Cardiac fibroma.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen. It usually arises within the ventricular myocardium or interventricular septum and can show prominent delayed enhancement on cardiac MRI because of its fibrous tissue content.

Cardiac hemangioma.description: A rare benign vascular tumor of the heart composed of capillary, cavernous, or mixed vascular channels. It may occur in the ventricular wall and can be asymptomatic when small.

Cardiac myofibroma.description: A benign mesenchymal tumor composed of spindle-shaped myofibroblasts, often with a biphasic pattern of fibrous tissue and branching vascular channels. Cardiac involvement is rare and is more often described in infants or children.

Cardiac angiofibroma.description: A rare benign fibrous tumor with a prominent vascular component, consisting of collagen-rich stroma containing small blood vessels. It can resemble a fibroma or hemangioma on imaging and pathology.

Splenic infarction.description: Ischemic necrosis of splenic tissue caused by impaired splenic arterial or venous blood flow. Imaging commonly shows peripheral wedge-shaped hypoechoic or nonenhancing splenic lesions; the provided ultrasound and MRI appearances are most compatible with infarction.

Splenic infarction associated with Mycop.normalized_text: Splenic infarction associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
Splenic infarction associated with Mycop.description: Mycoplasma pneumoniae respiratory infection can rarely cause extrapulmonary thrombosis or vasculitis, including splenic infarction. Respiratory symptoms accompanied by fever, inflammation, and imaging-confirmed splenic ischemic lesions support this possibility.

Splenic abscess.description: A splenic abscess is a focal bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infection of the spleen that can cause fever and left upper quadrant pain. It may appear as a hypoechoic splenic lesion on ultrasound, although the wedge-shaped, perfusion-deficient MRI pattern more strongly favors infarction than abscess.

Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histoly.normalized_text: Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica hepatic abscess)
Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histoly.description: An invasive intestinal amoebic infection that can spread through the portal circulation to cause a usually solitary liver abscess. It may occur months to years after travel to endemic regions and can cause diaphragmatic or pleuritic pain when the left hepatic lobe is involved.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection producing a pus-filled collection in the liver, commonly caused by enteric organisms such as Klebsiella species, Escherichia coli, streptococci, or anaerobes. It often presents with fever and high inflammatory markers; left-lobe abscesses may cause upper abdominal or diaphragmatic discomfort.

Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.normalized_text: Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection)
Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.description: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired from contaminated soil or water in endemic areas including parts of northern and western Australia and Southeast Asia. It can cause acute febrile illness, pneumonia, sepsis, and visceral abscesses involving the liver and spleen.

Septic portal vein thrombophlebitis (pyl.normalized_text: Septic portal vein thrombophlebitis (pylephlebitis) associated with a hepatic abscess
Septic portal vein thrombophlebitis (pyl.description: Pylephlebitis is infected thrombosis of the portal venous system, usually arising from an intra-abdominal infection such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, or liver abscess. The CT image may suggest a focal hepatic abscess with adjacent portal venous involvement.

OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.normalized_text: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome (DOA+)
OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by OPA1 variants, classically producing slowly progressive bilateral optic atrophy and sometimes additional neurologic features such as spastic paraplegia, ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, or parkinsonism.

SPG7-associated hereditary spastic parap.normalized_text: SPG7-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy
SPG7-associated hereditary spastic parap.description: A complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG7 variants. It commonly causes adult-onset progressive lower-limb spasticity and may include optic neuropathy/optic atrophy, ataxia, neuropathy, and bladder dysfunction.

Multiple sclerosis, progressive course.description: An immune-mediated central nervous system demyelinating disease that can cause progressive spastic paraparesis, bladder dysfunction, sensory symptoms, and optic neuritis/optic atrophy. Oligoclonal bands in CSF support intrathecal immune activity.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder affecting optic nerves and spinal cord, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies and causing severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis.

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degener.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of impaired copper excretion caused by ATP7B mutations, resulting in copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. The homozygous ATP7B c.2333G>T (p.Arg778Leu) pathogenic variant, Kayser-Fleischer corneal ring, and basal-ganglia MRI abnormalities strongly support this diagnosis.

Herb-induced liver injury (drug-induced.normalized_text: Herb-induced liver injury (drug-induced liver injury from Chinese herbal medicines)
Herb-induced liver injury (drug-induced.description: Liver injury caused by hepatotoxic medications or herbal products, which can present with hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed hepatitis and may cause jaundice and pruritus.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: A chronic immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that often affects girls and young women and can cause jaundice, progressive liver dysfunction, and, in advanced disease, coagulopathy.

Cholestatic hepatitis or biliary cholest.description: Reduced bile formation or bile flow, from intrahepatic liver disease or obstruction, causing retention of bilirubin and bile acids that commonly produces jaundice and itching.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome (.description: An idiosyncratic immune-mediated reaction to azathioprine, usually occurring within days to a few weeks of starting treatment, characterized by fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.normalized_text: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), potentially azathioprine-induced
Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory dermatosis causing abrupt fever, neutrophilia, painful erythematous papules, nodules, or plaques, often accompanied by arthralgia. It can be drug-induced, including after azathioprine exposure.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory panniculitis presenting with painful erythematous subcutaneous nodules, classically on the anterior lower legs, often associated with fever, malaise, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Drug-induced leukocytoclastic vasculitis.description: A small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis that may be triggered by medications and commonly causes palpable purpura or painful erythematous lesions on dependent areas, sometimes with fever and arthralgia.

Reactive arthritis.description: An inflammatory arthritis occurring after an infection, typically involving asymmetric lower-extremity joints and sometimes associated with fever, skin lesions, conjunctivitis, urethritis, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Hemorrhage into the retropharyngeal/prevertebral soft tissues after blunt neck trauma, which can expand and compress the pharynx and upper airway. The CT image shows marked prevertebral/retropharyngeal soft-tissue expansion consistent with hematoma.

Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.description: Injury to the larynx after anterior neck trauma may cause edema, mucosal bleeding, cartilage injury, and progressive airway narrowing.

Prevertebral soft-tissue hematoma from o.normalized_text: Prevertebral soft-tissue hematoma from occult cervical spine or ligamentous injury
Prevertebral soft-tissue hematoma from o.description: Trauma to the cervical spine or its supporting ligaments can produce bleeding and prevertebral swelling, sometimes without obvious tenderness or fracture on initial examination.

Traumatic pharyngeal injury with retroph.normalized_text: Traumatic pharyngeal injury with retropharyngeal edema
Traumatic pharyngeal injury with retroph.description: Blunt trauma can injure the pharyngeal wall and surrounding tissues, causing edema or hemorrhage in the retropharyngeal space and narrowing of the airway.

Insulinoma.description: A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin autonomously, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia (endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia).

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN.normalized_text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) with insulinoma
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN.description: An inherited endocrine tumor syndrome involving parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors; insulinoma may be the presenting pancreatic tumor.

Factitious or surreptitious sulfonylurea.description: Hypoglycemia caused by hidden ingestion of insulin secretagogue medications such as sulfonylureas, which stimulates endogenous insulin and C-peptide secretion.

Exogenous insulin-induced hypoglycemia.description: Hypoglycemia caused by administration of insulin from an external source, either accidental, intentional, or iatrogenic.

Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia.description: Hypoglycemia caused by tumors producing insulin-like growth factor 2 or consuming large amounts of glucose; it is usually associated with large mesenchymal, hepatic, or other non-pancreatic tumors.

Slipping rib syndrome (hypermobile 8th c.description: A mechanical pain syndrome caused by excessive mobility or subluxation of a false rib costal cartilage, usually involving ribs 8-10. Dynamic ultrasound may show abnormal movement/overlap of the involved rib cartilage relative to adjacent ribs.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overstretching or microscopic tearing of the intercostal muscles, commonly caused by strenuous trunk movement, repetitive exercise, coughing, or twisting.

Costochondral or interchondral joint str.description: Mechanical irritation or sprain at the junction between a rib and its cartilage, or between adjacent costal cartilages, often after repetitive loading of the chest wall.

Rib stress injury or occult stress fract.normalized_text: Rib stress injury or occult stress fracture
Rib stress injury or occult stress fract.description: A repetitive-load injury of a rib that can occur after abrupt increases in athletic activity; early stress injuries may be difficult to detect on plain radiographs.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent eosinophilia, dysplastic/immature eosinophil precursors, blasts or other abnormal myeloid cells, and cytogenetic abnormalities. It can cause pulmonary eosinophilic infiltration and respiratory symptoms.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase gene rearrangement
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms, often involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2 rearrangements, that produce marked eosinophilia and may infiltrate the lungs, heart, skin, gastrointestinal tract, or nervous system.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with pulmonary involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A syndrome of persistent eosinophilia associated with organ damage after secondary causes and defined clonal eosinophilic neoplasms have been excluded. Lung involvement may mimic asthma or eosinophilic pneumonia.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophilic lung disease characterized by subacute cough, dyspnea, wheezing, pulmonary infiltrates, and eosinophilic inflammation; it can be associated with adult-onset asthma but usually responds well to systemic corticosteroids.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma,.normalized_text: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-positive (ALCL)
Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma,.description: An aggressive CD30-positive T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly affects children and adolescents. It often causes prolonged fever, systemic inflammation, anemia, lymphadenopathy, and extranodal disease. The imaging suggests extensive abdominal nodal disease, and the histology shows large atypical cells with strong CD30-type membranous/Golgi staining, supporting ALCL.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by malignant Reed-Sternberg cells, frequently associated with fever, weight loss, inflammatory-marker elevation, anemia, and lymph-node enlargement. CD30 expression can overlap with ALCL, although the histologic and immunophenotypic pattern shown is more suggestive of ALCL.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-ce.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-ce.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma that may present with rapidly enlarging abdominal masses or lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, bowel involvement, gastrointestinal bleeding, and anemia. However, the CD30-positive anaplastic histologic appearance favors ALCL rather than diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Abdominal tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the peritoneum, bowel, or abdominal lymph nodes can cause prolonged fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and necrotic lymphadenopathy. Travel to an endemic region raises consideration, but the lymphoma-type histology and immunostaining argue against tuberculosis.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Severe mosquito-borne malaria caused by P. falciparum, often acquired in sub-Saharan Africa and capable of causing hemolysis, jaundice, kidney injury, and cerebral or visual symptoms. The rapid malaria test and blood smear show findings consistent with P. falciparum, including multiple delicate ring forms within erythrocytes and an appliqué form.

Severe falciparum malaria with blackwate.normalized_text: Severe falciparum malaria with blackwater fever
Severe falciparum malaria with blackwate.description: A severe hemolytic manifestation of P. falciparum malaria characterized by massive intravascular red-cell destruction, dark hemoglobin-containing urine, jaundice, and possible acute kidney injury.

Leptospirosis.description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, jaundice, dark urine, and acute kidney injury.

Dengue fever.description: A mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause abrupt fever, severe headache, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, and occasionally hepatitis or kidney injury. It is an important alternative diagnosis in febrile returning travelers.

Esophageal perforation caused by erosion.normalized_text: Esophageal perforation caused by erosion of cervical spine hardware
Esophageal perforation caused by erosion.description: A delayed complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which a plate or screw erodes into the pharynx or esophagus, producing a perforation and allowing contamination of deep neck and mediastinal spaces.

Descending necrotizing mediastinitis.description: A severe infection of the mediastinum caused by spread of infection from the neck, pharynx, or esophagus; it may produce purulent mediastinal collections and systemic illness.

Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.normalized_text: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with extensive paraspinal abscess
Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.description: Infection involving prior cervical fixation hardware and adjacent soft tissues, causing a deep paraspinal abscess that can spread longitudinally through fascial planes into the thorax.

Retropharyngeal/deep neck space abscess.normalized_text: Retropharyngeal/deep neck space abscess with extension to the mediastinum
Retropharyngeal/deep neck space abscess.description: A purulent infection in the retropharyngeal or prevertebral deep neck spaces that may descend into the mediastinum and cause life-threatening mediastinal sepsis.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous transmur.description: A full-thickness rupture of the esophagus, usually in the distal thoracic esophagus, caused by a sudden rise in intrathoracic pressure during forceful vomiting. It can cause mediastinal air, pleural contamination, pleural effusions, and rapidly progressive mediastinitis.

Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophag.normalized_text: Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophageal perforation
Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophag.description: Inflammation and infection of the mediastinum caused by leakage of esophageal contents after perforation. Early cases may initially have normal laboratory values before fever and leukocytosis develop.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum after vomi.description: Air in the mediastinum caused by alveolar rupture or, less commonly, esophageal injury after increased intrathoracic pressure from vomiting or Valsalva. It may produce chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema.

Aspiration pneumonitis or aspiration pne.normalized_text: Aspiration pneumonitis or aspiration pneumonia following emesis
Aspiration pneumonitis or aspiration pne.description: Chemical lung injury or infection caused by inhalation of gastric contents during vomiting. It commonly affects dependent lower-lobe lung regions and may cause hypoxemia, cough, fever, and infiltrates.

Functional seizures (psychogenic nonepil.description: Functional seizures are paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are not caused by abnormal epileptic cortical discharges. They are commonly associated with trauma-related, mood, anxiety, and dissociative disorders. The EEG image is most consistent with prominent movement/electrode artifact during an event without a convincing evolving ictal epileptiform pattern.

Generalized tonic-clonic epileptic seizu.description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures involve sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening followed by bilateral rhythmic clonic jerking, and often a postictal period. They may cause falls, injuries, urinary incontinence, lactate elevation, and creatine kinase elevation.

Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.normalized_text: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, possibly occipital onset
Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.description: Focal seizures arise from one cerebral region and may spread to produce bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions. Occipital seizures can include visual symptoms, and focal autonomic symptoms can include nausea and palpitations before convulsive activity.

Convulsive syncope.description: Convulsive syncope is transient loss of consciousness from reduced cerebral perfusion, often due to vasovagal or cardiac causes, with brief stiffening or myoclonic jerks that can mimic a seizure. Palpitations may suggest a cardiac trigger.

Right obturator hernia with incarcerated.normalized_text: Right obturator hernia with incarcerated small bowel causing small-bowel obstruction
Right obturator hernia with incarcerated.description: A pelvic hernia in which small bowel protrudes through the obturator canal. It classically occurs in thin, elderly multiparous women and may compress the obturator nerve, producing medial thigh or knee pain (Howship-Romberg sign). The CT images show a bowel-containing hernia in the right obturator region.

Strangulated or incarcerated right obtur.normalized_text: Strangulated or incarcerated right obturator hernia
Strangulated or incarcerated right obtur.description: An obturator hernia may trap bowel tightly within the obturator canal, causing incarceration and potentially bowel ischemia or strangulation. It commonly presents as an acute mechanical small-bowel obstruction in frail elderly women.

Femoral hernia causing small-bowel obstr.description: A femoral hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. It is more common in older women and can incarcerate bowel, although the imaging location and knee pain more strongly favor an obturator hernia.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune endotheliopathy causing microvascular occlusion in the brain, retina, and cochlea; classically presents with encephalopathy/headache, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss. MRI commonly shows characteristic corpus callosum lesions.

Multiple sclerosis.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that commonly affects young women and can cause episodic visual, sensory, and other neurologic deficits with white-matter lesions on MRI.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder that can produce arterial or venous thrombosis, including retinal vascular occlusion and cerebral ischemic lesions.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with retina.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with retinal vasculopathy
Systemic lupus erythematosus with retina.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that may cause retinal vascular occlusion, central nervous system involvement, headache, and neurologic deficits, often with systemic inflammatory or connective-tissue manifestations.

Cogan syndrome.description: A rare inflammatory disorder characterized mainly by interstitial keratitis and audiovestibular dysfunction, including sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo; systemic vasculitis can occur.

Mitochondrial myopathy due to an mtDNA m.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy due to an mtDNA mutation (likely MELAS-spectrum or m.3243A>G-related disease)
Mitochondrial myopathy due to an mtDNA m.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder causing impaired oxidative phosphorylation. It can produce proximal and axial myopathy, ragged-red/oxidative-enzyme-abnormal muscle fibers, hearing loss, cardiac conduction abnormalities, cognitive changes, and variable cerebellar involvement.

Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.normalized_text: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF syndrome)
Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.description: A mitochondrial disease, most often associated with an MT-TK mutation, characterized by myoclonus, generalized epilepsy, ataxia, myopathy, hearing impairment, and ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy. Clinical severity can vary considerably within maternal families.

Mitochondrial spinocerebellar ataxia wit.normalized_text: Mitochondrial spinocerebellar ataxia with myopathy (POLG-related or other nuclear mitochondrial disease)
Mitochondrial spinocerebellar ataxia wit.description: Nuclear-gene mitochondrial disorders can cause cerebellar ataxia, external ophthalmoplegia, neuropathy, seizures, myopathy, and mitochondrial abnormalities on muscle biopsy. POLG-related disease may present in adulthood but is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive or dominant nuclear pattern rather than a maternal mtDNA pattern.

Myofibrillar myopathy presenting as bent.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy presenting as bent-spine syndrome
Myofibrillar myopathy presenting as bent.description: Myofibrillar myopathies are inherited muscle diseases that can preferentially affect paraspinal, neck-flexor, and proximal muscles, causing camptocormia or bent-spine syndrome. Some forms are associated with cardiomyopathy or arrhythmias and modest CK elevation.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: A lysosomal glycogen-storage myopathy caused by acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Adult-onset disease produces slowly progressive limb-girdle and axial weakness, including paraspinal involvement, often with respiratory muscle weakness and sometimes elevated CK.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia (mature B-cell.normalized_text: Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia (mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with MYC rearrangement)
Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia (mature B-cell.description: An aggressive mature germinal-center B-cell lymphoma of childhood, commonly associated with MYC rearrangement, often involving lymph nodes, extranodal soft tissue, bone marrow, and peripheral blood. The images show highly proliferative atypical lymphoid cells with basophilic/vacuolated cytoplasm and cytogenetic/FISH findings compatible with a MYC-associated rearrangement.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rearrangement
High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.description: A category of aggressive mature B-cell lymphomas with MYC rearrangement that can resemble Burkitt lymphoma morphologically and immunophenotypically but may have more complex cytogenetic abnormalities or atypical clinical/pathologic features.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-center B-cell type
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma composed of large transformed B cells. It can present as nodal or extranodal soft-tissue disease and may express CD20 and CD10, although classic pediatric Burkitt lymphoma is more strongly favored here.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors that commonly affects children and may involve bone marrow, blood, lymph nodes, and bone. It is an important differential diagnosis for pediatric lymphoid malignancy but is poorly supported by the mature B-cell phenotype in this case.

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni with periportal fibrosis (Symmers fibrosis)
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.description: Chronic intestinal schistosomiasis can cause egg deposition in portal tracts, producing characteristic periportal fibrosis, hepatosplenomegaly, and portal hypertension. Ultrasound and CT commonly show echogenic/thickened periportal tracts and a heterogeneous liver with periportal bands.

Portal hypertension secondary to schisto.normalized_text: Portal hypertension secondary to schistosomal periportal fibrosis
Portal hypertension secondary to schisto.description: Periportal fibrosis from chronic S. mansoni infection may obstruct portal venous flow while preserving hepatocellular function, causing portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and potentially varices or ascites.

Intestinal schistosomiasis due to Schist.normalized_text: Intestinal schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
Intestinal schistosomiasis due to Schist.description: S. mansoni infection involves the mesenteric venous circulation; eggs lodged in the intestinal wall cause chronic inflammatory colitis, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and may progress to hepatosplenic disease.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (anterior STEMI)
Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute myocardial infarction due to coronary arterial occlusion, with ECG evidence of marked ST-segment elevation in the anterior precordial leads (especially V3-V5/V6).

Polycythemia vera.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by increased red blood cell mass and often associated leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, commonly causing aquagenic pruritus and arterial or venous thrombosis.

Essential thrombocythemia.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm with persistent excessive platelet production that can cause microvascular symptoms and major arterial thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis and myocardial infarction.

Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary thrombosis associated with a myeloproliferative neoplasm
Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.description: Acute coronary ischemia caused by thrombotic coronary occlusion in the setting of a hypercoagulable myeloproliferative disorder, most likely polycythemia vera in this case.

Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic her.normalized_text: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic liver herniation
Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic her.description: A congenital defect in the diaphragm allowing abdominal organs, particularly the liver, to enter the thorax, causing lung compression, pulmonary hypoplasia, and severe respiratory failure at birth.

Congenital diaphragmatic eventration.description: Abnormal elevation and thinning or paralysis of the diaphragm that permits cephalad displacement of abdominal contents without a true diaphragmatic defect, potentially causing neonatal respiratory distress.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), possibly with air trapping
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A developmental cystic malformation of the lung that may appear as a hyperlucent, cystic, or mass-like lesion and can cause respiratory distress through compression of normal lung tissue.

Bronchopulmonary sequestration.description: Nonfunctioning congenital lung tissue, usually in a lower lobe, that receives anomalous systemic arterial blood supply from the aorta and may be associated with other thoracoabdominal malformations.

Neonatal pneumothorax, including tension.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse; in a ventilated or resuscitated neonate it can rapidly worsen respiratory and cardiovascular status.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, aHUS)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: A complement-dysregulation disorder causing endothelial injury, arteriolar and glomerular thrombosis, hemolysis, severe hypertension, and acute kidney injury. The biopsy images show thrombotic microangiopathy with concentric intimal thickening ('onion-skin' arteriolopathy).

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe hypertension can cause endothelial damage, fibrinoid vascular injury, microangiopathic hemolysis, and rapidly progressive kidney failure. Renal pathology commonly shows marked arteriolar intimal thickening with onion-skin lesions, as seen in the images.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.normalized_text: Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangiopathy and malignant hypertension
Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: Cocaine can cause intense vasoconstriction, severe hypertension, endothelial injury, platelet activation, and thrombotic microangiopathy, resulting in acute kidney injury and hemolysis.

Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.normalized_text: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, often with low complement levels, proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive renal impairment.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system, usually associated with aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibodies. Involvement of the dorsal medulla/area postrema can cause otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, and hiccups. The sagittal MRI images are consistent with a lesion in the dorsal medulla near the area postrema.

Area postrema syndrome due to NMOSD.normalized_text: Area postrema syndrome due to NMOSD
Area postrema syndrome due to NMOSD.description: Area postrema syndrome is a core clinical manifestation of NMOSD caused by inflammatory lesions in the area postrema of the dorsal medulla. It presents with otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, and/or hiccups and may precede other neurological deficits.

Brainstem encephalitis/demyelinating les.normalized_text: Brainstem encephalitis/demyelinating lesion involving the medulla
Brainstem encephalitis/demyelinating les.description: Inflammation or demyelination of the brainstem can produce vomiting, nystagmus, bulbar dysfunction, long-tract signs, weakness, and respiratory compromise. In this case, the AQP4-IgG-positive status and area postrema lesion make NMOSD the most likely specific cause.

Lactobacillus infective endocarditis of.normalized_text: Lactobacillus infective endocarditis of the aortic valve
Lactobacillus infective endocarditis of.description: Subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Lactobacillus species, an uncommon opportunistic Gram-positive bacillus. Lactobacilli may show intrinsic high-level vancomycin resistance and poor susceptibility to cephalosporins; infection can cause destructive native-valve disease and severe aortic regurgitation.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infective e.description: A rare Gram-positive bacillary infection that can cause severe, often subacute native-valve endocarditis, frequently involving the aortic valve. The organism is characteristically resistant to vancomycin and generally susceptible to penicillin-class agents.

Enterococcus faecalis native aortic-valv.normalized_text: Enterococcus faecalis native aortic-valve infective endocarditis
Enterococcus faecalis native aortic-valv.description: A common cause of subacute infective endocarditis, particularly in patients with underlying cardiac disease. It can involve the aortic valve and produce progressive valvular destruction and aortic regurgitation.

Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.normalized_text: Venous air embolism with paradoxical systemic embolization through a patent foramen ovale
Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.description: Entry of air into the venous circulation during venesection, with passage from the right to left atrium through a patent foramen ovale, allowing air emboli to reach the coronary and cerebral arterial circulations.

Acute pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by embolic material. The CT pulmonary angiographic image shows an intraluminal filling defect in a left pulmonary arterial branch, compatible with pulmonary embolism; in this clinical context, embolic air may have contributed.

Paradoxical embolic transient ischemic a.normalized_text: Paradoxical embolic transient ischemic attack or acute ischemic stroke
Paradoxical embolic transient ischemic a.description: A transient cerebral arterial occlusion caused by embolic material crossing a right-to-left intracardiac shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale. Air emboli or thromboemboli can produce this mechanism.

Acute coronary syndrome due to paradoxic.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to paradoxical coronary air embolism
Acute coronary syndrome due to paradoxic.description: Acute myocardial ischemia caused by embolic obstruction of a coronary artery, potentially from air entering the venous system and crossing a patent foramen ovale into the systemic arterial circulation.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO.normalized_text: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO grade 2, BRAF V600E-mutant
Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO.description: A rare, usually superficial cerebral astrocytic tumor that often arises in the temporal lobe of younger patients and commonly presents with longstanding seizures. BRAF V600E mutation is frequent. The MRI appearance may include a cortical or superficial temporal lesion with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and variable enhancement.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.normalized_text: Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (anaplastic PXA, WHO grade 3)
Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: A higher-grade or transformed form of PXA characterized by increased mitotic activity and more aggressive behavior. It may develop after an initially grade 2 PXA and can show enlarging or newly enhancing tumor on follow-up MRI. BRAF V600E mutations are also common.

Ganglioglioma.description: A typically low-grade mixed neuronal-glial tumor that often occurs in the temporal lobe and causes chronic focal seizures. Some gangliogliomas harbor BRAF V600E mutations and may have cystic, solid, or variably enhancing MRI appearances.

Epithelioid glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype.description: A rare aggressive glioblastoma subtype that can occur in younger patients, often involves the temporal lobe, and may carry a BRAF V600E mutation. Imaging commonly shows an enhancing lesion with surrounding FLAIR abnormality and mass effect.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal muscle weakness due to muscle inflammation.

Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis.description: A dermatomyositis subtype often associated with painful ulcerative or violaceous skin lesions, periungual changes, arthritis, and a high risk of rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease; muscle disease can range from absent to severe.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome associated with myositis, interstitial lung disease, inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and mechanic's hands; it may overlap with dermatomyositis.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy, sometimes associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies, that causes rapidly progressive symmetric proximal weakness and markedly elevated muscle enzymes but usually has little or no rash.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, without the characteristic skin manifestations of dermatomyositis.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia.description: Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through accelerated vitamin D metabolism leading to vitamin D deficiency, impaired mineralization of osteoid, bone pain, muscle weakness, and insufficiency fractures.

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia.description: A disorder of defective bone mineralization caused by inadequate vitamin D availability, resulting in hypocalcemia or hypophosphatemia, diffuse bone pain, proximal myopathy, and Looser's zones.

Anticonvulsant-associated metabolic bone.description: Bone loss and impaired mineralization associated with enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications such as phenytoin; the spectrum includes vitamin D deficiency, osteomalacia, osteoporosis, and fragility fractures.

Osteoporosis with insufficiency fracture.description: Reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration causing fragility or insufficiency fractures, which can produce focal or multifocal pain and increased uptake on bone scans.

Group A streptococcal native mitral-valv.normalized_text: Group A streptococcal native mitral-valve infective endocarditis
Group A streptococcal native mitral-valv.description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, here most consistent with a large vegetation on the mitral valve caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. The echocardiographic image shows a valvular mass compatible with vegetation.

Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embo.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embolism
Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embo.description: An acute cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected material from a left-sided cardiac valve vegetation. The brain MRI image shows an acute infarct in the left cerebral hemisphere, consistent with the patient's focal neurologic deficits.

Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to.normalized_text: Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to infective endocarditis
Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to.description: Mitral-valve infection can damage leaflets or chordae and produce severe mitral regurgitation. The apical pansystolic murmur, displaced apex beat, elevated NT-pro-BNP, respiratory distress, and color Doppler regurgitant jet support significant mitral regurgitation.

Acute decompensated heart failure due to.normalized_text: Acute decompensated heart failure due to infective mitral-valve disease
Acute decompensated heart failure due to.description: Acute severe mitral regurgitation from endocarditis can elevate cardiac filling pressures and cause congestive heart failure. The elevated NT-pro-BNP, dyspnea/respiratory distress, tachycardia, and displaced apex beat are compatible with this complication.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A rare autosomal-recessive ciliopathy characterized by cranial shape abnormalities, distinctive facial appearance, ectodermal abnormalities of hair, teeth and nails, skeletal dysplasia with a narrow thorax and short limbs, and progressive renal disease, often resembling nephronophthisis or tubulointerstitial nephropathy.

Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by SMARCAL1 variants, characterized by steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome or progressive renal failure, disproportionate short stature from skeletal dysplasia, facial differences and variable immune deficiency with recurrent infections.

Lowe syndrome (oculocerebrorenal syndrom.description: An X-linked disorder caused by OCRL variants that produces proximal renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome), ocular abnormalities and neurodevelopmental impairment; affected boys may develop chronic kidney disease.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: A ciliopathy characterized by nephronophthisis-related kidney disease, skeletal dysplasia with cone-shaped epiphyses and shortened phalanges, and retinal dystrophy; some individuals have cerebellar or hepatic involvement.

Pierson syndrome.description: A severe congenital nephrotic syndrome due to LAMB2 variants, classically associated with diffuse mesangial sclerosis, early renal failure and characteristic ocular abnormalities such as microcoria; neurologic involvement may occur.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle inflammation and distinctive cutaneous lesions, including Gottron papules over the finger joints. It can cause severe creatine kinase elevation and dysphagia.

Cancer-associated (paraneoplastic) derma.description: Dermatomyositis may occur as a paraneoplastic autoimmune syndrome, particularly in older adults. The classic skin findings and inflammatory myopathy can precede or accompany detection of an internal malignancy.

Esophageal carcinoma, potentially associ.normalized_text: Esophageal carcinoma, potentially associated with paraneoplastic dermatomyositis
Esophageal carcinoma, potentially associ.description: Esophageal cancer is a malignant tumor of the esophagus that commonly presents with progressive dysphagia. In this context, an abnormal endoscopy and focal PET uptake raise suspicion for an esophageal malignancy, which could be associated with paraneoplastic dermatomyositis.

Legg-Calve-Perthes disease.description: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, causing sclerosis, fragmentation, flattening, and possible deformity of the femoral head. The radiographs show changes consistent with femoral-head collapse/fragmentation on the symptomatic side.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).description: Displacement of the femoral-head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually occurring in older children or adolescents and often associated with obesity.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, commonly following a viral illness, that causes acute hip pain and a limp in children.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: A bacterial infection within the hip joint that usually causes acute severe pain, inability to bear weight, fever, systemic illness, and rapidly progressive joint damage if untreated.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial collection of pus within the liver, sometimes containing gas-producing organisms. The imaging shows a large gas-containing fluid collection in the right hepatic lobe, explaining the apparent subdiaphragmatic free air on chest radiography.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: A liver abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica, typically producing fever and right upper quadrant pain and most often involving the right lobe of the liver.

Perforated peptic ulcer with pneumoperit.description: Perforation of a gastric or duodenal ulcer releases air and gastrointestinal contents into the peritoneal cavity, causing acute peritonitis and free subdiaphragmatic air.

Acute cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, usually due to biliary obstruction, causing fever, abdominal pain, and systemic inflammation; it can occasionally lead to hepatic abscess formation.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and variable congenital heart and brain abnormalities.

Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.description: A chromosomal deletion syndrome caused by loss of material from chromosome 4p. It causes growth and developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia, congenital heart defects, seizures, and characteristic craniofacial features.

22q11.2 deletion syndrome.description: A genetic microdeletion disorder with variable developmental delay, hypotonia, congenital heart defects, palatal abnormalities, immune dysfunction, and characteristic facial features.

Rett syndrome.description: An X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder, usually caused by pathogenic MECP2 variants, characterized by apparently normal early development followed by developmental regression, loss of purposeful hand use, stereotypic hand movements, impaired gait, and acquired microcephaly.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragon.normalized_text: Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragonadal yolk sac tumor)
Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragon.description: A rare malignant germ-cell tumor arising outside the gonads, capable of producing very high alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). In this case, the jejunal full-thickness mass, markedly elevated AFP, metastatic abdominal lymphadenopathy, peritoneal fluid, PET-avid lesion, and histology with glandular/reticular tumor architecture support this diagnosis.

Primary intestinal hepatoid adenocarcino.description: A rare AFP-producing adenocarcinoma with morphologic and immunohistochemical features resembling hepatocellular differentiation. It can arise in the gastrointestinal tract and metastasize to lymph nodes, but it is exceptionally uncommon in children and in the jejunum.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can produce a circumferential or full-thickness bowel mass and spread to regional or retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Conventional small-bowel adenocarcinoma generally does not cause substantial AFP elevation.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small bowel
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small.description: Pediatric non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve the bowel wall and produce abdominal pain, bowel masses, ascites, and extensive abdominal lymphadenopathy. However, lymphoma would not usually produce markedly elevated AFP or a glandular epithelial histology.

Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.normalized_text: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting ectopic gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ulceration and significant lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The radionuclide images show a right-sided abdominal focus with uptake timing similar to the stomach, supporting ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel diverticulum.

Intussusception.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, most often ileocolic in infants. It causes episodic severe colicky abdominal pain, vomiting or lethargy, and may produce bloody mucus stools due to bowel ischemia.

Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead poi.normalized_text: Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead point for intussusception
Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead poi.description: A Meckel diverticulum can serve as a pathologic lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception. This can combine features of Meckel-related bleeding with episodic obstructive abdominal pain.

Acute lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage.normalized_text: Acute lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage from an intestinal duplication containing ectopic gastric mucosa
Acute lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage.description: An enteric duplication cyst or tubular duplication can contain ectopic gastric mucosa, producing ulceration, abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal bleeding; it can occasionally be positive on technetium-pertechnetate scintigraphy.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.description: A rare proliferative disorder of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells that occurs predominantly in older nonsmoking women and commonly causes constrictive bronchiolitis. CT typically shows multiple small pulmonary nodules with mosaic attenuation and air trapping.

Constrictive bronchiolitis associated wi.description: Fibrotic narrowing and obliteration of small bronchioles, often caused by DIPNECH in older nonsmoking women. It produces fixed airflow obstruction and mosaic attenuation from regional air trapping.

Pulmonary carcinoid tumor(s) arising in.normalized_text: Pulmonary carcinoid tumor(s) arising in the setting of DIPNECH
Pulmonary carcinoid tumor(s) arising in.description: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors. DIPNECH can progress from neuroendocrine-cell hyperplasia and tumorlets to one or more carcinoid tumors, which may appear as larger rounded pulmonary nodules.

Asthma or non-smoking-related chronic ob.normalized_text: Asthma or non-smoking-related chronic obstructive airway disease
Asthma or non-smoking-related chronic ob.description: Chronic inflammatory airway disease can cause airflow limitation, wheeze, dyspnea, and air trapping. In this case, the imaging pattern and patient demographic make this less likely as the primary diagnosis.

Multiple pulmonary metastases.description: Hematogenous spread of malignancy to the lungs may produce multiple rounded pulmonary nodules. However, metastatic disease alone would not usually explain marked obstructive small-airway physiology and mosaic air trapping.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with possible coe.normalized_text: Pulmonary tuberculosis with possible coexisting unicentric hyaline-vascular Castleman disease
Pulmonary tuberculosis with possible coe.description: Pulmonary tuberculosis commonly causes upper-lobe cavitary infiltrates, hemoptysis, fever, and granulomatous inflammation. The longstanding supraclavicular node and its image appearance with regressed follicles and concentric mantle zones are compatible with a separate unicentric hyaline-vascular Castleman disease.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary d.description: Nontuberculous mycobacteria can produce chronic upper-lobe cavitary disease, bronchiectatic change, cough, hemoptysis, fever, and granulomatous lung inflammation; repeated mycobacterial cultures are usually needed for confirmation.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often involving the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes. Cavitary lung disease and substantial hemoptysis are uncommon but can occur in advanced or atypical pulmonary disease.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can cause pulmonary nodules or cavities, cough, hemoptysis, systemic inflammation, and granulomatous inflammation on tissue biopsy.

Unicentric hyaline-vascular Castleman di.description: Unicentric Castleman disease is a localized benign lymphoproliferative disorder, usually presenting as a single enlarged lymph node. Hyaline-vascular histology typically shows small regressed germinal centers with concentric mantle-zone lymphocytes and prominent vascular proliferation.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.normalized_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus, typically occurring in immunosuppressed individuals. Natalizumab exposure, high anti-JCPyV antibody index, subsequent fingolimod treatment, and profound leukopenia substantially increase risk.

Multiple sclerosis relapse.description: An acute or subacute episode of new inflammatory demyelination in a person with multiple sclerosis, causing new focal neurological deficits lasting more than 24 hours in the absence of infection or another explanation.

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndr.description: An inflammatory worsening of pre-existing or recently developing JC-virus PML that can occur after withdrawal of natalizumab or changes in immunomodulatory therapy, as immune surveillance returns and produces inflammation around infected brain tissue.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, usually affecting posterior cerebral regions, that commonly presents with seizures, visual disturbances, headache, and altered mental status. It is often associated with severe hypertension, renal disease, cytotoxic drugs, or immune-modulating treatments.

Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.normalized_text: Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)
Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants resulting in deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity and accumulation of globotriaosylceramide. It causes neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, corneal verticillata, kidney disease, and cardiomyopathy. The ECG/echocardiographic findings are compatible with Fabry cardiac involvement, and the electron microscopy appearance is consistent with lamellar lysosomal inclusions (zebra bodies).

Fabry cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiac involvement from Fabry disease, characterized by glycosphingolipid accumulation in cardiomyocytes that commonly produces concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities, chest pain, arrhythmias, and later myocardial fibrosis or heart failure.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A myocardial disease characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, often due to sarcomeric gene variants, which can cause chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, and ECG evidence of hypertrophy. Fabry disease is an important metabolic mimic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Anderson-Fabry nephropathy.description: Renal involvement of Fabry disease caused by glycolipid accumulation in podocytes, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and vascular cells. It commonly presents initially with proteinuria and may progress to chronic kidney disease.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma (post-tra.description: A traumatic liver hematoma can become secondarily infected during ICU admission, forming an abscess-like collection. Ultrasound may show a complex hypoechoic intrahepatic collection with internal debris.

Post-traumatic biloma.description: A biloma is an encapsulated collection of bile caused by disruption of intrahepatic bile ducts, often after liver trauma. It may become infected and cause fever and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a localized bacterial infection within the liver, producing a fluid-containing lesion and systemic inflammatory signs. In this setting, it may arise from infection of a traumatic hepatic collection.

Bullous iododerma (iodine-induced neutro.description: A rare severe cutaneous hypersensitivity/toxic reaction to iodinated compounds, including radiographic contrast, characterized by pustules, vesicles, bullae, and sometimes vegetating plaques with neutrophilic inflammation.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.normalized_text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) induced by iodinated contrast
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: An acute drug-induced pustular eruption, commonly caused by medications and occasionally iodinated contrast media, with numerous sterile nonfollicular pustules and neutrophilia.

Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.normalized_text: Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption caused by iodinated contrast
Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.description: A severe drug eruption in which well-demarcated erythematous or dusky plaques blister after medication exposure; generalized bullous forms can mimic epidermal necrolysis and may occur after contrast agents.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-.normalized_text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-like drug reaction
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-.description: A life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction marked by widespread keratinocyte death, epidermal detachment, bullae, and frequent mucosal involvement.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.description: A rapidly progressive bloodstream infection caused by a dog-associated, fastidious gram-negative fusiform bacillus. It is particularly severe in people with heavy alcohol use, impaired splenic function, or other immune compromise and can cause septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpuric skin necrosis, and multiorgan failure.

Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associat.normalized_text: Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation
Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associat.description: A life-threatening thrombotic and bleeding disorder, usually triggered by severe sepsis, in which widespread microvascular clotting causes rapidly progressive purpura, ecchymoses, skin necrosis, shock, and possible limb ischemia.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection of the.normalized_text: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection of the forearm from dog-bite wound
Necrotizing soft-tissue infection of the.description: A rapidly progressive bacterial infection involving deep skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, or muscle. It can follow animal bites and may produce severe pain, necrosis, violaceous discoloration, systemic toxicity, and septic shock.

Pasteurella multocida infection after do.normalized_text: Pasteurella multocida infection after dog bite
Pasteurella multocida infection after do.description: A gram-negative coccobacillary infection commonly transmitted through dog or cat bites. It typically causes rapidly developing cellulitis at the bite site and can occasionally cause bacteremia or severe sepsis in medically vulnerable patients.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic.normalized_text: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS syndrome) due to MT-TL1 m.3303C>T mutation
Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by impaired oxidative phosphorylation, characterized by myopathy, lactic acidosis, neurologic deficits, and recurrent stroke-like episodes at a young age. MT-TL1 mutations affecting mitochondrial tRNA leucine are a well-established cause.

Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke due.normalized_text: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke due to left ventricular thrombus
Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke due.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolization of a thrombus from the heart into a cerebral artery. The brain diffusion MRI demonstrates an acute right hemispheric infarct, while MR angiography suggests major intracranial arterial obstruction and echocardiographic images appear to show a left ventricular intracavitary thrombus.

Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy with left v.normalized_text: Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy with left ventricular thrombus formation
Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy with left v.description: Cardiac involvement in mitochondrial disease can include cardiomyopathy, impaired ventricular contractility, arrhythmia, and intracardiac thrombus formation. A ventricular thrombus can lead to systemic embolism and ischemic stroke.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreas. A tumor in the pancreatic head can obstruct the distal common bile duct, causing painless or minimally painful obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, gallbladder distention, and elevated CA 19-9. The imaging and pathology are consistent with an infiltrative pancreatic-region adenocarcinoma with biliary obstruction.

Distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: Cholangiocarcinoma is an adenocarcinoma arising from biliary duct epithelium. Distal common-bile-duct tumors produce obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, anorexia, and biliary dilatation; CA 19-9 may be elevated.

Ampullary adenocarcinoma.description: Ampullary carcinoma arises at the ampulla of Vater, where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct drain into the duodenum. It can cause early biliary obstruction, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and elevated CA 19-9, often with less extensive symptoms than pancreatic cancer.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causing.normalized_text: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causing biliary obstruction
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causing.description: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is a neoplasm arising from endocrine cells of the pancreas. A nonfunctioning tumor in the pancreatic head may compress the bile duct and cause jaundice, although its pathology is usually neuroendocrine rather than conventional ductal adenocarcinoma.

Gallstone ileus with rectal gallstone im.normalized_text: Gallstone ileus with rectal gallstone impaction
Gallstone ileus with rectal gallstone im.description: Mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by a gallstone that has entered the bowel, usually through a biliary-enteric fistula, and has become impacted distally in the rectum.

Cholecystoenteric fistula, most likely c.normalized_text: Cholecystoenteric fistula, most likely cholecystoduodenal fistula
Cholecystoenteric fistula, most likely c.description: An abnormal communication between the gallbladder and bowel that permits a gallstone to migrate directly into the gastrointestinal tract. The abdominal images are consistent with a biliary-enteric fistulous route near the gallbladder and adjacent duodenum.

Crohn's disease with possible intestinal.normalized_text: Crohn's disease with possible intestinal stricture or anorectal involvement
Crohn's disease with possible intestinal.description: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause bowel-wall inflammation, strictures, fissures, and anorectal symptoms. It may contribute to impaired intestinal passage and increase the likelihood of a migrating stone becoming impacted.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella to the lateral side of the knee, commonly occurring in adolescents with ligamentous laxity and often associated with injury to the medial patellofemoral ligament.

Osteochondral fracture following patella.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, typically from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after a lateral patellar dislocation. A fragment may detach and become an intra-articular loose body.

Intra-articular osteochondral loose body.normalized_text: Intra-articular osteochondral loose body of the knee
Intra-articular osteochondral loose body.description: A free fragment of cartilage and bone within the knee joint, often produced by an osteochondral injury after patellar dislocation. It can cause episodic locking, swelling, and pain.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by the triad of cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring alopecia of axillary/pubic hair, and widespread follicular keratotic or spiny papules (lichen spinulosus-like eruption).

Lichen planopilaris.description: A primary lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia in which inflammation targets the upper hair follicle, causing permanent hair loss; it can be associated with perifollicular scale, itching, and follicular keratotic papules.

Lichen spinulosus.description: A follicular keratotic disorder producing groups of tiny rough, spine-tipped papules, often on the trunk and extremities; it may resemble keratosis pilaris but has more prominent follicular spines.

Follicular lichen planus.description: A lichen planus variant with follicular hyperkeratotic papules and perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation; when the scalp is involved, it may overlap clinically and histologically with lichen planopilaris.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.normalized_text: Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), pregnancy-associated
Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period. It produces microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, severe kidney injury, hypertension, and may cause thrombotic skin lesions.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can damage small arteries and arterioles, causing endothelial injury, platelet consumption, mechanical hemolysis, renal failure, and ischemic skin injury.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy usually caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with variable neurologic, renal, fever, and skin manifestations.

Pregnancy-related HELLP syndrome or pers.normalized_text: Pregnancy-related HELLP syndrome or persistent preeclampsia-associated thrombotic microangiopathy
Pregnancy-related HELLP syndrome or pers.description: Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome are pregnancy-related endothelial disorders causing hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and sometimes kidney injury. They usually improve after delivery.

Antiphospholipid syndrome with thromboti.normalized_text: Antiphospholipid syndrome with thrombotic vasculopathy (including catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome)
Antiphospholipid syndrome with thromboti.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable condition that can cause pregnancy morbidity, hypertension-related placental disease, renal thrombotic microangiopathy, thrombocytopenia, and ischemic skin ulcers.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Small-intestinal gastrointestinal stroma.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract derived from interstitial cells of Cajal. Ileal GISTs commonly express KIT (CD117) and may harbor activating KIT exon 11 mutations, as in this case.

Small-bowel leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise from the intestinal wall and present as a bleeding small-bowel mass. It is generally positive for smooth-muscle markers such as desmin and SMA rather than KIT-driven.

Small-bowel neuroendocrine tumor (ileal.description: A neuroendocrine neoplasm frequently arising in the distal ileum. These tumors may cause obstruction, mesenteric fibrosis, or metastatic disease and can occasionally bleed.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.description: An epithelial malignancy of the small intestine that can produce anemia, bleeding, abdominal pain, obstruction, or weight loss. It usually has gland-forming histology rather than a KIT-mutant mesenchymal phenotype.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A rare malignant exocrine pancreatic tumor, usually occurring in older adults, often presenting as a large, well-circumscribed pancreatic mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Histology typically shows acinar or solid growth of relatively uniform cells with granular cytoplasm.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A pancreatic neoplasm arising from neuroendocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors can become large before causing symptoms and may produce abdominal fullness, digestive symptoms, or a palpable mass.

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor that is typically large, encapsulated, and contains mixed solid, hemorrhagic, and cystic areas. It most often occurs in young women but can rarely occur in older men.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from pancreatic ductal epithelium. It commonly causes obstructive, digestive, and constitutional symptoms and is often associated with diabetes in older patients.

Hailey-Hailey disease (benign familial p.description: An autosomal-dominant acantholytic blistering disorder caused by ATP2C1 mutations, producing recurrent painful erosions, fissures, crusting, and maceration in flexural areas. It commonly worsens with heat, sweating, and friction. Histology typically shows widespread suprabasal acantholysis with a "dilapidated brick wall" appearance.

Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).description: An inherited acantholytic keratinization disorder caused by ATP2A2 mutations. It causes persistent greasy, crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas and may worsen with heat and sweating. Histology shows acantholysis with dyskeratosis, including corps ronds and grains.

Pemphigus vegetans.description: A rare vegetating form of pemphigus vulgaris in which flaccid bullae evolve into painful, malodorous, vegetating erosions and plaques, often in intertriginous regions. It is autoimmune and usually has mucosal involvement; histology may show acantholysis with eosinophilic inflammation.

Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or c.normalized_text: Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or candidal infection
Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or c.description: Inflammation of opposing skin surfaces caused by moisture, heat, friction, and sweating, often complicated by Candida or bacterial overgrowth. It produces erythema, maceration, fissuring, erosions, odor, and discomfort in axillae, groin, or inframammary folds.

Acanthosis nigricans.description: A velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, commonly associated with obesity, insulin resistance, or diabetes mellitus. Skin tags may coexist, particularly in the axillae and neck.

Extraskeletal mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.description: A rare malignant cartilage-forming soft-tissue tumor that often occurs in young adults and may arise in the pelvis. Imaging commonly shows a lobulated soft-tissue mass with prominent calcified chondroid matrix, adjacent bone erosion or invasion, and increased FDG uptake.

Extraskeletal osteosarcoma.description: A malignant soft-tissue sarcoma that produces osteoid or bone outside the skeleton. It can present as a calcified pelvic mass with local invasion and marked metabolic activity, although it is more common in older adults.

Synovial sarcoma.description: A malignant mesenchymal soft-tissue tumor affecting adolescents and young adults. It may occur near the hip or pelvic joints, can contain calcifications, and may cause pressure erosion of adjacent bone.

Conventional chondrosarcoma of the ilium.normalized_text: Conventional chondrosarcoma of the ilium with extraosseous soft-tissue extension
Conventional chondrosarcoma of the ilium.description: A malignant cartilaginous tumor arising from bone, often in the pelvis, with lobulated architecture and characteristic rings-and-arcs or stippled calcification. Larger lesions can extend into surrounding soft tissues.

Chondroblastoma of the pelvic bone with.normalized_text: Chondroblastoma of the pelvic bone with soft-tissue extension
Chondroblastoma of the pelvic bone with.description: A benign but locally aggressive cartilage tumor that usually affects adolescents and young adults. It can show matrix calcification and bone-scan uptake, although pelvic location and a large soft-tissue mass are uncommon.

Stiff-person syndrome (SPS).description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb muscle rigidity, painful stimulus-sensitive spasms, hyperreflexia, and exaggerated startle responses; it is often associated with antibodies to GAD65 or related inhibitory-synapse proteins. The electrophysiology shown is compatible with excessive stimulus-triggered muscle activation and an enhanced late blink-reflex response.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe autoimmune stiff-person-spectrum disorder, frequently associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, causing rigidity, painful spasms, myoclonus or exaggerated startle, hyperreflexia, brainstem involvement, and sometimes autonomic or respiratory dysfunction.

Glycine receptor antibody-associated sti.normalized_text: Glycine receptor antibody-associated stiff-person spectrum disorder
Glycine receptor antibody-associated sti.description: An autoimmune disorder of inhibitory glycinergic neurotransmission that may present as stiff-person syndrome or PERM, with exaggerated startle, axial and limb spasms, hyperexcitability of brainstem/spinal reflex circuits, and potential respiratory involvement.

Hyperekplexia (exaggerated startle syndr.description: A disorder of impaired glycinergic inhibition, usually genetic but occasionally acquired/autoimmune, causing an excessive startle reflex with generalized stiffening after unexpected stimuli. Electrophysiology may show abnormal startle-related recruitment across multiple muscles.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia or other u.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia or other upper-motor-neuron spastic paraparesis
Hereditary spastic paraplegia or other u.description: A group of disorders causing progressive bilateral lower-limb spasticity, weakness, hyperreflexia, and clonus due to corticospinal-tract dysfunction. Some forms can produce substantial gait disability.

Takayasu arteritis (aortic arch syndrome.normalized_text: Takayasu arteritis (aortic arch syndrome) with carotid/subclavian arterial stenosis
Takayasu arteritis (aortic arch syndrome.description: A large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often causing stenosis or occlusion of carotid and subclavian arteries. Reduced scalp and cerebral perfusion can cause scalp ischemia, ulceration, syncope, and stroke.

Severe carotid artery occlusive disease.normalized_text: Severe carotid artery occlusive disease causing scalp ischemic necrosis
Severe carotid artery occlusive disease.description: Critical stenosis or occlusion of the common or internal carotid circulation can impair flow through the external carotid branches supplying the scalp, producing ischemic scalp ulceration and cerebral hypoperfusion symptoms.

Atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease.normalized_text: Atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease with recurrent carotid stenosis or occlusion
Atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the carotid and great vessels can recur after carotid endarterectomy and may cause transient cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemic stroke, and rarely external-carotid territory ischemia such as scalp necrosis.

Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia/necrosis
Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia.description: Giant cell arteritis is an inflammatory vasculitis of medium and large arteries that can cause scalp tenderness, ischemic scalp ulceration or necrosis, and ischemic neurologic complications. It usually occurs in adults older than 50 years.

Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania infan.description: A systemic protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies, often acquired in Mediterranean regions. In immunosuppressed patients, it can cause fever, pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, autoimmune-like serology, and may occur without splenomegaly. The image is consistent with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages, and the serum appearance is compatible with hypergammaglobulinemia.
