Felty syndrome.description: A complication of longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, usually splenomegaly, and increased susceptibility to infection. It may be associated with anemia, thrombocytopenia, high rheumatoid factor, and hypergammaglobulinemia.

Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumato.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis-systemic lupus overlap syndrome (rhupus)
Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumato.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory polyarthritis, fever, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, positive ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, cryoglobulins, and cutaneous vasculitic lesions. In this case, some lupus-like laboratory findings may instead be induced by visceral leishmaniasis.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).normalized_text: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), potentially secondary to visceral leishmaniasis
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, immune activation, and macrophage activation. Infections, including visceral leishmaniasis, can trigger secondary HLH in immunosuppressed adults.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous dermatosis strongly associated with diabetes mellitus. It typically presents on the shins as slowly enlarging red-brown plaques that develop a yellow-brown, atrophic, indented center with a raised erythematous border. Histology shows dermal collagen degeneration (necrobiotic collagen) with granulomatous inflammation.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign granulomatous inflammatory skin disorder that may produce slowly enlarging papules or plaques, often on the extremities. Histology can show palisading granulomas around degenerated collagen, but lesions are usually annular and lack the prominent yellow atrophic center typical of necrobiosis lipoidica.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A common diabetes-associated skin finding consisting of small, round or oval, brown, slightly depressed macules on the shins, often called shin spots. It is related to diabetic microangiopathy and usually causes no symptoms.

Lipodermatosclerosis.description: A chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disorder of the lower legs caused by chronic venous insufficiency. It can produce tender, hyperpigmented, indurated plaques and eventually atrophic or scarred skin, most often around the lower calves and ankles.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B).normalized_text: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B), likely due to a GNAS methylation defect
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B).description: An inherited or sporadic disorder of parathyroid-hormone resistance, primarily in the renal proximal tubules. It causes hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH despite adequate parathyroid hormone production. The image shows abnormal GNAS methylation in the patient, supporting PHP1B.

Symptomatic hypocalcemia with tetany/lar.description: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability and can cause muscle stiffness, tetany, dysphagia, laryngospasm or stridor, anxiety, vomiting, and reduced oral intake. In this case, the hypocalcemia is most likely secondary to pseudohypoparathyroidism.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A).normalized_text: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A) / Albright hereditary osteodystrophy spectrum
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A).description: A GNAS-related disorder causing resistance to PTH and sometimes other hormones, usually associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features such as short stature, obesity, brachydactyly, and subcutaneous ossifications. It is a differential diagnosis for hypocalcemia with elevated PTH, but the methylation findings favor PHP1B rather than PHP1A.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, often involving the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and reticuloendothelial system. Tissue typically shows granulomatous inflammation with small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.

Dabrafenib-trametinib associated pyrexia.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, characterized by recurrent fever, chills, diaphoresis, malaise, nausea, and occasionally hypotension or laboratory inflammatory abnormalities. Symptoms often improve with treatment interruption and antipyretics.

Hepatosplenic candidiasis.description: An invasive Candida infection that can produce persistent fever and multiple small liver and splenic lesions, particularly in patients with malignancy or immunosuppression. Histology may show granulomas and fungal elements.

Sarcoid-like granulomatous reaction indu.normalized_text: Sarcoid-like granulomatous reaction induced by BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy
Sarcoid-like granulomatous reaction indu.description: BRAF and MEK inhibitors can rarely trigger sarcoid-like inflammatory reactions, with noncaseating granulomas involving the skin, lungs, lymph nodes, liver, or other organs.

Gallbladder metastasis from prostate ade.description: Metastatic spread of prostate cancer to the gallbladder, an extremely uncommon site of involvement. The imaging demonstrates a gallbladder mass, and the cytology/histology with prostate-lineage immunostaining is consistent with metastatic prostatic adenocarcinoma rather than a primary gallbladder tumor.

Primary gallbladder adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the gallbladder mucosa, often presenting late with right upper quadrant pain, biliary obstruction, cholecystitis-like symptoms, or a gallbladder mass. In this case it is less favored because pathology supports prostatic origin.

Acute cholecystitis due to malignant cys.normalized_text: Acute cholecystitis due to malignant cystic-duct obstruction
Acute cholecystitis due to malignant cys.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder caused by obstruction of cystic-duct outflow, in this case potentially from a gallbladder metastatic deposit or tumor rather than gallstones. It can mimic typical calculous cholecystitis clinically.

Allgrove syndrome (Triple-A syndrome; AA.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by alacrima, achalasia, ACTH-resistant primary adrenal insufficiency, and progressive neurologic/autonomic dysfunction. A '4A' phenotype may include amyotrophy and other neurologic manifestations.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, including.normalized_text: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, including adolescent cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy or early adrenomyeloneuropathy
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, including.description: An X-linked peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 variants that produces adrenal insufficiency and progressive central nervous system white-matter or spinal-cord disease. It can cause spasticity, weakness, gait impairment, and visual or cognitive decline.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency with.normalized_text: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency with neurologic involvement
Familial glucocorticoid deficiency with.description: A group of inherited causes of ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency, usually presenting in childhood with severe cortisol deficiency, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, and typically preserved mineralocorticoid function. Certain genetic forms can include developmental or neurologic abnormalities.

Cerebral fat embolism syndrome secondary.normalized_text: Cerebral fat embolism syndrome secondary to metastatic bone disease/bone marrow necrosis
Cerebral fat embolism syndrome secondary.description: A neurologic manifestation of fat embolism in which marrow fat enters the circulation and causes diffuse cerebral microvascular occlusion, edema, and petechial hemorrhage. MRI commonly shows numerous bilateral diffusion-restricting lesions (the "starfield" pattern) and microhemorrhages on susceptibility imaging.

Multifocal embolic ischemic stroke due t.normalized_text: Multifocal embolic ischemic stroke due to cancer-associated hypercoagulability
Multifocal embolic ischemic stroke due t.description: Advanced malignancy can produce a hypercoagulable state, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, or tumor-associated thrombosis, leading to multiple acute embolic cerebral infarcts in different vascular territories.

Cerebral tumor embolism from metastatic.normalized_text: Cerebral tumor embolism from metastatic breast carcinoma
Cerebral tumor embolism from metastatic.description: Tumor cells can embolize to cerebral arteries in patients with disseminated cancer, causing multifocal ischemic lesions and occasionally hemorrhagic infarction. It is rare but can occur in advanced metastatic breast cancer.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, usually involving posterior cerebral regions, associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic therapies, eclampsia, or severe systemic illness. It can cause seizures and altered mental status.

Brain metastases from breast carcinoma.description: Breast cancer may spread to the brain, producing focal or multifocal enhancing masses with vasogenic edema, seizures, headache, and focal neurologic deficits. Some metastases can bleed.

Isolated spinal cord neurosarcoidosis.description: Neurosarcoidosis is granulomatous inflammation caused by sarcoidosis involving the nervous system. In this case, imaging shows an enhancing cervical intramedullary lesion and pathology shows noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells; absence of systemic organ involvement supports isolated spinal neurosarcoidosis.

Idiopathic transverse myelitis.description: Idiopathic transverse myelitis is an inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord causing acute or subacute motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction, usually with a sensory level and MRI evidence of myelitis.

Cervical intramedullary spinal cord tumo.normalized_text: Cervical intramedullary spinal cord tumor (especially ependymoma or astrocytoma)
Cervical intramedullary spinal cord tumo.description: Intramedullary tumors such as ependymoma or astrocytoma can produce a slowly progressive cervical myelopathy through expansion and compression of spinal cord tracts and may enhance on MRI.

Infectious granulomatous myelitis (tuber.normalized_text: Infectious granulomatous myelitis (tuberculous or fungal myelitis)
Infectious granulomatous myelitis (tuber.description: Tuberculosis and certain fungal infections can cause granulomatous inflammation of the spinal cord, sometimes forming an intramedullary tuberculoma or inflammatory mass with enhancing MRI abnormalities.

Right lower lobe lung abscess / necrotiz.normalized_text: Right lower lobe lung abscess / necrotizing bacterial pneumonia
Right lower lobe lung abscess / necrotiz.description: A destructive bacterial lung infection causing consolidation with areas of tissue necrosis and cavitation; imaging commonly shows a thick-walled cavity or multiple small cavities within an area of pneumonia.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A chronic suppurative lung infection caused by Actinomyces species, often producing mass-like consolidation, abscesses, cavitation, and extension across tissue planes. Histology may show suppurative inflammation and sulfur-granule-like bacterial colonies.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with cavitary pne.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause persistent cough, sputum production, focal consolidation, cavitation, and granulomatous inflammation. Although classically upper-lobe predominant, lower-lobe disease can occur.

Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia w.description: Bacterial pneumonia produces cough, purulent sputum, focal crackles, and lobar consolidation. More severe infections, including those caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or anaerobic organisms, may cavitate.

Pulmonary fungal infection, including pu.normalized_text: Pulmonary fungal infection, including pulmonary cryptococcosis
Pulmonary fungal infection, including pu.description: Pulmonary fungal infections can present with subacute cough and focal nodules, consolidation, or cavitary lesions. Histologic evaluation may demonstrate granulomatous inflammation with yeast-containing macrophages, depending on the organism.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.normalized_text: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually involving dogs as reservoir hosts. In humans, Dirofilaria repens commonly causes a solitary or migrating painless subcutaneous nodule. Histology typically shows a nematode with a thick multilayered cuticle and characteristic external longitudinal ridges.

Human subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to.normalized_text: Human subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria immitis
Human subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to.description: An uncommon human infection with the dog heartworm, transmitted by mosquitoes. Human infection more often causes pulmonary nodules, but rare subcutaneous lesions can occur. Histology may show a Dirofilaria species, although D. immitis is less consistent with the cuticular morphology and clinical presentation than D. repens.

Sparganosis.description: A tissue infection caused by larval Spirometra tapeworms, acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or undercooked intermediate hosts. It may present as slowly migrating subcutaneous nodules, but the parasite morphology differs substantially from the filarial nematode shown.

Progressive supranuclear palsy, Richards.description: A rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonian tauopathy characterized by early unexplained backward falls, axial rigidity, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal-subcortical dysfunction. The MRI appearance is compatible with midbrain atrophy, often termed the 'hummingbird' or 'penguin' sign.

Multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian ty.description: An alpha-synuclein neurodegenerative disorder causing parkinsonism, autonomic failure, gait impairment, dysarthria, dysphagia, and sometimes eye-movement abnormalities. However, severe early vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and early backward falls favor PSP over MSA.

Corticobasal syndrome / corticobasal deg.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy that usually causes asymmetric parkinsonism, limb dystonia, apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien-limb phenomena, and cognitive impairment; eye-movement abnormalities and dysphagia may occur later.

Parkinson disease.description: A common alpha-synuclein disorder causing bradykinesia with rigidity, resting tremor, and later postural instability. Advanced disease can produce dysarthria and dysphagia, but early falls and vertical gaze palsy are not typical.

Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococ.normalized_text: Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans
Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococ.description: Opportunistic fungal meningitis caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeast, especially in advanced HIV/AIDS. The images show round budding yeasts with prominent clear capsules/halos, characteristic of Cryptococcus on India ink or capsule-staining microscopy.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, typically producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated protein, reduced glucose, and elevated intracranial pressure. It is more common in people with advanced HIV.

Viral meningitis or meningoencephalitis.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as herpesviruses, enteroviruses, or HIV-associated infections. CSF usually has lymphocytic pleocytosis with relatively preserved glucose.

Acute left pontine ischemic infarction c.normalized_text: Acute left pontine ischemic infarction causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Acute left pontine ischemic infarction c.description: A small acute ischemic stroke in the left medial pons involving the medial longitudinal fasciculus, producing impaired left eye adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus. The diffusion-weighted MRI appearance is consistent with an acute pontine infarct.

Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.description: A disorder of horizontal eye movement caused by interruption of the medial longitudinal fasciculus. It produces ipsilateral impaired adduction and nystagmus of the opposite abducting eye; in this case it is most likely due to a small pontine infarct.

Posterior-circulation transient ischemic.normalized_text: Posterior-circulation transient ischemic attack or ischemic stroke due to atrial fibrillation
Posterior-circulation transient ischemic.description: Atrial fibrillation can cause cardioembolic ischemia in the posterior circulation, including small brainstem infarcts. Persistent focal eye movement findings and diffusion restriction favor completed ischemic stroke rather than transient ischemia.

Multiple sclerosis causing internuclear.description: Multiple sclerosis can produce internuclear ophthalmoplegia through demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, but it is substantially less likely in an elderly patient with abrupt symptoms and an acute diffusion-restricting pontine lesion.

Congenital Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Malaria acquired transplacentally or during delivery, most often presenting in early infancy with fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and parasitemia. The smear appearance of multiple delicate ring forms within individual erythrocytes strongly supports P. falciparum.

Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium viv.normalized_text: Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium vivax
Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium viv.description: A transplacentally acquired malaria infection that can cause fever, anemia, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and parasitemia in neonates. P. vivax typically infects enlarged young red cells and usually has only one parasite per erythrocyte, unlike the multiple-ring-form pattern seen here.

Neonatal babesiosis.description: Babesia is an intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and splenomegaly. It may resemble malaria on smear; however, Babesia classically shows tetrads forming a Maltese-cross pattern and is generally acquired by tick exposure, transfusion, or rarely vertically.

Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis wit.normalized_text: Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis wit.description: Systemic bacterial infection in an infant can cause fever, tachycardia, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, anemia, and multiorgan dysfunction. It is an important initial consideration in a toxic-appearing febrile infant but does not explain malarial parasites on smear.

Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.normalized_text: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal involvement
Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with locally invasive pelvic/rectal disease and distant metastases. The CT images appear to show a pelvic rectal-region mass, hepatic lesion, and multiple pulmonary nodules, compatible with disseminated malignancy.

Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with hepat.normalized_text: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with hepatic and pulmonary metastases
Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with hepat.description: A colorectal malignancy arising in the rectum can cause tenesmus and rectal pain and commonly metastasizes to the liver and lungs. The pelvic abnormality and distant lesions on CT are compatible with advanced metastatic rectal cancer.

Metastatic malignancy of uncertain prima.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy of uncertain primary origin involving rectum, liver, and lungs
Metastatic malignancy of uncertain prima.description: Widespread cancer can present with constitutional decline and focal symptoms from pelvic or rectal involvement. The combination of a pelvic lesion, liver mass, and pulmonary nodules suggests disseminated malignant disease, although tissue diagnosis is needed to establish the primary site.

Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypoka.normalized_text: Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypoka.description: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins. The ultrasound appearance of diffuse thyroid enlargement with marked hypervascularity ('thyroid inferno') and histology showing diffuse hyperplastic follicles with scalloped colloid are consistent with Graves disease. Severe thyrotoxicosis can cause intracellular potassium shifting and acute flaccid weakness.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.description: An episodic, potentially life-threatening neuromuscular complication of thyrotoxicosis in which thyroid hormone excess increases cellular potassium uptake, producing profound hypokalemia and sudden weakness. It commonly affects young men and may be precipitated by medications, supplements, carbohydrate intake, exertion, or stress.

Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxico.normalized_text: Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or thyroid hormone exposure
Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxico.description: Some herbal or 'stress-reducing' supplements may contain undisclosed thyroid hormone, iodine, stimulants, or other compounds that precipitate or worsen hyperthyroidism. In a person with underlying Graves disease, such exposure can trigger a thyrotoxic periodic paralysis episode.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of weakness with low serum potassium, often triggered by carbohydrate intake, rest after exertion, stress, or certain medications. Thyroid disease can mimic or exacerbate this syndrome.

Guillain-Barre syndrome.description: An acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy that causes progressive, usually symmetric weakness and classically reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes. It is an important alternative diagnosis for acute limb weakness but does not explain the severe hypokalemia or thyroid findings well.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign, non-neoplastic bony exostosis arising from the midline hard palate. It is often nodular or lobulated, covered by normal mucosa, slowly enlarges over time, and is usually asymptomatic.

Palatal exostosis.description: A benign localized overgrowth of mature bone on the palate. Palatal exostoses can resemble torus palatinus but may be less strictly midline or have an irregular nodular contour.

Peripheral osteoma of the palate.description: A benign, slow-growing tumor composed of mature bone. In the oral cavity it typically presents as a firm, painless, well-circumscribed bony mass.

Fibrous hamartoma or congenital oral ham.normalized_text: Fibrous hamartoma or congenital oral hamartoma
Fibrous hamartoma or congenital oral ham.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of normal tissue components that can be present from birth and may form a painless, soft-tissue mass in the oral cavity.

Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.description: A benign salivary-gland tumor that commonly occurs on the palate and usually presents as a painless, slowly enlarging, firm submucosal mass.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Large L4-L5 lumbar disc herniation with.normalized_text: Large L4-L5 lumbar disc herniation with nerve-root compression
Large L4-L5 lumbar disc herniation with.description: A protruded or extruded degenerative disc at L4-L5 compressing the thecal sac and adjacent lumbar nerve roots. The sagittal MRI shows a prominent posterior L4-L5 disc herniation with marked central canal narrowing.

Lumbar radiculopathy, likely involving t.normalized_text: Lumbar radiculopathy, likely involving the L5 nerve root
Lumbar radiculopathy, likely involving t.description: Radiculopathy is pain, weakness, or sensory disturbance caused by compression or irritation of a spinal nerve root. In this case it is most likely due to the large L4-L5 disc herniation seen on MRI, which commonly affects the traversing L5 root.

Degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosi.normalized_text: Degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosis, exacerbated by L4-L5 disc protrusion
Degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosi.description: Lumbar spinal stenosis is narrowing of the spinal canal from degenerative disc disease, disc bulging/herniation, and facet or ligamentous degeneration. The MRI demonstrates substantial lower-lumbar central canal narrowing, most pronounced at L4-L5.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with multiorgan involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated injury to organs, commonly the heart, nervous system, lungs, skin, and gastrointestinal tract. In this case, cerebral ischemic lesions and cardiac injury are compatible with eosinophilic vascular and cardiac involvement.

Eosinophilic myocarditis/endomyocardial.normalized_text: Eosinophilic myocarditis/endomyocardial disease secondary to hypereosinophilic syndrome
Eosinophilic myocarditis/endomyocardial.description: Eosinophil infiltration of the myocardium and endocardium can produce myocardial injury, ventricular dysfunction, mural thrombus formation, and systemic embolic stroke. It is a major cardiac complication of hypereosinophilic syndrome.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.normalized_text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA; Churg-Strauss syndrome)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A necrotizing eosinophilic small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly causes asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, peripheral eosinophilia, lung infiltrates or nodules, neuropathy, cardiac disease, and occasionally cerebral infarction or hemorrhage.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: An inflammatory vasculitis limited to cerebral and spinal cord vessels that can cause multifocal ischemic strokes, intracranial hemorrhage, encephalopathy, and segmental arterial narrowing or irregularity on angiography.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other c.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other clonal myeloid hypereosinophilic neoplasm
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other c.description: A clonal hematologic disorder in which excessive eosinophil production can lead to tissue infiltration, thrombosis, cardiac damage, pulmonary abnormalities, and central nervous system ischemic events. It must be excluded in otherwise unexplained hypereosinophilia.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis (Stage II).description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving intrathoracic lymph nodes and lungs. Stage II disease includes bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy with pulmonary parenchymal involvement.

Sarcoid-like reaction associated with pr.normalized_text: Sarcoid-like reaction associated with prior breast cancer or cancer therapy
Sarcoid-like reaction associated with pr.description: A noninfectious granulomatous reaction resembling sarcoidosis that can occur in regional or distant lymph nodes after malignancy, chemotherapy, radiation, or other immune-modulating treatments, without representing tumor recurrence.

Metastatic breast cancer to mediastinal/.normalized_text: Metastatic breast cancer to mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes and lungs
Metastatic breast cancer to mediastinal/.description: Recurrent breast carcinoma can metastasize to thoracic lymph nodes and lungs and may show intense FDG uptake on PET imaging.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with granulomatou.description: Tuberculosis is a mycobacterial infection that can cause pulmonary infiltrates and granulomatous lymphadenitis; granulomas are classically caseating but may occasionally be noncaseating.

IgG kappa multiple myeloma.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder characterized by clonal bone-marrow plasma-cell infiltration, monoclonal immunoglobulin production, osteolytic bone disease, anemia, hypercalcemia, and possible renal impairment. The marrow images show extensive plasma-cell infiltration, and the pelvic radiograph shows lytic bone lesions.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic plasma-cell neoplasm with a substantial monoclonal protein and/or increased marrow plasma cells but without myeloma-defining end-organ damage. It may progress to symptomatic multiple myeloma.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.normalized_text: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), IgG kappa type
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A premalignant clonal plasma-cell condition with a low-level monoclonal protein and no attributable anemia, hypercalcemia, renal injury, bone lesions, or significant marrow plasma-cell burden.

Bifocal intracranial germinoma (suprasel.normalized_text: Bifocal intracranial germinoma (suprasellar and pineal germinoma)
Bifocal intracranial germinoma (suprasel.description: A primary central nervous system germ-cell tumor that commonly affects adolescent and young adult males. It often involves the pineal region and/or suprasellar-hypothalamic-pituitary region, producing diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism, visual-field defects, and sometimes multifocal enhancing brain lesions.

Suprasellar germinoma with multifocal in.normalized_text: Suprasellar germinoma with multifocal intracranial dissemination
Suprasellar germinoma with multifocal in.description: A suprasellar germinoma is a germ-cell tumor involving the pituitary stalk, hypothalamus, or posterior pituitary. It frequently presents with central diabetes insipidus and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies; additional pineal or ventricular lesions may represent synchronous or disseminated disease.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving.description: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is an infiltrative inflammatory-neoplastic disorder that can involve the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, most often causing central diabetes insipidus and pituitary hormone deficiencies. It is a differential diagnosis for pituitary-stalk thickening, although the pineal and multifocal intracranial imaging pattern is more suggestive of germinoma.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.normalized_text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus native aortic-valve infective endocarditis
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.description: Infection of the native aortic valve by MRSA, producing valvular vegetations and systemic embolic phenomena. The echocardiographic images are consistent with aortic-valve vegetation, and the clinical findings fulfill major features of infective endocarditis.

Aortic root abscess complicating aortic-.normalized_text: Aortic root abscess complicating aortic-valve infective endocarditis
Aortic root abscess complicating aortic-.description: A periannular infection extending from aortic-valve endocarditis into the aortic root, potentially causing abscess formation, aortic regurgitation, and conduction-system disturbance. The ECG images suggest PR-interval prolongation/conduction delay, while echocardiography suggests periannular involvement adjacent to the aortic valve.

Septic cerebral embolic stroke secondary.normalized_text: Septic cerebral embolic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
Septic cerebral embolic stroke secondary.description: Embolization of infected valvular material from endocarditis to cerebral arteries, causing acute ischemic stroke and potentially cerebral infection. This is a common neurological complication of left-sided infective endocarditis.

Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (a.normalized_text: Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency; glycogen storage disease type II)
Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (a.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal glycogen-storage disorder caused by severe deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA), resulting in glycogen accumulation in cardiac, skeletal, and respiratory muscle. The classic infantile form commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, muscle weakness, and markedly reduced GAA activity.

CRIM-negative or functionally CRIM-defic.normalized_text: CRIM-negative or functionally CRIM-deficient infantile-onset Pompe disease
CRIM-negative or functionally CRIM-defic.description: A severe subtype of infantile-onset Pompe disease in which little or no endogenous immunologically detectable GAA protein is produced, often due to null or severe splice variants. It carries a high risk of anti-drug antibody formation during enzyme-replacement therapy and requires early immune-tolerance consideration.

Pompe disease with hypertrophic cardiomy.description: Cardiac involvement from glycogen accumulation in Pompe disease, typically producing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and an enlarged cardiac silhouette in infants. Cardiac disease may be detectable before substantial skeletal-muscle symptoms appear.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: A milder GAA-deficiency phenotype that usually presents later in childhood or adulthood with progressive proximal muscle weakness and respiratory muscle weakness, typically without severe infantile cardiomyopathy.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts involving bone marrow and potentially extramedullary sites. The marrow morphology and flow-cytometry images showing a blast population with B-cell markers including CD19 and CD10 strongly support this diagnosis.

Neuroblastoma.description: An embryonal tumor of sympathetic nervous system origin, usually arising from the adrenal gland or paraspinal sympathetic chain. It can metastasize to bone marrow, bone, orbit, liver, and lymph nodes, causing bone pain and periorbital ecchymoses.

Burkitt lymphoma with bone marrow involv.normalized_text: Burkitt lymphoma with bone marrow involvement
Burkitt lymphoma with bone marrow involv.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can involve the abdomen, bone marrow, central nervous system, and extranodal soft tissues. It may produce abdominal enlargement, constitutional symptoms, anemia, and bone pain when marrow is involved.

Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarc.normalized_text: Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarcoma
Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarc.description: Acute myeloid leukemia is a clonal myeloid blast malignancy that can infiltrate marrow and form extramedullary tumor masses called myeloid sarcomas. Such lesions can involve bone, orbit, soft tissue, and lymph nodes.

Acute bacterial cellulitis of the glutea.normalized_text: Acute bacterial cellulitis of the gluteal region
Acute bacterial cellulitis of the glutea.description: A bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, most often caused by streptococci or staphylococci. The photographs show diffuse erythema and swelling, while ultrasound appears consistent with subcutaneous edema/cobblestoning without a well-defined drainable collection.

Erysipelas.description: A superficial acute bacterial skin infection, usually due to beta-hemolytic streptococci, characterized by painful erythema and edema. It is closely related to cellulitis but more often involves the upper dermis and lymphatics.

Early necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive, potentially life-threatening infection involving deep fascia and soft tissue. Early disease may initially resemble cellulitis, but worsening pain, systemic toxicity, skin necrosis, bullae, crepitus, or fascial fluid/gas would raise concern.

Gluteal soft-tissue abscess.description: A localized collection of pus within soft tissue, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, which can produce painful erythema and swelling and may coexist with surrounding cellulitis.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD), sclerodermatous/dermatomyositis-like cutaneous phenotype
Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.description: A late immune-mediated complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Cutaneous cGVHD can cause lichenoid or sclerodermoid skin changes, pigmentary changes, restricted joint mobility, and occasionally dermatomyositis-like eruptions.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive skin findings, including facial erythema, shawl-distribution rash, Gottron papules/sign, and periungual changes. It may occur after transplantation or in association with chronic GVHD.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.description: A systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disease that can cause photosensitive facial and generalized rashes, constitutional symptoms, musculoskeletal complaints, and positive antinuclear antibodies. A lupus-like syndrome may rarely occur in the post-transplant setting.

Systemic sclerosis-like chronic GVHD / e.normalized_text: Systemic sclerosis-like chronic GVHD / eosinophilic fasciitis-like syndrome
Systemic sclerosis-like chronic GVHD / e.description: A fibrosing disorder of skin and fascia that can occur as a manifestation of chronic GVHD after stem-cell transplantation. It causes skin induration, reduced joint range of motion, contractures, and a positive prayer sign; inflammatory rash may coexist.

Multiple keratoacanthomas (eruptive kera.description: Keratoacanthomas are rapidly growing crateriform keratinizing epidermal tumors that can occur as multiple lesions in eruptive forms. They may be associated with immunologic dysfunction, chronic renal failure, medications, ultraviolet exposure, or trauma.

Generalized eruptive keratoacanthomas of.description: A rare eruptive keratoacanthoma syndrome characterized by the development of many small keratinizing papules, often with severe itch and prominent involvement of sun-exposed skin. Lesions may be persistent and difficult to manage.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.normalized_text: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma type
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.description: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a keratinocyte malignancy that may present as a hyperkeratotic papule, nodule, ulcer, or crateriform keratoacanthoma-like lesion. Multiple tumors can occur in patients with immune dysfunction or prior immunosuppression.

Acquired perforating dermatosis associat.normalized_text: Acquired perforating dermatosis associated with chronic renal failure (Kyrle disease spectrum)
Acquired perforating dermatosis associat.description: Acquired perforating dermatosis is an intensely pruritic disorder seen particularly in patients with diabetes or end-stage renal disease on dialysis. It causes excoriated hyperkeratotic papules, often on the extremities, due to transepidermal elimination of dermal material.

Anterior spinal artery syndrome due to s.normalized_text: Anterior spinal artery syndrome due to spinal cord infarction
Anterior spinal artery syndrome due to s.description: Acute ischemic injury of the spinal cord, usually involving the anterior two-thirds of the cord and producing motor weakness, loss of pain/temperature sensation, and autonomic dysfunction. The MRI appearances are compatible with intramedullary T2 hyperintensity in an ischemic distribution.

Fibrocartilaginous embolism causing spin.normalized_text: Fibrocartilaginous embolism causing spinal cord infarction
Fibrocartilaginous embolism causing spin.description: A rare cause of spinal cord infarction in children and young adults, caused by embolization of intervertebral-disc fibrocartilage into spinal cord vessels. It typically presents with abrupt spinal or limb pain followed by rapidly progressive motor, sensory, and bladder dysfunction, often with normal CSF.

Acute transverse myelitis.description: An inflammatory spinal cord disorder causing acute or subacute motor weakness, sensory impairment with a spinal sensory level, and autonomic dysfunction. MRI usually shows intramedullary T2-hyperintense lesions.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune demyelinating disorder that can cause severe myelitis with weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder dysfunction. It often produces longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions, although confirmatory antibody testing and clinical correlation are required.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.normalized_text: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), with TCRAD-associated chromosomal rearrangement
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive precursor T-lymphoid neoplasm characterized by marrow and blood replacement by lymphoblasts. The images show blast-rich peripheral blood and marrow, while the immunophenotype demonstrates T-lineage markers (cytoplasmic/surface CD3, CD2, CD5, and CD7). The karyotype/FISH findings support rearrangement involving the T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus at 14q11, with additional involvement of Xq22.3/IRS4.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: A mature, aggressive T-cell leukemia that commonly presents with marked lymphocytosis and a mature post-thymic T-cell phenotype, often expressing CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It is usually a disease of older adults and frequently has splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and skin involvement.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).description: A mature peripheral T-cell malignancy caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Leukemic ATLL generally expresses mature T-cell markers, often CD2, CD3, CD4, and CD25, and may present with high LDH, blood involvement, lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, and organ enlargement.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, leading to cytokine storm, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, coagulopathy, multiorgan failure, and very high ferritin. The marrow images show hemophagocytosis.

Disseminated tuberculosis with tuberculo.description: Widespread infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis can trigger secondary HLH, especially when there is bone-marrow, hepatic, splenic, and pulmonary involvement. It may present with prolonged fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse lung infiltrates, and hemophagocytosis.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with seconda.description: Disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum infection can involve the reticuloendothelial system, including bone marrow, liver, and spleen, and may trigger HLH. It commonly causes fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, markedly elevated ferritin, and diffuse pulmonary disease.

Visceral leishmaniasis with secondary HL.description: Visceral leishmaniasis is a systemic protozoal infection involving macrophages in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. It can produce prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and secondary HLH.

Severe viral infection causing infection.normalized_text: Severe viral infection causing infection-associated HLH, especially Epstein-Barr virus-associated HLH
Severe viral infection causing infection.description: Acute Epstein-Barr virus infection and other systemic viral infections can trigger HLH in previously healthy adults. EBV-associated HLH commonly causes persistent fever, cytopenias, liver/spleen enlargement, coagulopathy, hyperferritinemia, and rapid multiorgan deterioration.

Dengue virus encephalitis with cerebral.normalized_text: Dengue virus encephalitis with cerebral vasculitis/ischemic strokes
Dengue virus encephalitis with cerebral.description: A severe neurologic complication of dengue infection in which encephalitis and inflammatory vascular injury can cause multifocal cerebral ischemia. Dengue is endemic in several Pacific islands, including Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands.

Chikungunya virus encephalitis with cere.normalized_text: Chikungunya virus encephalitis with cerebral vasculitis
Chikungunya virus encephalitis with cere.description: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne alphavirus infection that can cause fever and rash; severe encephalitis, encephalopathy, and vascular complications occur particularly in older adults.

Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with.normalized_text: Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with VZV cerebral vasculopathy
Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with.description: Varicella-zoster virus can infect cerebral arteries, producing vasculopathy with multifocal infarctions, encephalitis, altered consciousness, and focal deficits; rash may be absent, remote, or transient.

West Nile virus encephalitis.description: West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that can cause severe meningoencephalitis in older adults, with fever, coma, focal neurologic deficits, and occasionally rash.

Bacterial meningitis with infectious cer.normalized_text: Bacterial meningitis with infectious cerebral vasculitis or septic embolic infarction
Bacterial meningitis with infectious cer.description: Acute bacterial meningitis can cause coma and focal deficits through meningeal inflammation, vasculitis, arterial thrombosis, or septic emboli, producing ischemic lesions on brain imaging.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition in vessel walls. It commonly follows an upper respiratory infection and causes palpable purpura of the lower extremities, arthralgia or arthritis, gastrointestinal involvement, and sometimes kidney disease. The biopsy images show leukocytoclastic vasculitis with vascular IgA, C3, and fibrin deposition, strongly supporting this diagnosis.

Adalimumab-associated IgA vasculitis.description: A drug-associated immune-complex vasculitis in which tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors, including adalimumab, can rarely trigger IgA-mediated leukocytoclastic vasculitis. It may present with lower-extremity palpable purpura and joint symptoms, sometimes after prolonged exposure.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis.description: A histopathologic pattern of immune-mediated inflammation of small dermal vessels, typically producing palpable purpura on dependent areas of the legs. It may be caused by infection, medications, inflammatory bowel disease, or systemic vasculitis. In this case, the IgA staining indicates that it is most specifically IgA vasculitis.

Crohn's disease-associated peripheral in.normalized_text: Crohn's disease-associated peripheral inflammatory arthritis with vasculitic skin manifestation
Crohn's disease-associated peripheral in.description: Crohn's disease can cause extraintestinal manifestations including peripheral arthritis, usually affecting large joints of the lower limbs, and inflammatory skin disorders. Immune-complex vasculitis can rarely occur in association with inflammatory bowel disease, although the biopsy pattern here is more specifically diagnostic of IgA vasculitis.

HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.normalized_text: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the left base of tongue with cervical nodal metastasis
HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.description: A squamous-cell cancer arising in the oropharynx, commonly the lingual tonsil/base of tongue. HPV-associated disease often occurs in relatively young patients with little or no smoking history and commonly presents with a cystic or firm upper-neck lymph-node metastasis. The CT and PET-CT show an FDG-avid left oropharyngeal/base-of-tongue mass and an FDG-avid left cervical nodal mass.

Non-HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamou.description: Squamous cell carcinoma can arise from the base of tongue, tonsil, or other oropharyngeal mucosa and spread to upper cervical lymph nodes. It classically occurs in patients with substantial tobacco and alcohol exposure, although it can occur without these risk factors.

Oropharyngeal lymphoma involving the lin.normalized_text: Oropharyngeal lymphoma involving the lingual tonsil/base of tongue with cervical lymphadenopathy
Oropharyngeal lymphoma involving the lin.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve Waldeyer's ring, including the lingual tonsils at the base of tongue, and may produce a pharyngeal mass with enlarged FDG-avid cervical lymph nodes.

Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in a.normalized_text: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in a cervical lymph node from an occult oropharyngeal primary
Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in a.description: Cervical nodal metastasis from an initially occult head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma is common, particularly from the palatine tonsil or base of tongue. PET-CT may reveal the small mucosal primary responsible for an apparently isolated neck mass.

Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.normalized_text: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in extranodal mucosal tissue. Primary bladder MALT lymphoma is rare and is often associated with longstanding chronic cystitis or recurrent bacterial urinary infections. The images show a dense small lymphoid infiltrate beneath urothelium, compatible with lymphoma involving the bladder.

Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the uri.normalized_text: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the urinary bladder (chronic follicular cystitis)
Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the uri.description: A benign reactive accumulation of lymphoid tissue in the bladder wall caused by chronic irritation or recurrent infection. It may produce lymphoid aggregates and can mimic low-grade bladder lymphoma histologically.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can rarely involve the bladder, either as primary disease or as part of systemic lymphoma. It usually consists of large atypical lymphoid cells and tends to have a more clinically aggressive presentation than MALT lymphoma.

Emphysematous cystitis.description: A complicated urinary tract infection characterized by gas production within the bladder wall and/or lumen, most often caused by gas-forming organisms such as Klebsiella pneumoniae. It occurs particularly in older adults with diabetes.

Complicated lower urinary tract infectio.normalized_text: Complicated lower urinary tract infection (acute cystitis) due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
Complicated lower urinary tract infectio.description: A bacterial infection of the urinary bladder; in frail older adults it may present with nonspecific features and systemic inflammatory-marker elevation rather than classic dysuria or urinary frequency.

Enterovesical fistula with intravesical.description: An abnormal communication between bowel and bladder that can cause gas in the bladder and recurrent urinary infections, usually associated with diverticular disease, bowel malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, or prior surgery.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the medial.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans of the medial femoral condyle
Osteochondritis dissecans of the medial.description: An osteochondral disorder in which subchondral bone and overlying cartilage of the femoral condyle become damaged and may partially detach, producing an unstable fragment or loose body. The radiographs show a subchondral osteochondral defect/sclerotic lesion in the femoral condyle, a typical location for knee osteochondritis dissecans.

Unstable osteochondral fragment or intra.normalized_text: Unstable osteochondral fragment or intra-articular loose body secondary to osteochondritis dissecans
Unstable osteochondral fragment or intra.description: A detached or partially detached cartilage-and-bone fragment within the knee joint, often arising from an osteochondral lesion such as osteochondritis dissecans. It can intermittently obstruct joint movement and cause locking and effusions.

Meniscal tear.description: A tear of the medial or lateral meniscus, commonly associated with twisting sports injuries and capable of causing pain, recurrent effusions, catching, and locking. It is an important clinical alternative for mechanical knee symptoms, although the radiographic osteochondral lesion favors osteochondritis dissecans.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the pancreas, often presenting as a pancreatic head mass causing biliary obstruction. The imaging and histology are compatible with a lymphomatous pancreatic mass composed of large atypical lymphoid cells; immunohistochemical nuclear/cytoplasmic staining patterns support lymphoid malignancy rather than adenocarcinoma.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreas, most commonly arising in the pancreatic head and causing obstruction of the common bile duct. It commonly produces painless obstructive jaundice and elevated CA19-9.

Primary pancreatic lymphoma, follicular.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic lymphoma, follicular lymphoma subtype
Primary pancreatic lymphoma, follicular.description: An uncommon B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the pancreas that may form a pancreatic mass and obstruct the bile duct. Follicular lymphoma is typically composed of centrocyte-like and centroblast-like cells and is often associated with germinal-center immunophenotypic markers.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma.description: A bile-duct adenocarcinoma arising in the distal common bile duct, often causing obstructive jaundice and elevated CA19-9. It may appear as a mass near the pancreatic head and can mimic a pancreatic neoplasm.

Uremic tumoral calcinosis (secondary tum.normalized_text: Uremic tumoral calcinosis (secondary tumoral calcinosis due to chronic renal failure)
Uremic tumoral calcinosis (secondary tum.description: A periarticular lobulated mass composed of calcium-phosphate deposits, occurring in patients with long-standing renal failure and dialysis, usually driven by hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Imaging typically shows dense, multilobulated 'cloud-like' calcified masses.

Calcinosis cutis secondary to chronic ki.normalized_text: Calcinosis cutis secondary to chronic kidney disease
Calcinosis cutis secondary to chronic ki.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts within the skin and subcutaneous tissues. In chronic kidney disease, metastatic calcification may occur because of disturbed calcium-phosphate metabolism, especially severe hyperphosphatemia.

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolo.description: A severe dialysis-associated disorder involving calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels, usually causing intensely painful ischemic skin lesions that may ulcerate and become necrotic.

Myositis ossificans / heterotopic ossifi.description: Abnormal bone formation in soft tissues, often after trauma, surgery, neurologic injury, or prolonged immobilization. It commonly produces a painful or stiff periarticular mass with organized peripheral ossification.

Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.normalized_text: Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-depression type, Schatzker II)
Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.description: An intra-articular fracture of the lateral upper tibia involving a split component and depression of the tibial plateau. The radiographs show an irregular fracture line involving the lateral tibial plateau with articular surface disruption.

Tibial plateau fracture with traumatic k.normalized_text: Tibial plateau fracture with traumatic knee hemarthrosis
Tibial plateau fracture with traumatic k.description: A fracture extending into the knee joint can cause bleeding into the joint space, producing rapid diffuse swelling and pain. The imaging supports a proximal tibial articular fracture.

Associated internal derangement of the k.normalized_text: Associated internal derangement of the knee (meniscal and/or anterior cruciate ligament injury)
Associated internal derangement of the k.description: Tibial plateau fractures from high-energy knee trauma are frequently associated with meniscal, cruciate ligament, and other soft-tissue injuries; these are not directly confirmed on the supplied plain radiographs and would require MRI or operative assessment.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (G.description: A rare mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal. Rectal GISTs commonly present as well-circumscribed submucosal spindle-cell masses and may show KIT or PDGFRA mutations; immunohistochemistry is typically positive for KIT (CD117) and DOG1.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor arising from the muscularis mucosae or muscularis propria of the rectum. It typically forms a slow-growing, well-circumscribed submucosal mass and may cause obstructive symptoms when large.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum. It can present as a large intramural or submucosal spindle-cell mass with local invasion and symptoms of rectal obstruction.

Rectal schwannoma.description: An uncommon peripheral-nerve sheath tumor arising in the rectal wall. Most are benign and present as slow-growing submucosal spindle-cell masses; tumor cells are generally S100 and SOX10 positive rather than KIT/DOG1 positive.

SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1-related SHORT syn.description: A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PIK3R1 variants, characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, partial lipodystrophy/lipoatrophy, thin or aged-appearing skin, characteristic facial features, delayed dentition, and metabolic risk including insulin resistance or diabetes later in life. SHORT refers to short stature, hyperextensibility/hernia, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and teething delay, although not all features are required.

Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome.description: A premature-aging disorder, usually caused by de novo LMNA variants, with postnatal growth failure, loss of subcutaneous fat, thin wrinkled skin, and a characteristic aged facial appearance. Cardiovascular disease and skeletal complications typically develop over time.

Berardinelli-Seip congenital lipodystrop.description: A severe generalized congenital lipodystrophy, usually caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in genes such as AGPAT2 or BSCL2, characterized by near-complete lack of body fat, muscular prominence, acromegaloid features, hepatomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and early insulin resistance.

Silver-Russell syndrome.description: A growth-restriction syndrome most commonly related to abnormalities of chromosome 11p15 imprinting or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7. It features prenatal and postnatal growth failure, triangular face, prominent forehead, feeding difficulty, body asymmetry, and relative macrocephaly at birth.

Hallermann-Streiff syndrome.description: A rare craniofacial developmental syndrome characterized by a bird-like facies with micrognathia, dental abnormalities, hypotrichosis, skin atrophy, ocular abnormalities such as microphthalmia or cataracts, and proportionate short stature.

Good syndrome (thymoma-associated immuno.description: A rare adult-onset combined immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by profound B-cell lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, impaired T-cell function, and recurrent bacterial and opportunistic infections.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring primarily in patients with impaired cellular immunity; imaging commonly shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates, though atypical nodular or cavitary disease can occur.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterial infection of the lungs that can cause chronic constitutional symptoms and cavitary lung lesions, particularly in individuals from endemic regions or those with impaired immunity.

Pulmonary infection due to Moraxella cat.normalized_text: Pulmonary infection due to Moraxella catarrhalis
Pulmonary infection due to Moraxella cat.description: A bacterial respiratory infection that may cause acute bronchitis, pneumonia, or exacerbations of chronic airway disease, especially in individuals with humoral immunodeficiency or recurrent respiratory infections.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A primary antibody deficiency characterized by low immunoglobulins, poor vaccine responses, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, gastrointestinal symptoms, and sometimes reduced B-cell numbers; it can be complicated by chronic lung disease and opportunistic infections.

Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.normalized_text: Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy)
Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.description: A rare benign non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder, usually presenting with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Histology characteristically shows large S100-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis (intact lymphocytes within histiocyte cytoplasm), typically with negative or weak CD1a staining.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that commonly affects young adults and can present with painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A clonal histiocytic disorder characterized by Langerhans cells, often involving bone, skin, lungs, or lymph nodes. The lesional cells are generally positive for CD1a and langerin and may be S100-positive.

Fulminant viral myocarditis (likely aden.description: Acute inflammation of the heart muscle caused by a viral infection, potentially producing severe ventricular dysfunction, cardiogenic shock, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest. The preceding conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, and respiratory illness are compatible with adenovirus infection.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation involving both the myocardium and pericardium, often after a viral respiratory infection. Severe myocardial involvement can cause heart failure, chest pain, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and sudden cardiac arrest.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy.description: Pregnancy-associated systolic heart failure that develops late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery. Twin gestation, obesity, gestational diabetes, and advanced hemodynamic stress of pregnancy may increase risk. Severe cases can cause pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, and ventricular arrhythmias.

Pulmonary embolism with right-heart stra.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, often arising from deep venous thrombosis. Pregnancy, obesity, twin pregnancy, and reduced mobility are important risk factors. Massive pulmonary embolism can cause shock and cardiac arrest.

Acute coronary syndrome from pregnancy-a.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome from pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD)
Acute coronary syndrome from pregnancy-a.description: SCAD is a nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma of a coronary artery that can occur during pregnancy or postpartum and may cause myocardial infarction, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac arrest.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and arteriovenous malformations in organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, and gastrointestinal tract.

Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.normalized_text: Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due to hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.description: Abnormal direct connections between hepatic arterial, portal venous, and hepatic venous vessels. Doppler findings may show turbulent, high-velocity, and abnormally pulsatile flow, while CT can demonstrate enlarged tortuous hepatic vessels. These shunts can cause high-output heart failure, portal hypertension, biliary ischemia, or encephalopathy.

Hepatic encephalopathy or portosystemic.description: A neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by impaired hepatic detoxification or portosystemic shunting, resulting in accumulation of neurotoxins such as ammonia. It commonly produces fluctuating attention, somnolence, confusion, irritability, and severe psychomotor slowing.

Acute metabolic encephalopathy from dehy.normalized_text: Acute metabolic encephalopathy from dehydration, diarrhea, acute kidney injury, and electrolyte disturbance
Acute metabolic encephalopathy from dehy.description: Acute delirium caused by systemic illness and metabolic derangements. Volume depletion from diarrhea and poor oral intake can produce prerenal azotemia, hypokalemia, weakness, and altered mental status, particularly in an older adult with cardiac and hepatic comorbidity.

Macular cutaneous mastocytosis (urticari.description: A childhood form of cutaneous mastocytosis caused by increased mast cells in the skin, typically producing tan, brown, or orange-brown macules or patches on the trunk and proximal limbs.

Juvenile xanthogranuloma, macular varian.description: A benign non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis of infancy and childhood. Typical lesions are yellow-orange papules or nodules, but uncommon early or macular lesions may appear as flat orange-brown patches or macules.

Benign cephalic histiocytosis.description: A self-limited non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis occurring in infants, characterized by asymptomatic red-brown, yellow-brown, or orange papules that may spread from the head to the trunk and limbs.

Café-au-lait macules.description: Flat, well-demarcated hyperpigmented patches caused by increased epidermal melanin. Multiple lesions can occur in otherwise healthy children but may warrant assessment for neurofibromatosis type 1 or other genetic syndromes.

Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.description: Residual darkening of the skin after dermatitis, infection, insect bites, trauma, or other inflammation; lesions may be brown and persist for weeks to months.

Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (Wil.description: Mechanical compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, usually after loss of retroperitoneal fat from significant weight loss. The CT images show marked gastric and proximal duodenal dilatation with a narrowed aortomesenteric angle and distance.

Anorexia nervosa or another restrictive.normalized_text: Anorexia nervosa or another restrictive eating disorder
Anorexia nervosa or another restrictive.description: A psychiatric eating disorder characterized by restricted caloric intake, low body weight, endocrine consequences of malnutrition, and potentially severe gastrointestinal dysmotility. Severe weight loss can precipitate superior mesenteric artery syndrome.

Gastroparesis.description: Delayed gastric emptying due to impaired gastric motility, causing retention of food and gastric dilatation, nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. It may occur idiopathically or secondary to systemic disease.

Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastri.normalized_text: Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastric pouch and transverse colon after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastri.description: An abnormal communication between the gastric pouch and colon, allowing gastric contents to pass directly into the colon and colonic contents/gas to reflux into the stomach. The contrast study demonstrates a fistulous tract from the gastric pouch to the transverse/descending colon, and endoscopy shows an abnormal gastric opening.

Marginal ulcer with fistulization into t.normalized_text: Marginal ulcer with fistulization into the colon
Marginal ulcer with fistulization into t.description: A marginal ulcer is a peptic ulcer near the gastrojejunal anastomosis after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Deep ulceration can rarely erode into adjacent structures, including the transverse colon, producing a gastrocolic fistula.

Severe protein-calorie malnutrition and.normalized_text: Severe protein-calorie malnutrition and dehydration secondary to gastrointestinal fistula-associated malabsorption
Severe protein-calorie malnutrition and.description: Severe nutritional depletion and volume loss can occur when food bypasses normal intestinal digestion and absorption through a gastrocolic fistula, causing chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea-like stools, electrolyte abnormalities, and muscle wasting.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (S.normalized_text: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) after altered Roux-en-Y anatomy
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (S.description: Excess bacterial colonization of the small bowel can occur after surgically altered gastrointestinal anatomy and may cause diarrhea, gas, malabsorption, steatorrhea-like stools, and weight loss.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum.description: Free air in the mediastinum, often caused by alveolar rupture during coughing or an asthma exacerbation. Chest radiography may show subtle linear mediastinal air outlining the heart or great vessels.

Acute asthma exacerbation.description: Acute worsening of reversible lower-airway obstruction, commonly causing wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and breathlessness. Poor adherence to inhalers is a common trigger.

Small spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial lung collapse; it can occur as a complication of asthma and may produce acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea.

Acute bronchitis or lower respiratory tr.normalized_text: Acute bronchitis or lower respiratory tract infection triggering asthma
Acute bronchitis or lower respiratory tr.description: Inflammation of the bronchi, usually viral, can cause cough, sputum production, mild inflammatory-marker elevation, and worsening of underlying asthma.

Pellagra (niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency).description: A nutritional deficiency disorder, often related to malnutrition, poverty, malabsorption, or substance use, characterized by photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and peripheral neuropathic complaints.

Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.normalized_text: Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobulinemia with peripheral neuropathy
Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.description: An immune-complex vasculitic disorder associated with chronic hepatitis C that can cause painful distal sensory neuropathy, purpura, arthralgias, renal disease, and skin ulcers.

Nutritional peripheral neuropathy due to.normalized_text: Nutritional peripheral neuropathy due to vitamin B6, vitamin B12, thiamine, or other micronutrient deficiency
Nutritional peripheral neuropathy due to.description: Malnutrition-related vitamin deficiencies can produce distal symmetric sensory neuropathy, burning pain, paresthesias, gait impairment, and sometimes skin or mucosal findings depending on the deficient nutrient.

Arsenic toxicity.description: Chronic arsenic exposure can cause painful peripheral neuropathy and characteristic skin changes, including diffuse hyperpigmentation, raindrop pigmentation, and palmar or plantar hyperkeratosis.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA, Bruton.normalized_text: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA, Bruton agammaglobulinemia) due to BTK deficiency
X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA, Bruton.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked BTK gene, leading to failure of B-cell maturation, profoundly reduced or absent mature B cells, very low immunoglobulins, and recurrent bacterial respiratory infections. The image demonstrates a BTK c.494G>A (p.Cys165Tyr) variant in the patient, absent/reduced BTK expression, and low-level maternal mosaicism.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).description: A group of severe inherited immunodeficiencies characterized by major impairment of T-cell development or function, usually with secondary B-cell dysfunction and severe early-life infections.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A heterogeneous antibody-deficiency disorder with impaired antibody production, low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. It usually presents later in childhood or adulthood.

Autosomal-recessive agammaglobulinemia o.normalized_text: Autosomal-recessive agammaglobulinemia or other early B-cell developmental defect
Autosomal-recessive agammaglobulinemia o.description: Rare inherited defects affecting B-cell development, such as defects in IGHM, CD79A, CD79B, BLNK, PIK3R1, or related pathways, can cause absent/very low B cells, hypogammaglobulinemia, and recurrent bacterial infections resembling XLA.

Penile fracture (right corpus cavernosum.normalized_text: Penile fracture (right corpus cavernosum tunica albuginea rupture)
Penile fracture (right corpus cavernosum.description: Acute rupture of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually during sexual intercourse. The MRI demonstrates a defect in the tunica albuginea of the right corpus cavernosum near the penile base with adjacent soft-tissue hematoma extending into the scrotum.

Proximal penile fracture with extravasat.normalized_text: Proximal penile fracture with extravasated hematoma into the scrotum
Proximal penile fracture with extravasat.description: A subtype of penile fracture in which a proximal corporal tear near the penile root permits blood to track into the perineum and scrotal sac, potentially leaving the penile shaft relatively spared externally.

Rupture of the superficial dorsal penile.normalized_text: Rupture of the superficial dorsal penile vein
Rupture of the superficial dorsal penile.description: Traumatic tearing of the superficial dorsal vein during intercourse can cause penile or scrotal bruising and hematoma and may clinically mimic penile fracture, but it does not produce a tunica albuginea defect.

Traumatic scrotal hematoma secondary to.normalized_text: Traumatic scrotal hematoma secondary to genital soft-tissue injury
Traumatic scrotal hematoma secondary to.description: Blood accumulation within scrotal soft tissues after trauma may cause painful scrotal enlargement and bruising. In this case, imaging indicates that the hematoma is secondary to a proximal corporal tear rather than an isolated scrotal injury.

Muscle-eye-brain disease (MEB disease; P.description: An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy caused most often by defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation. It combines severe congenital hypotonia and weakness, developmental impairment, eye abnormalities, elevated CK, and structural brain malformations.

Walker-Warburg syndrome.description: A severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy characterized by congenital muscular weakness, eye malformations, cobblestone cortical malformation, hydrocephalus, and profound developmental disability. It is usually autosomal recessive and can result from variants in POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, FKTN, FKRP, or related genes.

Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy.description: An alpha-dystroglycanopathy causing congenital muscular dystrophy, intellectual disability, brain malformations, elevated CK, and sometimes ocular abnormalities. It is classically associated with FKTN variants and is most prevalent in Japan but can occur in other populations.

LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystro.description: A recessive congenital muscular dystrophy due to laminin-alpha-2 deficiency, causing severe neonatal hypotonia, weakness, absent reflexes, contractures, and elevated CK. Brain MRI commonly shows diffuse white-matter signal abnormalities.

Primary seminal vesicle adenocarcinoma.description: A rare malignant gland-forming tumor arising from the seminal vesicle, typically occurring in older men and presenting as a pelvic mass that may invade the bladder, prostate, or rectum. The pelvic location and glandular malignant cytology/histology support this consideration.

Prostatic adenocarcinoma, including duct.description: Prostatic adenocarcinoma is a common malignancy in older men. Ductal variants can form glandular lesions near the prostatic urethra or bladder base and may present as a pelvic mass with malignant glandular cytology.

Primary urinary bladder adenocarcinoma.description: Primary bladder adenocarcinoma is an uncommon gland-forming carcinoma of the bladder, often arising near the trigone or bladder dome and potentially producing a mass with malignant glandular cells in urine or aspirate cytology.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic ex.normalized_text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic extension or metastasis
Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic ex.description: Colorectal adenocarcinoma is a common gland-forming cancer in older adults and can present with lower abdominal pain and a pelvic mass when locally advanced or metastatic.

Propylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxicity from propylene glycol, a solvent found in some intravenous medications and occasionally ingested products, causing high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hyperosmolality, elevated osmolality gap, and lactic acidosis.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Ethylene glycol is a toxic alcohol, commonly found in antifreeze, that produces an early osmolality gap followed by severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis as toxic metabolites accumulate.

Methanol poisoning.description: Methanol is a toxic alcohol that causes an elevated osmolality gap early and severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis after metabolism to formic acid; neurologic and visual toxicity are common.

Metformin-associated lactic acidosis.description: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is severe lactic acidosis occurring after metformin overdose or accumulation, especially in renal failure, hypoxia, shock, or liver dysfunction.

Cyanide poisoning.description: Cyanide toxicity inhibits cellular oxygen utilization and can rapidly cause severe lactic acidosis, altered consciousness, cardiovascular collapse, and respiratory failure.

diagnoses.icd11_title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site
