Ovarian yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus.normalized_text: Ovarian yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor)
Ovarian yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus.description: A highly malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor occurring mainly in children and adolescents. It typically presents as a rapidly enlarging unilateral adnexal mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. The pathology images are compatible with a yolk sac tumor, including reticular/microcystic architecture, Schiller-Duval body-like structures, and hyaline globules.

Ovarian dysgerminoma.description: A malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor that most often affects adolescents and young women. It usually forms a large unilateral solid ovarian mass and may cause abdominal pain, distension, and constitutional or inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.normalized_text: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.description: A sex-cord stromal ovarian tumor that occurs predominantly in children and adolescents. It may become large and present with abdominal pain or distension; many tumors produce estrogen and cause precocious puberty or abnormal uterine bleeding.

Ovarian torsion involving a large ovaria.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion involving a large ovarian neoplasm
Ovarian torsion involving a large ovaria.description: Twisting of the ovarian vascular pedicle, usually due to an enlarged ovary or ovarian mass, causing venous obstruction, edema, hemorrhagic infarction, and abdominal pain. The imaging appearance of a very large adnexal mass with possible twisted pedicle and hemorrhagic changes can suggest torsion complicating a tumor.

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, resulting in dermatan/heparan sulfate accumulation. Severe forms cause progressive developmental delay, coarse facial features, skeletal deformities and joint contractures; leukocytes may show coarse granulations (Alder-Reilly-like inclusions) on peripheral smear.

Mucolipidosis II alpha/beta (I-cell dise.description: A severe autosomal-recessive lysosomal trafficking disorder caused by defective mannose-6-phosphate targeting of lysosomal enzymes. It produces congenital skeletal abnormalities, joint contractures, coarse facial features, severe developmental delay and cellular inclusions/vacuolation.

GM1 gangliosidosis, late-infantile/type.description: A lysosomal storage disease caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency, leading to GM1 ganglioside accumulation in the brain and other tissues. The late-infantile form causes hypotonia, developmental delay or regression, seizures, dysmorphic/coarse facial features and skeletal abnormalities; vacuolated lymphocytes may be present.

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disease due to alpha-mannosidase deficiency. It commonly causes developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, coarse facial features, skeletal deformities, hearing impairment, immune dysfunction and vacuolated lymphocytes.

Fucosidosis.description: A rare autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency. It can cause progressive intellectual disability, hypotonia, seizures, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, recurrent infections, behavioral problems and cytoplasmic vacuoles in leukocytes.

Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis (verteb.normalized_text: Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis (vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis) with left psoas abscess
Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis (verteb.description: Bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral endplates, often causing severe back pain, fever, inflammatory-marker elevation, and extension into the psoas muscle as an abscess. The CT appearance is consistent with lumbar disc/endplate involvement and an adjacent left psoas collection.

Secondary iliopsoas abscess.description: A collection of pus within the iliopsoas muscle, usually caused by spread from nearby spinal, gastrointestinal, urinary, or pelvic infection. In this case, the psoas abnormality is likely secondary to adjacent lumbar spondylodiscitis.

Spinal epidural abscess complicating pyo.normalized_text: Spinal epidural abscess complicating pyogenic vertebral infection
Spinal epidural abscess complicating pyo.description: A purulent infection in the epidural space that may arise from vertebral osteomyelitis or bacteremia. It presents with fever and focal spinal pain and can progress to radicular pain, weakness, sensory loss, or bladder dysfunction; MRI is required to assess it reliably.

Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.normalized_text: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disease) with psoas abscess
Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine can cause vertebral destruction, disc-space disease, paraspinal or psoas abscesses, and constitutional symptoms. It is an important differential diagnosis for spondylodiscitis with a psoas collection, although the acute high-grade inflammatory presentation favors pyogenic infection.

Re-expansion pulmonary edema.description: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema occurring after rapid re-expansion of a chronically collapsed lung following thoracentesis or drainage of a large pleural effusion. Imaging commonly shows unilateral ground-glass and alveolar opacities in the re-expanded lung.

Aspiration pneumonia.description: Pulmonary infection or chemical pneumonitis caused by aspiration of gastric or oropharyngeal contents, often producing dependent unilateral consolidation and hypoxemic respiratory symptoms.

Hospital-acquired or community-acquired.description: Infectious inflammation of lung parenchyma that may cause focal or multilobar consolidation, cough, crackles, tachypnea, and hypoxemic respiratory failure.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema.description: Pulmonary interstitial and alveolar fluid accumulation due to elevated cardiac filling pressures, usually causing dyspnea, crackles, hypoxemia, and bilateral perihilar or diffuse pulmonary opacities.

Multifocal fibromuscular dysplasia invol.normalized_text: Multifocal fibromuscular dysplasia involving the renal and right iliac arteries
Multifocal fibromuscular dysplasia invol.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arteriopathy affecting medium-sized arteries, classically producing a 'string-of-beads' angiographic appearance from alternating stenoses and small aneurysmal dilatations. Renal artery involvement can cause hypertension, while iliac involvement can cause exertional claudication.

Right external iliac artery fibromuscula.normalized_text: Right external iliac artery fibromuscular dysplasia causing proximal lower-extremity claudication
Right external iliac artery fibromuscula.description: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the external iliac artery may produce segmental arterial stenoses and beading, limiting blood flow to the buttock and thigh during exertion. It may occur with fibromuscular dysplasia in other vascular beds, particularly the renal arteries.

Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia cau.normalized_text: Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia causing renovascular hypertension
Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia cau.description: Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia is a common cause of secondary hypertension in women and typically has a multifocal 'string-of-beads' appearance on angiography. It may coexist with fibromuscular dysplasia in iliac, carotid, vertebral, or other medium-sized arteries.

Atherosclerotic aortoiliac peripheral ar.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the aortoiliac arteries can cause buttock, hip, or thigh claudication due to reduced blood flow during exertion. It is more common in patients with smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, or advanced age.

External iliac artery endofibrosis.description: External iliac artery endofibrosis is a nonatherosclerotic arterial narrowing seen most often in high-level endurance athletes, particularly cyclists and runners. It causes exertional thigh, buttock, or leg symptoms, often with near-normal findings at rest.

Drug-induced torsades de pointes (polymo.normalized_text: Drug-induced torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia due to QT prolongation)
Drug-induced torsades de pointes (polymo.description: A potentially life-threatening polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that occurs in the setting of a prolonged QT interval. In this case, sotalol, potentiated by concomitant verapamil-related bradycardia, is a strong precipitating factor. The ECG shows prolonged repolarization followed by a rapid polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia with changing QRS axis/amplitude, consistent with torsades de pointes.

Sotalol-induced acquired long QT syndrom.description: An acquired prolongation of ventricular repolarization caused by medications, particularly class III antiarrhythmics such as sotalol. It predisposes to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes, especially in older women and in the presence of bradycardia or concomitant rate-slowing drugs.

Recurrent atrial tachycardia.description: A supraventricular tachyarrhythmia arising from an atrial focus or re-entry circuit. This patient has a prior history of recurrent atrial tachycardia after left atrial myxoma surgery and recently required cardioversion for persistent atrial tachycardia.

Systemic sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas. The chest radiograph suggests bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and the skin biopsy is consistent with noncaseating granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

Lofgren syndrome (acute sarcoidosis).description: An acute sarcoidosis phenotype classically characterized by bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, acute ankle-predominant arthritis or periarthritis, and fever.

Tuberculosis with cutaneous and musculos.normalized_text: Tuberculosis with cutaneous and musculoskeletal involvement
Tuberculosis with cutaneous and musculos.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can produce fever, lymphadenopathy, granulomatous skin lesions, hepatomegaly, and inflammatory arthritis; tissue granulomas are often caseating but may occasionally appear noncaseating.

Disseminated fungal infection causing gr.normalized_text: Disseminated fungal infection causing granulomatous disease
Disseminated fungal infection causing gr.description: Disseminated fungal infections, such as histoplasmosis, can cause fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, skin lesions, and granulomatous inflammation, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis.description: A rare systemic histiocytic disorder causing papulonodular skin lesions and destructive inflammatory polyarthritis, usually affecting the hands and face and often associated with malignancy.

Kienböck disease (avascular necrosis/ost.normalized_text: Kienböck disease (avascular necrosis/osteonecrosis of the lunate)
Kienböck disease (avascular necrosis/ost.description: Osteonecrosis of the lunate bone caused by impaired blood supply. The coronal wrist MRI shows abnormal low marrow signal in the lunate relative to the surrounding carpal bones, supporting lunate osteonecrosis.

Treatment-associated osteonecrosis of th.description: Medication- or cancer-treatment-associated impairment of bone vascularity can cause focal osteonecrosis. In this case, the imaging appearance is most consistent with lunate osteonecrosis, while the absence of corticosteroid or bisphosphonate exposure suggests another treatment-related or multifactorial mechanism.

Lunate stress injury or occult fracture.normalized_text: Lunate stress injury or occult fracture
Lunate stress injury or occult fracture.description: An occult carpal stress injury can produce wrist pain, tenderness, and marrow-signal abnormality on MRI. However, the relatively diffuse low signal of the lunate and the clinical context favor osteonecrosis over a fracture.

Menkes disease (ATP7A-related copper tra.description: An X-linked disorder of copper transport causing systemic copper deficiency, impaired copper-dependent enzymes, neurodegeneration, characteristic sparse/kinky hair, vascular tortuosity, and failure to thrive.

Occipital horn syndrome (mild ATP7A-rela.normalized_text: Occipital horn syndrome (mild ATP7A-related copper transport disorder)
Occipital horn syndrome (mild ATP7A-rela.description: A milder allelic form of ATP7A-related copper transport disease, characterized by connective-tissue abnormalities, vascular tortuosity, bladder diverticula, lax skin/joints, and sometimes low copper and ceruloplasmin.

Nutritional or acquired copper deficienc.description: Copper deficiency due to inadequate intake, malabsorption, excessive zinc exposure, or prolonged parenteral nutrition; it can cause low serum copper and ceruloplasmin, anemia, impaired growth, and neurologic dysfunction.

Adrenal oncocytoma.description: A rare adrenal cortical tumor composed of oncocytic cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. Most are nonfunctioning and are discovered incidentally; they may become large and can appear heterogeneous on imaging.

Adrenocortical adenoma.description: A common benign tumor of the adrenal cortex. Many adenomas are nonfunctioning incidentalomas, although some produce cortisol or aldosterone.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-producing tumor arising from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells. It may be incidentally detected and can be radiologically heterogeneous, especially when large; some tumors are biochemically silent.

Adrenocortical carcinoma.description: A rare malignant tumor of the adrenal cortex that often presents as a large enlarging adrenal mass. It may be hormonally functional or nonfunctioning and can cause symptoms from hormone secretion or local invasion.

Lupus erythematosus profundus (lupus pan.description: A chronic cutaneous lupus variant causing lymphocytic inflammation of subcutaneous fat, often producing firm indurated plaques, lipoatrophy, and scalp alopecia. The biopsy appearance of deep lymphocytic inflammation involving adipose tissue supports this diagnosis.

Linear morphea (linear scleroderma, incl.normalized_text: Linear morphea (linear scleroderma, including en coup de sabre variant)
Linear morphea (linear scleroderma, incl.description: A localized scleroderma subtype characterized by a linear band of skin thickening and fibrosis, commonly affecting the forehead and scalp in the en coup de sabre pattern and potentially causing hair loss.

Morphea profunda.description: A deep form of localized scleroderma involving the dermis, subcutis, fascia, or muscle, causing firm bound-down plaques and sometimes atrophy.

Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp.normalized_text: Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp
Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp.description: A chronic cutaneous lupus disorder that commonly affects sun-exposed skin and scalp, producing inflammatory plaques and potentially permanent scarring alopecia.

Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell ly.description: A rare cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that infiltrates subcutaneous adipose tissue and can clinically resemble inflammatory panniculitis, often with persistent plaques or nodules.

ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.normalized_text: ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus enteritis (mesenteric vasculitis) and intussusception
ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus can rarely be ANA-negative by indirect immunofluorescence, particularly when other lupus-specific antibodies are present. Lupus enteritis results from immune-complex-mediated small-vessel inflammation and bowel-wall edema, which may cause obstruction or intussusception. The imaging is consistent with dilated bowel loops and bowel-wall edema/target appearance compatible with intussusception or lupus enteritis.

Lupus-associated small-bowel intussuscep.description: Intussusception is telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, causing bowel obstruction, vomiting, abdominal pain, and a target-like appearance on CT. In lupus, bowel-wall edema from mesenteric vasculitis can act as a transient lead point.

Behçet disease with gastrointestinal inv.description: Behçet disease is a multisystem inflammatory vasculitis characterized primarily by recurrent oral and genital ulceration, ocular inflammation, skin lesions, and sometimes intestinal ulceration causing abdominal pain or obstruction.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.normalized_text: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) with gastrointestinal involvement
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: IgA vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis in children that can cause colicky abdominal pain, bowel-wall edema, gastrointestinal bleeding, and intussusception. It is usually associated with palpable purpura, arthralgia, and sometimes renal involvement.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.normalized_text: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) of the left anterior descending coronary artery
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: A nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma within a coronary artery wall that narrows the true lumen and can cause myocardial ischemia or infarction. The coronary angiogram is compatible with a long, smooth narrowing/dissection of the LAD.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) secondary to SCAD
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute myocardial infarction caused by reduced coronary blood flow without persistent diagnostic ST-segment elevation. In this case, the likely mechanism is LAD spontaneous coronary artery dissection rather than atherosclerotic plaque rupture.

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) with coron.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder that commonly affects renal and cerebrovascular arteries and is strongly associated with SCAD. The abdominal vascular images show multifocal arterial irregularity/beading compatible with renal-artery FMD.

Vascular connective-tissue disorder, inc.normalized_text: Vascular connective-tissue disorder, including vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Vascular connective-tissue disorder, inc.description: Inherited connective-tissue disorders can predispose to arterial fragility, aneurysm, and spontaneous arterial dissection. Although the family history specifically reports hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, the combination of arterial dissection and a family history of cerebral aneurysm warrants consideration of a vascular connective-tissue disorder.

Infantile achalasia.description: A rare esophageal motility disorder caused by impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. The contrast study appearance is consistent with a dilated esophagus and smooth distal tapering at the gastroesophageal junction ("bird-beak" appearance), with delayed passage into the stomach.

Congenital esophageal stenosis.description: A congenital fixed narrowing of the esophagus, often in the distal esophagus, which can cause impaired swallowing, proximal esophageal dilatation, feeding intolerance, and poor weight gain in infancy.

Esophageal stricture.description: Narrowing of the esophageal lumen, usually acquired from reflux injury, caustic exposure, infection, or prior instrumentation. It may produce feeding intolerance and poor growth due to obstruction of swallowed feeds.

Dermatomyositis with prominent facial, p.normalized_text: Dermatomyositis with prominent facial, pharyngeal, and subcutaneous edema (edematous dermatomyositis)
Dermatomyositis with prominent facial, p.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by immune-mediated skeletal-muscle inflammation, typically causing proximal weakness, elevated creatine kinase, dysphagia, and characteristic skin findings. Rarely, marked periorbital, facial, limb, and upper-airway edema can be a presenting feature. The MRI pattern of diffuse edema in facial, tongue, pharyngeal, and cervical muscles and the biopsy showing perivascular inflammation and MHC class I expression support this diagnosis.

Polymyositis / overlap inflammatory myop.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal skeletal-muscle weakness, myalgia, elevated muscle enzymes, and possible bulbar or pharyngeal muscle involvement. It may occur with positive ANA and may lack myositis-specific antibodies, although the marked edema and periorbital changes favor dermatomyositis over classic polymyositis.

Angioedema.description: Acute noninfectious swelling of deeper skin and mucosal tissues, often involving the eyelids, lips, tongue, pharynx, and larynx. It can cause throat tightness, voice change, and dysphagia. However, it does not explain the subsequent inflammatory myopathy, severe creatine kinase elevation, proximal weakness, MRI muscle inflammation, or biopsy findings.

Allergic contact dermatitis due to parap.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis due to paraphenylenediamine (PPD) in black henna tattoo
Allergic contact dermatitis due to parap.description: A delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to PPD, a common additive in black henna that intensifies and accelerates tattoo staining. It typically develops days to weeks after exposure and closely follows the tattoo design.

Bullous allergic contact dermatitis with.normalized_text: Bullous allergic contact dermatitis with secondary impetiginization
Bullous allergic contact dermatitis with.description: Severe allergic contact dermatitis causing vesicles or bullae, with secondary superficial bacterial infection—usually Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes—producing honey-colored or golden crusts.

Bullous impetigo.description: A superficial Staphylococcus aureus skin infection characterized by fragile flaccid bullae that rupture and leave erosions with yellow crusting. It may occur secondarily in skin damaged by dermatitis.

Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo.normalized_text: Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo chemicals
Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo.description: Inflammation caused by direct chemical injury to the skin from tattoo ingredients or solvents. It often causes burning, erythema, scaling, and occasionally blistering, generally soon after exposure.

Cellulitis complicating damaged tattooed.description: A bacterial infection of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually causing spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness, and swelling. It can complicate excoriated or blistered dermatitis.

Chronic tophaceous gout.description: Advanced gout caused by longstanding monosodium urate crystal deposition, producing large subcutaneous and periarticular tophi, erosive joint disease, and deformity.

Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nod.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that can cause symmetric hand deformities and firm subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules, usually over pressure points.

Calcinosis cutis / tumoral calcinosis.description: Deposition of calcium salts in skin and periarticular soft tissues, sometimes producing large calcified nodules around joints and restricting movement.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: A subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly affects young adults and typically presents with cervical/supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and a bulky anterior mediastinal mass. It is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells that are usually CD15-positive, CD30-positive, and CD45-negative, often within a background of fibrosis and mixed inflammatory cells.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in the anterior mediastinum, often causing a bulky mediastinal mass with respiratory symptoms. It is more common in young women and usually expresses B-cell markers such as CD20, PAX5, and CD45.

Mediastinal gray-zone lymphoma.description: A rare lymphoma with overlapping clinical, morphologic, and immunophenotypic features of classical Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma. It often involves the mediastinum and may express CD30 and sometimes CD15 along with B-cell markers.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma that can present with lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms. ALK-positive disease often affects younger patients, but the tumor cells typically express leukocyte and T-cell-associated markers rather than the classic Hodgkin immunophenotype.

T-lymphoblastic lymphoma.description: An aggressive immature T-cell neoplasm that frequently presents in adolescent or young adult males with a large anterior mediastinal mass, lymphadenopathy, and respiratory symptoms due to thymic involvement.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP/PC.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring most commonly in advanced HIV infection, typically causing subacute nonproductive cough, progressive dyspnea, hypoxemia, and bilateral diffuse interstitial or perihilar ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis.description: A viral opportunistic pneumonia seen in severely immunocompromised patients, including people with advanced HIV, which may produce diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates and respiratory symptoms.

Pulmonary tuberculosis in HIV infection.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can present atypically in HIV, with diffuse or lower-lung infiltrates rather than the classic upper-lobe cavitary pattern; cough and dyspnea may occur.

Atypical community-acquired pneumonia.description: Atypical bacterial or viral pneumonias can cause dry cough, dyspnea, and bilateral patchy or interstitial radiographic infiltrates, although HIV-associated opportunistic infection is more concerning in this setting.

Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis (l.normalized_text: Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis (likely from occult primary lung adenocarcinoma)
Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis (l.description: Diffuse infiltration of pulmonary lymphatic vessels by metastatic carcinoma, often from lung adenocarcinoma or another solid malignancy. CT typically shows asymmetric or unilateral interlobular septal and peribronchovascular thickening, sometimes with a small pleural effusion.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial circulation by thrombus, commonly causing acute or subacute dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope, and an elevated D-dimer. It may coexist with an underlying malignancy.

Unilateral pulmonary oedema due to cardi.normalized_text: Unilateral pulmonary oedema due to cardiac disease
Unilateral pulmonary oedema due to cardi.description: Pulmonary oedema is accumulation of fluid in the lung interstitium and alveoli, usually from elevated pulmonary venous pressure. It can produce septal thickening and pleural effusions; marked unilateral oedema is uncommon and may occur with asymmetric pulmonary venous flow or mitral regurgitation.

Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.normalized_text: Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with possible acute cardiopulmonary decompensation
Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.description: COPD is chronic airflow limitation, usually caused by cigarette smoking, and commonly produces progressive exertional dyspnoea. It may coexist with coronary disease, pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary embolism, or lung cancer.

Right hemidiaphragm eventration with com.normalized_text: Right hemidiaphragm eventration with compressive right middle/lower lobe atelectasis
Right hemidiaphragm eventration with com.description: Eventration is an abnormal, usually longstanding elevation of an intact hemidiaphragm due to thinning or weakness of diaphragmatic muscle. The chest radiograph and sagittal CT show marked smooth elevation of the right hemidiaphragm with compression/collapse of adjacent right lung.

Right unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis.description: Paralysis or marked weakness of the right phrenic nerve/hemidiaphragm causes elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and reduced ventilation of the ipsilateral lung. It may produce basal atelectasis and clinically important dyspnea, particularly in obese patients or those with underlying lung disease.

Compressive atelectasis of the right lun.normalized_text: Compressive atelectasis of the right lung secondary to elevated hemidiaphragm
Compressive atelectasis of the right lun.description: Atelectasis is partial collapse or underinflation of lung tissue. In this case, the elevated right hemidiaphragm compresses the adjacent lung, producing reduced basal ventilation and contributing to hypoxemia.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease ex.description: COPD is chronic airflow limitation, most commonly related to cigarette smoking. An acute exacerbation can cause worsening dyspnea, wheeze, and hypoxemia, often triggered by a viral upper-respiratory infection.

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL-NOS), activated B-cell phenotype
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can arise at extranodal sites, including the oral cavity and maxilla. The images show a soft-tissue maxillary mass and sheets of atypical large lymphoid cells; BCL6 and MUM1 positivity with limited/negative CD10 staining supports a non-germinal-center/activated B-cell phenotype.

Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin B-cell ly.normalized_text: Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma of the maxilla
Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin B-cell ly.description: A lymphoma originating in the maxillary alveolus, gingiva, palate, or adjacent soft tissues rather than in lymph nodes. DLBCL is the most common histologic subtype of oral/maxillary extranodal B-cell lymphoma.

Post-extraction odontogenic infection or.normalized_text: Post-extraction odontogenic infection or maxillary osteomyelitis
Post-extraction odontogenic infection or.description: Bacterial infection involving an extraction socket, maxillary alveolar bone, or adjacent soft tissues can produce swelling, delayed healing, and inflammatory marker elevation. It is an important clinical mimic of malignancy after dental extraction.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the maxilla/oral cavity
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: Colorectal carcinoma can rarely metastasize to the oral cavity or jaw and may present as a rapidly enlarging gingival or extraction-socket mass, particularly in a patient with a prior cancer history.

Plasmablastic lymphoma.description: An aggressive lymphoma with plasmablastic morphology that commonly involves the oral cavity, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It usually shows plasma-cell-associated markers and often lacks conventional B-cell marker expression.

Tinea incognito (steroid-modified tinea.normalized_text: Tinea incognito (steroid-modified tinea corporis and tinea cruris)
Tinea incognito (steroid-modified tinea.description: A dermatophyte fungal infection whose usual ring-shaped, scaly border has been altered and allowed to spread by potent topical corticosteroid use. It commonly affects the groin, thighs, and trunk.

Extensive tinea corporis with tinea crur.normalized_text: Extensive tinea corporis with tinea cruris
Extensive tinea corporis with tinea crur.description: A superficial dermatophyte infection of glabrous skin and the groin, typically producing pruritic expanding annular plaques with an active scaly edge and relative central clearing.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption characterized by slowly enlarging ring-shaped erythematous lesions, sometimes with trailing scale inside the advancing border.

Nummular eczema (discoid dermatitis).description: A pruritic eczematous disorder causing coin-shaped erythematous, scaly plaques, often on the limbs; lesions may become widespread but usually lack a true advancing ring border.

Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (lin.description: An infiltrative gastric cancer, often composed of poorly cohesive/signet-ring cells, that diffusely thickens and stiffens the stomach wall and may cause gastric outlet obstruction without a discrete intraluminal mass.

Gastric signet-ring cell carcinoma.description: A subtype of diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma characterized histologically by mucin-containing signet-ring cells. It commonly infiltrates the gastric wall diffusely, producing linitis plastica and obstruction.

Gastric outlet obstruction due to infilt.normalized_text: Gastric outlet obstruction due to infiltrative gastric malignancy
Gastric outlet obstruction due to infilt.description: Mechanical obstruction at the distal stomach or pylorus caused by an infiltrating gastric tumor. This produces delayed gastric emptying, severe gastric retention, vomiting or nausea, and inability to tolerate oral intake.

Primary gastric lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the stomach that can cause wall thickening, enlarged folds, early satiety, and occasionally gastric outlet obstruction. It is a differential diagnosis for diffuse gastric infiltration but is less supported when pathology shows carcinoma-type cells.

Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytope.description: A rare inherited bone-marrow failure disorder caused most often by biallelic MPL variants, resulting in markedly reduced megakaryocytes and severe thrombocytopenia beginning at birth. The parent-child sequencing image supports consideration of an inherited genetic disorder.

Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocyt.description: An immune disorder in which maternal antibodies against paternally inherited fetal platelet antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal/neonatal platelets. It commonly presents in an otherwise healthy newborn with severe petechiae, purpura, and bruising.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome / X-linked thro.description: An X-linked inherited platelet disorder affecting males, caused by WAS gene variants. It can produce congenital thrombocytopenia with petechiae and bruising; eczema and immune dysfunction may develop later.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome.description: A rare inherited platelet adhesion disorder involving the GPIb-IX-V complex. It causes thrombocytopenia with giant platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding, including petechiae, bruising, and bleeding after procedures.

Neonatal thrombocytopenia due to materna.normalized_text: Neonatal thrombocytopenia due to maternal immune thrombocytopenia (maternal ITP-associated neonatal thrombocytopenia)
Neonatal thrombocytopenia due to materna.description: Maternal antiplatelet autoantibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal platelet destruction. Affected newborns may develop petechiae, purpura, and bruising soon after delivery.

Subacute/chronic subdural hematoma relat.normalized_text: Subacute/chronic subdural hematoma related to repetitive headbanging
Subacute/chronic subdural hematoma relat.description: A subdural hematoma is blood collected between the dura and brain surface, often from tearing of bridging veins after acceleration-deceleration forces. The CT appearance of a crescentic extra-axial collection and the delayed progressive headache after vigorous headbanging strongly support this diagnosis.

Traumatic cerebral contusion with associ.normalized_text: Traumatic cerebral contusion with associated intracranial hemorrhage
Traumatic cerebral contusion with associ.description: A cerebral contusion is bruising and bleeding within brain tissue caused by rapid head acceleration or deceleration. Temporal and frontal regions are common sites, and contusions may coexist with subdural bleeding after repetitive head movement.

Acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma.description: An acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma occurs when recent bleeding develops into a pre-existing or evolving chronic subdural collection. It can cause progressively worsening headache and may follow seemingly minor or repetitive mechanical head trauma.

Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.normalized_text: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor (pPNET) of the omentum or abdominal wall
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.description: A malignant small round cell sarcoma occurring in soft tissue rather than bone. It commonly harbors an EWSR1 gene rearrangement and may show neural/neuroendocrine marker expression, including synaptophysin and PGP9.5. The imaging shows a sizable anterior intra-abdominal/abdominal-wall soft-tissue mass.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor (DSR.description: A rare aggressive small round cell sarcoma that usually arises in the peritoneum or omentum of young people and can present as an abdominal mass. It is genetically characterized by an EWSR1-WT1 fusion rather than the classic Ewing-family fusion.

Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine car.description: An aggressive epithelial malignancy composed of poorly differentiated neuroendocrine cells, often arising in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, or other organs. These tumors typically express neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).normalized_text: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) secondary to dabrafenib plus trametinib
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by excessive activation of macrophages and T cells, resulting in cytokine release, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and hyperferritinemia. In this case, the rapid onset after dabrafenib-trametinib strongly supports drug-associated HLH.

Dabrafenib-trametinib-associated drug hy.normalized_text: Dabrafenib-trametinib-associated drug hypersensitivity reaction with rash
Dabrafenib-trametinib-associated drug hy.description: A medication-related immune reaction to BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy that can produce fever, diffuse morbilliform erythema, liver injury, and systemic inflammation. Severe reactions may overlap with or trigger HLH.

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.normalized_text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.description: A severe delayed drug hypersensitivity syndrome characterized by fever, widespread rash, hematologic abnormalities, and internal-organ involvement, especially hepatitis. It can occasionally be associated with hemophagocytic syndromes.

Malignancy-associated hemophagocytic lym.description: HLH can be triggered by advanced malignancy, including metastatic melanoma, through tumor-driven immune dysregulation. It produces the same inflammatory and hematologic pattern as drug-induced HLH.

Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to tran.normalized_text: Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to transorbital gunshot injury involving the sellar/pituitary region
Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to tran.description: Loss of multiple anterior pituitary hormone functions caused by direct traumatic injury to the pituitary gland or pituitary stalk. Imaging shows a retained metallic projectile in the central skull base/sellar region, supporting pituitary-region trauma.

Central adrenal insufficiency (secondary.description: Adrenal cortisol deficiency resulting from inadequate pituitary ACTH secretion, most likely from traumatic pituitary damage. It can be life-threatening during acute illness or trauma.

Central hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.description: Deficient gonadotropin secretion from pituitary or hypothalamic injury causes inadequate testosterone production and delayed or arrested pubertal development.

Central hypothyroidism due to traumatic.normalized_text: Central hypothyroidism due to traumatic pituitary dysfunction
Central hypothyroidism due to traumatic.description: Insufficient pituitary TSH stimulation of the thyroid gland, producing low free thyroxine with a TSH level that is inappropriately normal or low rather than elevated.

Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congeni.normalized_text: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congenital aqueductal stenosis
Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congeni.description: Cerebrospinal-fluid flow is blocked at the cerebral aqueduct, producing enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles with relative sparing of the fourth ventricle. The MRI appearance is consistent with severe triventricular hydrocephalus and aqueductal obstruction.

Raised intracranial pressure secondary t.normalized_text: Raised intracranial pressure secondary to severe hydrocephalus
Raised intracranial pressure secondary t.description: Increased intracranial pressure occurs when excessive cerebrospinal fluid enlarges the ventricles and stretches the skull in infants with open sutures and fontanelles. It can cause episodic vomiting, somnolence, developmental decline, and motor abnormalities.

Hydrocephalus-associated seizures or sei.description: Severe hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure can lower the seizure threshold. The reported brief symmetric shaking events may represent epileptic myoclonus, tremulousness, or another seizure-like phenomenon, although EEG would be needed for confirmation.

Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome).description: A form of secondary hypertension caused by autonomous excess aldosterone production, usually from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. It commonly produces hypertension with suppressed renin and an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

Obstructive sleep apnea-associated hyper.description: Obstructive sleep apnea can cause persistent and resistant hypertension through recurrent nocturnal hypoxia, sympathetic nervous system activation, and sleep fragmentation.

Essential (primary) hypertension.description: Essential hypertension is the most common form of hypertension and is multifactorial, influenced by obesity, smoking, sleep apnea, genetic susceptibility, diet, and lifestyle factors.

Cushing syndrome.description: Cushing syndrome results from chronic glucocorticoid excess and may cause hypertension, weight gain, fatigue, glucose intolerance, proximal muscle weakness, and characteristic physical features.

Pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma.description: These catecholamine-secreting tumors can cause episodic or sustained hypertension, headaches, palpitations, sweating, anxiety, and tachycardia.

Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmet.normalized_text: Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmetal angina) causing acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction
Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmet.description: Transient intense constriction of an epicardial coronary artery, likely involving the left anterior descending artery, causing severe ischemia, ST elevation, myocardial injury, and potentially malignant ventricular arrhythmia/cardiac arrest.

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction due to acute left anterior descending coronary artery occlusion
Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute interruption of blood flow in the left anterior descending coronary artery, most often from plaque rupture and thrombosis, producing anterior myocardial infarction and risk of ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest.

Sumatriptan-associated coronary vasospas.normalized_text: Sumatriptan-associated coronary vasospasm with myocardial infarction
Sumatriptan-associated coronary vasospas.description: A medication-triggered coronary vasospastic reaction caused by a triptan, which can constrict coronary arteries and produce transient ST elevation, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, or cardiac arrest even in patients without obstructive coronary disease.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: A nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma within a coronary artery that can abruptly obstruct coronary blood flow, causing acute myocardial infarction, ST elevation, and ventricular arrhythmias; it occurs disproportionately in women.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.normalized_text: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) with megacolon
Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.description: Functional obstruction of the colon caused by severe autonomic and neuromuscular dysmotility without a mechanical obstructing lesion. It can cause massive colonic dilatation, ischemia, and perforation.

Fecal impaction causing acute large-bowe.normalized_text: Fecal impaction causing acute large-bowel obstruction (fecaloma-associated megacolon)
Fecal impaction causing acute large-bowe.description: A large, hardened accumulation of stool obstructs the distal colon or rectum, producing proximal colonic dilatation, vomiting, abdominal pain, and potentially ischemia or perforation.

Stercoral colitis with impending or cont.normalized_text: Stercoral colitis with impending or contained colonic perforation
Stercoral colitis with impending or cont.description: Inflammation, pressure necrosis, ulceration, and possible perforation of the colon caused by prolonged fecal impaction. It occurs particularly in patients with chronic constipation and neurologic impairment.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; A.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis, usually associated with cytoplasmic ANCA/PR3-ANCA, that can involve the lungs, kidneys, upper airways, joints, eyes, and nervous system. The CT abnormalities may represent pulmonary capillaritis/alveolar hemorrhage or inflammatory pulmonary nodules, and the immunofluorescence image is compatible with ANCA staining.

Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA).description: A pauci-immune ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis, commonly associated with MPO-ANCA, that frequently causes pulmonary capillaritis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.normalized_text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (anti-GBM disease/Goodpasture syndrome)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.description: An autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome caused by antibodies directed against the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. It produces rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage, often with diffuse ground-glass lung opacities.

Legionella pneumonia with neurologic man.description: Legionella is an atypical bacterial pneumonia acquired from contaminated water aerosols or healthcare-associated water systems. It can cause fever, cough, dyspnea, headache, myalgias, hyponatremia, and occasionally encephalopathy or aseptic-meningitis-like symptoms.

Renal-limited thrombotic microangiopathy.description: A renal vascular injury pattern caused by endothelial damage, platelet-rich microthrombi, arteriolar intimal swelling or concentric 'onion-skin' thickening, and glomerular ischemia. The biopsy images are most consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy, including vascular thrombotic/occlusive lesions and endothelial injury on electron microscopy.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A complement-mediated form of thrombotic microangiopathy that predominantly affects the kidneys and may occur without diarrheal illness. It causes microvascular thrombosis, hemolytic anemia, acute kidney injury, hematuria, and proteinuria; some cases are renal-limited.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A systemic thrombotic microangiopathy usually caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, leading to platelet-rich microthrombi, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and variable renal, neurologic, and febrile manifestations.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomeruli, producing fibrinoid vascular injury, thrombotic microangiopathy, ischemic glomerular collapse, renal dysfunction, hematuria, and proteinuria.

Uterine arteriovenous malformation (acqu.description: An abnormal high-flow connection between uterine arteries and veins, often acquired after pregnancy-related uterine trauma such as miscarriage, curettage, or delivery. It can cause recurrent, severe, sometimes life-threatening uterine bleeding.

Retained products of conception.description: Persistent placental or fetal tissue within the uterus after miscarriage, which may remain vascular and cause prolonged or heavy vaginal bleeding.

Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm.description: A contained injury to a uterine arterial wall that forms a vascular sac and can rupture intermittently, causing sudden severe vaginal bleeding. It may occur after miscarriage, uterine instrumentation, or pregnancy.

Gestational trophoblastic disease (persi.description: Abnormal persistence or proliferation of pregnancy-related trophoblastic tissue after a pregnancy event, which can present with irregular or heavy bleeding and a highly vascular uterine lesion.

Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infec.description: A recurrence of antibiotic-associated C. difficile infection causing toxin-mediated colitis, often occurring within weeks after an initial episode.

Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome.description: A functional bowel disorder that can develop after infectious gastroenteritis or colitis, characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits.

Asymptomatic Clostridioides difficile co.normalized_text: Asymptomatic Clostridioides difficile colonization with post-infectious bowel symptoms
Asymptomatic Clostridioides difficile co.description: Presence of C. difficile detected by PCR without active toxin-mediated infection; bowel symptoms may instead be due to post-infectious dysmotility or irritable bowel syndrome.

Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not cause.normalized_text: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not caused by Clostridioides difficile
Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not cause.description: Diarrhea related to disruption of normal intestinal microbiota by antibiotic treatment, usually mild and self-limited, without toxin-mediated colitis.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, especially severe in advanced HIV/AIDS. It can involve the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, lymph nodes, bone marrow, skin, liver, and spleen, and may produce diffuse pulmonary micronodules.

Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary pulmonary tuberculosis
Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.description: Hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing innumerable tiny lung nodules and possible involvement of lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, abdomen, and other organs. It is common in profoundly immunocompromised patients.

Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex.description: Disseminated infection with nontuberculous mycobacteria, usually occurring in patients with AIDS and CD4 counts below 50/mm3. It commonly causes fever, weight loss, anemia, hepatosplenic disease, lymphadenopathy, and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia in advanced HIV/AIDS, usually producing progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, fever, hypoxemia, and bilateral diffuse ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates.

AIDS-related lymphoma, such as non-Hodgk.normalized_text: AIDS-related lymphoma, such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma
AIDS-related lymphoma, such as non-Hodgk.description: Aggressive B-cell lymphomas can occur in advanced HIV and may involve lymph nodes, gastrointestinal organs, bone marrow, lungs, and abdominal lymph nodes. They often cause constitutional symptoms and abdominal pain.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) wi.normalized_text: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) with cutaneous involvement
Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) wi.description: An aggressive mature CD4-positive T-cell neoplasm caused by HTLV-1 infection. It commonly affects people from HTLV-1-endemic regions, including the Caribbean, and may produce pruritic papules, patches, plaques, tumors, lymphadenopathy, and systemic symptoms. The biopsy appearance of epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes is compatible with cutaneous involvement by a T-cell lymphoma.

Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymp.description: Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. It typically presents with slowly progressive pruritic patches and plaques and shows epidermotropism of atypical T lymphocytes, sometimes with Pautrier microabscesses, on skin biopsy.

Secondary syphilis.description: Secondary syphilis is a systemic manifestation of Treponema pallidum infection that may cause a diffuse papulosquamous eruption, often including the palms and soles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and constitutional symptoms. It is an important clinical mimic of cutaneous lymphoma.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive autoimmune inflammatory myocarditis characterized histologically by myocardial necrosis, lymphocytic inflammation, and multinucleated giant cells. It can cause ventricular arrhythmias, atrioventricular block, heart failure, and sudden cardiac death. The biopsy image is most consistent with giant cell myocarditis.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation involving the myocardium that may produce ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease, myocardial thickening or scar, and heart failure. Histology can show giant cells, although well-formed noncaseating granulomas would be more typical than the diffuse necrotizing giant-cell inflammation shown.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: An inherited disorder characterized by otherwise unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, often involving the interventricular septum, which can cause exertional chest pain, dyspnea, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.

Chronic coronary syndrome due to obstruc.normalized_text: Chronic coronary syndrome due to obstructive coronary artery disease
Chronic coronary syndrome due to obstruc.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries causing exertional myocardial ischemia, typically producing exertional chest pressure and dyspnea. Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity substantially increase risk.

Postoperative pyoderma gangrenosum.description: A rare neutrophilic inflammatory dermatosis causing rapidly progressive, painful sterile ulceration, often triggered by surgical trauma (pathergy). Cesarean-section wounds may enlarge and fail to heal despite antibiotics or debridement; lesions often have violaceous undermined borders and purulent-appearing bases.

Post-cesarean surgical-site infection wi.normalized_text: Post-cesarean surgical-site infection with wound dehiscence
Post-cesarean surgical-site infection wi.description: A bacterial infection involving a cesarean incision can cause fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis, wound separation, drainage, tissue breakdown, and delayed healing. Common organisms include polymicrobial genital-tract flora, Staphylococcus species, and streptococci.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (necro.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue that may occur after surgery or childbirth. It produces severe systemic illness, fever, rising inflammatory markers, tissue necrosis, and wound breakdown.

Intra-amniotic infection (chorioamnionit.description: Infection of the amniotic fluid, placenta, membranes, or uterine lining can cause maternal fever, uterine tenderness or pain, leukocytosis, fetal tachycardia, preterm labor, and postpartum fever. It may coexist with a postoperative wound complication.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) causing anterior cervical osteophyte compression
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.description: A noninflammatory disorder characterized by extensive flowing calcification and ossification along the anterior spine. Large anterior cervical osteophytes can mechanically compress the pharynx or esophagus, producing progressive dysphagia and aspiration. The image is suggestive of prominent anterior cervical bony overgrowth.

Cervical spondylosis with large anterior.normalized_text: Cervical spondylosis with large anterior cervical osteophytes
Cervical spondylosis with large anterior.description: Degenerative cervical spine disease can produce osteophytes. When unusually large, anterior osteophytes may indent the hypopharynx or cervical esophagus and cause swallowing difficulty, choking, and aspiration.

Ossification of the anterior longitudina.normalized_text: Ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament
Ossification of the anterior longitudina.description: Ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament, frequently occurring as part of DISH, may form a rigid bony prominence along the anterior cervical vertebrae. This can compress adjacent swallowing structures and lead to dysphagia and aspiration.

NUT carcinoma (NUTM1-rearranged poorly d.normalized_text: NUT carcinoma (NUTM1-rearranged poorly differentiated carcinoma of the mediastinum)
NUT carcinoma (NUTM1-rearranged poorly d.description: A rare, aggressive poorly differentiated carcinoma driven by a NUTM1 gene rearrangement, often arising in the midline thorax/mediastinum of young patients and frequently initially misclassified as thymic carcinoma.

Thymic carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the thymus, usually located in the anterior mediastinum. It can cause respiratory symptoms from compression of the lungs, airways, vessels, or pleura.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that commonly occurs in young women and presents as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass, often producing cough, dyspnea, and constitutional symptoms. Tissue flow cytometry can be nondiagnostic when the specimen is fibrotic or limited.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis type
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: A lymphoma that frequently affects young adults and may present with a large anterior mediastinal mass. Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma is especially common in young women and may have nondiagnostic flow cytometry because malignant Reed-Sternberg cells are sparse.

Mediastinal germ cell tumor.description: Primary mediastinal germ cell tumors arise in the anterior mediastinum and can become large enough to compress adjacent lungs and airways. Teratoma, seminoma, and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors are included in this category.

Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.normalized_text: Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (PBMAH) causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.description: A disorder characterized by bilateral adrenal enlargement with nodular hyperplasia and autonomous cortisol production, often presenting as mild or subclinical Cushing syndrome in older adults. The CT images show bilateral adrenal enlargement/nodularity.

ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to.normalized_text: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to.description: Endogenous cortisol excess caused by autonomous adrenal cortisol secretion rather than pituitary or ectopic ACTH stimulation. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is suggested by enlargement of both adrenal glands on the CT images.

Subclinical or mild autonomous cortisol.normalized_text: Subclinical or mild autonomous cortisol secretion from bilateral adrenal incidentalomas
Subclinical or mild autonomous cortisol.description: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion is a low-grade form of adrenal cortisol excess that may lack obvious classic Cushingoid appearance but can cause bruising, bone loss, metabolic complications, and abnormal cortisol suppression or circadian testing. Bilateral adrenal nodular lesions/enlargement support an adrenal source.

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.icd11_title: Glomerular disease associated with thin basement membrane nephropathy

Inferior vena cava thrombosis with bilat.normalized_text: Inferior vena cava thrombosis with bilateral iliac/renal venous thrombosis
Inferior vena cava thrombosis with bilat.description: Extensive thrombosis of the inferior vena cava and pelvic/renal venous drainage can cause severe bilateral lower-extremity edema, abdominal/flank pain, venous collateral formation, and abdominal wall/subcutaneous edema. The CT images show findings consistent with thrombosed central venous structures and extensive collateral veins.

Nephrotic syndrome.description: Nephrotic syndrome is heavy urinary protein loss due to glomerular disease, producing hypoalbuminemia, edema, and increased risk of venous thromboembolism, including renal-vein and inferior-vena-cava thrombosis.

Renal vein thrombosis.description: Renal vein thrombosis is a thrombotic occlusion of renal venous drainage, often associated with nephrotic syndrome. It may produce flank pain, hematuria, proteinuria, impaired renal drainage, and extension into the inferior vena cava.

Severe hypothyroidism (myxedema) contrib.description: Hypothyroidism can cause edema, weight gain, fatigue, serous-cavity effusions, and worsening of fluid retention. In this case it may contribute to edema but does not adequately explain the heavy proteinuria or CT evidence of extensive venous obstruction.

Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleo.normalized_text: Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis with cholestatic hepatitis
Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleo.description: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection can cause infectious mononucleosis with hepatitis, sometimes producing marked cholestasis and jaundice. Imaging may show periportal edema and gallbladder wall edema without biliary stones or duct obstruction.

Acute acalculous cholecystitis associate.normalized_text: Acute acalculous cholecystitis associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection
Acute acalculous cholecystitis associate.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones. It is an uncommon complication of Epstein-Barr virus infection and may result from gallbladder wall edema, biliary stasis, and systemic inflammation. Ultrasound and MRI can demonstrate gallbladder wall thickening/edema without calculi.

Acute bacterial cholangitis due to extra.normalized_text: Acute bacterial cholangitis due to extrahepatic biliary obstruction
Acute bacterial cholangitis due to extra.description: Cholangitis is infection of the biliary tract, usually caused by obstruction such as a common bile duct stone. It classically presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, but imaging generally shows biliary dilatation or an obstructing lesion.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal ar.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal arterial involvement
Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal ar.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause microaneurysms, stenoses, thrombosis, and renal infarctions. Renal angiography commonly shows multiple small aneurysms and irregular branch-vessel narrowing.

Renal infarction due to renal artery bra.normalized_text: Renal infarction due to renal artery branch thrombosis or embolism
Renal infarction due to renal artery bra.description: Acute interruption of renal arterial blood flow causes renal ischemia and infarction, producing sudden flank or abdominal pain, elevated LDH, kidney dysfunction, and wedge-shaped perfusion defects on contrast imaging.

Segmental arterial mediolysis (SAM).description: A rare noninflammatory arteriopathy of medium-sized abdominal visceral arteries that can produce arterial dissections, stenoses, aneurysms, thrombosis, and organ infarction, including renal infarction.

Fibromuscular dysplasia involving the re.normalized_text: Fibromuscular dysplasia involving the renal arteries
Fibromuscular dysplasia involving the re.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder causing alternating stenosis and dilation, often described as a string-of-beads appearance. It can rarely cause renal artery dissection, thrombosis, or renal infarction.

Ileocecal tuberculosis with tuberculous.normalized_text: Ileocecal tuberculosis with tuberculous aortitis (tuberculous mycotic abdominal aortic aneurysm)
Ileocecal tuberculosis with tuberculous.description: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis involving the ileocecal bowel and potentially the aortic wall, causing inflammatory aneurysmal degeneration. The imaging suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm with adjacent inflammatory change, ileocecal abnormality, and a pulmonary lesion compatible with disseminated or reactivated tuberculosis.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis involving the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly the ileocecal region, causing ulceration, bowel-wall thickening, abdominal pain, diarrhea, anorexia, and wasting. It may coexist with pulmonary tuberculosis.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma of the cecum o.normalized_text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma of the cecum or ascending colon
Colorectal adenocarcinoma of the cecum o.description: Cancer of the colon can present with constitutional symptoms, abdominal discomfort, altered bowel habits, and a mass or ulcerated lesion in the cecum/ascending colon. It may produce FDG uptake on PET imaging.

Amebic colitis (Entamoeba histolytica in.normalized_text: Amebic colitis (Entamoeba histolytica infection), possibly with ameboma
Amebic colitis (Entamoeba histolytica in.description: Invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection causes colitis with abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and colonic ulcerations. A mass-like inflammatory lesion, termed an ameboma, can occur in the cecum or ascending colon and mimic colon cancer.

Infected abdominal aortic aneurysm (myco.normalized_text: Infected abdominal aortic aneurysm (mycotic aneurysm), including Salmonella-associated infection
Infected abdominal aortic aneurysm (myco.description: A mycotic aneurysm is infection of the aortic wall resulting in rapid aneurysm formation, periaortic inflammation, pain, and risk of rupture. Elderly patients with diabetes and extensive atherosclerotic disease are at increased risk; Salmonella species are a classic cause.

Pancreatic panniculitis associated with.normalized_text: Pancreatic panniculitis associated with acute pancreatitis
Pancreatic panniculitis associated with.description: A rare form of lobular panniculitis caused by release of pancreatic enzymes into the bloodstream, leading to enzymatic fat necrosis in subcutaneous tissue. It is classically associated with acute pancreatitis, pancreatic pseudocyst, or pancreatic malignancy. The biopsy image is consistent with lobular fat necrosis with characteristic anucleate adipocytes ('ghost cells').

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas, commonly caused by alcohol use or gallstone disease. It typically presents with acute epigastric abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes; imaging may show pancreatic edema and peripancreatic inflammatory changes.

Erythema nodosum.description: A reactive inflammatory panniculitis that causes tender erythematous nodules, most commonly on the anterior lower legs. It is a septal panniculitis and may occur with infections, inflammatory disorders, medications, or systemic disease.

Multiple myeloma with extensive calvaria.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with extensive calvarial plasmacytoma
Multiple myeloma with extensive calvaria.description: A malignant clonal plasma-cell disorder causing monoclonal light-chain production, osteolytic bone disease, anemia, renal dysfunction, and hypercalcaemia. The skull mass represents an extensive osseous/extramedullary plasmacytoma involving the calvarium.

Macrofocal multiple myeloma.description: A variant of multiple myeloma characterized by multiple destructive bone or soft-tissue plasmacytomas despite relatively limited bone-marrow plasma-cell involvement. Monoclonal protein/light-chain production and end-organ injury may still occur.

Multiple osseous plasmacytomas.description: Plasmacytomas are localized masses of monoclonal plasma cells arising in bone or soft tissue. More than one osseous lesion, especially with systemic monoclonal light chains and CRAB features, generally represents systemic plasma-cell myeloma rather than truly isolated disease.

Solitary osseous plasmacytoma of the sku.normalized_text: Solitary osseous plasmacytoma of the skull
Solitary osseous plasmacytoma of the sku.description: A localized tumor of monoclonal plasma cells arising from a single bone, often presenting as a painless enlarging skull mass. It is distinguished from multiple myeloma by absent or minimal marrow involvement and no myeloma-related systemic end-organ damage.

Hepatic tuberculosis with tubercular liv.normalized_text: Hepatic tuberculosis with tubercular liver abscesses
Hepatic tuberculosis with tubercular liv.description: Tuberculous involvement of the liver can produce multiple hypodense nodules or larger coalescent abscess-like lesions with peripheral enhancement on contrast CT. It may occur as recurrence or reactivation in a patient with previous abdominal tuberculosis.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a bacterial collection of pus in the liver, often appearing on CT as a low-attenuation lesion with rim enhancement; multiple abscesses can occur.

Hepatic lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can involve the liver as solitary or multiple hypoattenuating masses and may cause abdominal pain, anorexia, and constitutional symptoms. In children, lymphomatous hepatic involvement is usually associated with nodal, splenic, or systemic disease.

Cholesterol embolization syndrome (ather.description: Systemic showering of cholesterol crystal emboli from disrupted atherosclerotic plaques, often after angiography or vascular surgery. It commonly causes blue/purple toes, livedo-like skin lesions, eosinophilia, and subacute kidney failure.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that can cause skin infarction, livedo reticularis, peripheral ischemia, renal injury, hypertension, and systemic inflammation.

Infective endocarditis with septic perip.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with septic peripheral emboli
Infective endocarditis with septic perip.description: Infection of a cardiac valve or endocardial surface that may produce embolic skin lesions, renal injury, neurologic manifestations, and systemic inflammatory findings.

Severe accidental hypothermia.description: A life-threatening reduction in core body temperature, often causing depressed consciousness, hypotension, marked bradycardia, and characteristic ECG J (Osborn) waves.

Myxedema coma.description: Decompensated severe hypothyroidism causing altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, and potentially respiratory failure.

Sepsis with hypothermia.description: Severe infection can produce altered mental status and shock; elderly patients may develop hypothermia rather than fever.

Hyperkalemia.description: An elevated serum potassium level can cause life-threatening bradyarrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, weakness, and altered mental status.

Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.normalized_text: Seronegative anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (atypical Goodpasture syndrome)
Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.description: An autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome caused by antibodies targeting basement membranes, usually producing diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Rarely, circulating anti-GBM antibodies are negative despite diagnostic linear IgG staining on tissue immunofluorescence.

Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis with.normalized_text: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis with mild renal immune-complex involvement
Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis with.description: A rare disorder characterized by recurrent diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, iron-deficiency anemia, and pulmonary hemosiderin deposition, usually without a defined autoimmune, infectious, cardiac, or renal cause.

ANCA-negative small-vessel vasculitis ca.normalized_text: ANCA-negative small-vessel vasculitis causing pulmonary capillaritis
ANCA-negative small-vessel vasculitis ca.description: A small-vessel inflammatory vasculitis can cause pulmonary capillaritis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis. Although commonly ANCA-positive, some cases are ANCA-negative.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (lupus pneumonitis/capillaritis)
Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus can produce immune-complex glomerulonephritis and, rarely, life-threatening diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Neurologic lupus may cause seizures and focal deficits.

IgA vasculitis or IgA nephropathy with d.normalized_text: IgA vasculitis or IgA nephropathy with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
IgA vasculitis or IgA nephropathy with d.description: IgA-mediated disease primarily affects the kidneys but can rarely involve pulmonary capillaries, causing hemoptysis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage; neurologic events are uncommon.

Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular ge.normalized_text: Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular germ-cell tumor (mixed germ-cell tumor) with gastrointestinal metastasis
Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular ge.description: An aggressive testicular cancer containing nonseminomatous elements, often including yolk-sac tumor and embryonal carcinoma, that can spread through retroperitoneal lymph nodes and rarely metastasize to the stomach or duodenum, causing ulceration and bleeding.

Testicular yolk-sac tumor with metastati.normalized_text: Testicular yolk-sac tumor with metastatic gastrointestinal involvement
Testicular yolk-sac tumor with metastati.description: A nonseminomatous germ-cell tumor characterized by production of alpha-fetoprotein. In adults it commonly occurs as part of a mixed testicular germ-cell tumor and may spread to retroperitoneal lymph nodes and distant organs.

Testicular choriocarcinoma or mixed germ.normalized_text: Testicular choriocarcinoma or mixed germ-cell tumor with choriocarcinoma component
Testicular choriocarcinoma or mixed germ.description: A highly vascular nonseminomatous germ-cell tumor component that produces beta-human chorionic gonadotropin and has a strong tendency toward hematogenous metastasis and hemorrhage, including bleeding from gastrointestinal metastases.

NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease wi.normalized_text: NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease wi.description: Gastric or duodenal mucosal injury caused by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which can produce painful ulcers, melena, and iron-deficiency anemia.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens.description: A severe form of extensive deep venous thrombosis causing near-total venous outflow obstruction, massive edema, cyanosis, pain, and potentially limb-threatening arterial compromise.

Extensive acute right iliofemoral deep v.normalized_text: Extensive acute right iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
Extensive acute right iliofemoral deep v.description: Acute thrombosis involving the deep veins of the lower extremity, especially the femoral and iliac venous system, producing unilateral pain, swelling, and venous congestion.

Gastric adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the stomach. Advanced gastric adenocarcinoma can cause weight loss and can produce a hypercoagulable state associated with venous thrombosis.

Malignancy-associated hypercoagulability.description: A cancer-related prothrombotic state in which occult or advanced malignancy, particularly adenocarcinoma, leads to recurrent or unusually extensive venous thromboembolism.

Penile leishmaniasis due to Leishmania d.normalized_text: Penile leishmaniasis due to Leishmania donovani complex
Penile leishmaniasis due to Leishmania d.description: A rare extrapulmonary manifestation of leishmaniasis in which amastigote-filled macrophages infiltrate penile/cavernosal tissue, potentially causing painful priapism. The histology is consistent with intracellular small oval organisms with kinetoplast-like structures, and the imaging shows metabolically active penile involvement.

Visceral leishmaniasis with isolated gen.normalized_text: Visceral leishmaniasis with isolated genital involvement
Visceral leishmaniasis with isolated gen.description: Visceral leishmaniasis is a systemic infection caused mainly by Leishmania donovani in South Asia. It usually affects the reticuloendothelial system but can rarely involve unusual sites such as the penis and corpora cavernosa.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with penile.description: Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection in which small intracellular yeast forms can be seen within macrophages and can resemble Leishmania on routine histology. Disseminated disease may produce fever and rare genitourinary involvement.

Struma ovarii with pseudo-Meigs syndrome.description: A rare monodermal ovarian teratoma composed predominantly of thyroid tissue. It may cause ascites, pleural effusion, marked CA-125 elevation, and occasionally pelvic radioiodine uptake despite normal cervical thyroid function.

Ovarian fibroma/thecoma with Meigs syndr.description: A benign sex-cord stromal ovarian tumor, often occurring in peri- or postmenopausal women, that can be associated with ascites and pleural effusion (Meigs syndrome). Fibrous tumors commonly show low T2 signal and enhancement.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma.description: Malignant epithelial ovarian tumors, particularly high-grade serous carcinoma, often present with an adnexal mass, ascites, abdominal symptoms, pleural effusion, and elevated CA-125.

Brenner tumor of the ovary.description: A usually benign epithelial ovarian tumor composed of transitional-type epithelium in a fibrous stroma. It can be solid, calcified, low on T2-weighted MRI, and may occasionally be associated with ascites or elevated CA-125.

Cervical spine chordoma.description: A rare, slow-growing but locally aggressive tumor derived from notochord remnants. It most often arises in the clivus, sacrum, or upper cervical spine and typically produces a destructive midline osseous mass with substantial soft-tissue extension.

Chondrosarcoma of the skull base or uppe.normalized_text: Chondrosarcoma of the skull base or upper cervical spine
