Chondrosarcoma of the skull base or uppe.description: A malignant cartilaginous tumor that can involve the skull base or cervical vertebrae. It may cause destructive bone change and a lobulated soft-tissue mass, although skull-base lesions are more often eccentric rather than strictly midline.

Primary bone lymphoma involving the cerv.normalized_text: Primary bone lymphoma involving the cervical spine
Primary bone lymphoma involving the cerv.description: Lymphoma can involve vertebral marrow and extend into adjacent epidural or paraspinal soft tissues. Radiographs may initially be unrevealing despite extensive marrow disease on MRI.

Cervical vertebral osteomyelitis/spondyl.description: Infection of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs can produce severe persistent neck pain, marrow edema or replacement, bony destruction, and prevertebral or epidural inflammatory soft tissue.

Metastatic disease involving the cervica.normalized_text: Metastatic disease involving the cervical spine
Metastatic disease involving the cervica.description: Metastases may infiltrate cervical vertebral marrow and create destructive lesions with epidural or paraspinal soft-tissue extension, causing persistent focal pain.

Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma.description: A benign congenital proliferation of dermal smooth-muscle bundles, often involving arrector pili muscles. It typically presents in infancy as a skin-colored or hyperpigmented plaque on the trunk, sometimes with hypertrichosis, firmness, or sweating.

Eccrine angiomatous hamartoma.description: A benign hamartoma composed of increased eccrine sweat glands and vascular structures, usually present at birth or during childhood. Localized hyperhidrosis is characteristic, and lesions may be painful, bluish, or nodular.

Fibrous hamartoma of infancy.description: A benign pediatric soft-tissue tumor that usually develops during the first two years of life as a painless, slowly enlarging, poorly circumscribed subcutaneous mass, commonly on the trunk or upper extremities.

Congenital melanocytic nevus.description: A benign melanocytic proliferation present at birth or appearing early in infancy, usually presenting as a pigmented plaque that may enlarge proportionally with the child and can develop hypertrichosis.

Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosi.normalized_text: Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis with pulmonary involvement
Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosi.description: A clonal histiocytic disorder that can involve skin, lungs, bone, liver, and other organs. Pulmonary disease characteristically produces a mixture of nodules, cavitated nodules, and irregular cysts, often most marked in the upper lungs; scalp lesions are a common cutaneous manifestation in children.

Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A lung-predominant form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterized on high-resolution CT by centrilobular nodules, cavitating nodules, and bizarre-shaped cysts, usually with relative sparing of the lung bases and costophrenic angles.

Cystic fibrosis with bronchiectasis.description: An inherited CFTR-related disease causing chronic suppurative airways disease, upper-lobe-predominant bronchiectasis, recurrent respiratory infection, nutritional impairment, and possible hepatobiliary disease.

Primary immunodeficiency with chronic su.normalized_text: Primary immunodeficiency with chronic suppurative lung disease, such as hyper-IgE syndrome
Primary immunodeficiency with chronic su.description: Some primary immunodeficiency disorders cause eczema-like skin disease, recurrent bacterial lung infections, pneumatoceles or bronchiectasis, and systemic inflammation. Hyper-IgE syndrome is one example, usually associated with markedly elevated IgE and eosinophilia.

Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.normalized_text: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (NST), grade 2, left breast
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.description: The most common form of invasive breast cancer, previously termed invasive ductal carcinoma. It arises from breast ducts and infiltrates surrounding breast tissue. In this case, biopsy has confirmed grade 2 invasive carcinoma NST.

Locally extensive or multifocal left bre.normalized_text: Locally extensive or multifocal left breast invasive carcinoma
Locally extensive or multifocal left bre.description: Breast MRI demonstrates a larger region of abnormal enhancement than may be visible on mammography, suggesting substantial local tumor extent and potentially multifocal or multicentric invasive disease within the left breast.

Internal mammary lymph-node metastasis f.normalized_text: Internal mammary lymph-node metastasis from left breast carcinoma
Internal mammary lymph-node metastasis f.description: Metastatic spread of breast carcinoma can involve internal mammary lymph nodes along the parasternal chest wall. The MRI images show a suspicious enhancing focus in the internal mammary nodal region, which may represent nodal metastatic involvement.

Hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy (.description: Dose- and duration-related toxic retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor injury caused by hydroxychloroquine, classically producing bilateral parafoveal damage, ring scotomas, and a bull's-eye macular appearance.

Cone-rod dystrophy.description: An inherited retinal degeneration in which cone dysfunction occurs first, causing impaired central vision, color vision deficits, photopsias, and progressive visual-field loss; pigmentary macular changes may resemble a bull's-eye pattern.

Age-related macular degeneration (dry/no.description: A degenerative macular disease of older adults characterized by drusen and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, resulting in central visual impairment and reduced contrast or color perception.

Cataract-related visual impairment.description: Lens opacification causing gradual painless reduction in visual acuity, glare, reduced contrast sensitivity, and sometimes reduced color discrimination.

Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, likely nodular.normalized_text: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, likely nodular sclerosis subtype, primary nasopharyngeal
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, likely nodular.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by rare Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background. The image shows large atypical cells with morphology compatible with Reed-Sternberg cells and immunoreactivity for CD30 and CD15, supporting classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Disease confined to the nasopharynx is consistent with stage IEA extranodal Hodgkin lymphoma.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma that can contain large pleomorphic malignant cells and may involve extranodal sites. It may mimic classic Hodgkin lymphoma histologically, but typical cases are usually CD15-negative and show T-cell-marker expression and/or ALK expression depending on subtype.

EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lympho.normalized_text: EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lympho.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that may occur in extranodal locations and can feature large atypical cells, occasionally with Hodgkin-like morphology. It generally requires confirmation of B-cell marker expression and Epstein-Barr virus positivity.

Ipilimumab-induced immune checkpoint inh.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory myocarditis caused by CTLA-4 checkpoint inhibition, potentially producing myocardial injury, ST-segment changes, arrhythmias, heart failure, and nonobstructive coronary angiography findings.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation of the myocardium, sometimes with associated pericardial inflammation, that can mimic acute myocardial infarction with chest pain, ST elevation, and troponin release despite unobstructed coronary arteries.

Acute coronary syndrome with nonobstruct.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Acute coronary syndrome with nonobstruct.description: Myocardial infarction or ischemic myocardial injury meeting acute coronary syndrome criteria but without a flow-limiting epicardial coronary obstruction; potential mechanisms include coronary spasm, microvascular dysfunction, embolism, or myocarditis mimicking infarction.

Stress-induced cardiomyopathy with dynam.normalized_text: Stress-induced cardiomyopathy with dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
Stress-induced cardiomyopathy with dynam.description: A catecholamine- and stress-associated transient cardiac syndrome that can cause chest pain, dyspnea, ECG changes, troponin elevation, systolic dysfunction, and dynamic LV outflow obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.

Syphilitic proctitis (anorectal secondar.description: Rectal infection with Treponema pallidum acquired through sexual contact, which can cause painful proctitis, rectal bleeding, fissure-like anal lesions, and inflammatory rectal mucosa. The biopsy pattern and brown spirochete immunostaining are highly supportive of this diagnosis.

Lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis (rect.normalized_text: Lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis (rectal Chlamydia trachomatis infection)
Lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis (rect.description: An invasive sexually transmitted rectal infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3, most commonly affecting men who have sex with men. It may cause painful proctitis, bleeding, rectal ulcers, and inflammatory endoscopic findings.

Herpes simplex virus proctitis.description: Sexually acquired HSV infection of the anus and rectum that can produce severe anorectal pain, painful defecation, rectal bleeding, ulcerations, and distal proctitis.

Inflammatory bowel disease, particularly.normalized_text: Inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn disease with perianal involvement
Inflammatory bowel disease, particularly.description: Crohn disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can involve the rectum and anus, producing proctitis, fissures, skin tags, rectal bleeding, and pain with defecation.

Gonococcal proctitis.description: Rectal infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae acquired through anal sexual contact. It can cause anorectal pain, rectal bleeding, inflammation, discharge, and tenesmus.

Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria.description: The presence of blood detected on urine testing without visible blood in the urine or urinary symptoms; it may be transient or due to urinary tract, kidney, or prostate conditions.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or u.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or upper urinary tract
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or u.description: Cancer arising from the lining of the bladder, ureters, or renal pelvis. Microscopic or visible hematuria can be the presenting finding, particularly in older adults.

Nephrolithiasis (kidney or ureteral ston.description: Mineral stones in the kidney or ureter that can cause microscopic hematuria, often with flank pain, nausea, or urinary symptoms.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia.description: Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that commonly occurs with aging and may occasionally be associated with hematuria or urinary obstruction symptoms.

Renal cell carcinoma.description: A kidney cancer that may present with microscopic hematuria; classic findings such as flank pain, a palpable mass, and visible hematuria are often absent early.

Congenital dysfibrinogenemia due to an F.normalized_text: Congenital dysfibrinogenemia due to an FGG gene variant
Congenital dysfibrinogenemia due to an F.description: An inherited qualitative fibrinogen disorder in which fibrinogen antigen concentration is normal or near normal, but the fibrinogen molecule functions poorly. The sequencing image indicates an FGG gene sequence abnormality, supporting a genetic fibrinogen disorder.

Congenital hypodysfibrinogenemia.description: A hereditary fibrinogen disorder characterized by both impaired fibrinogen function and reduced fibrinogen quantity. It may be caused by variants in FGA, FGB, or FGG and can cause bleeding, thrombosis, or no symptoms.

Congenital afibrinogenemia or severe hyp.description: A severe inherited quantitative fibrinogen deficiency that usually presents early in life with significant bleeding and markedly reduced or absent fibrinogen antigen and activity.

Acquired dysfibrinogenemia.description: An acquired qualitative fibrinogen abnormality, most often associated with liver disease, plasma-cell disorders, autoimmune disease, or certain medications. It can produce disproportionately low functional fibrinogen with a normal antigen concentration.

Large cell carcinoma of the lung (poorly.normalized_text: Large cell carcinoma of the lung (poorly differentiated non-small-cell lung carcinoma)
Large cell carcinoma of the lung (poorly.description: An aggressive non-small-cell lung cancer composed of large poorly differentiated malignant cells, often occurring in older heavy smokers. It may present as a central hilar mass with mediastinal invasion and metastases.

Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to.normalized_text: Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to malignant mediastinal compression
Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to.description: A syndrome caused by obstruction of the superior vena cava, most commonly from lung cancer or mediastinal malignancy, resulting in impaired venous drainage from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Imaging demonstrates severe SVC narrowing/occlusion with collateral venous channels.

Small-cell lung carcinoma.description: A highly aggressive neuroendocrine lung cancer strongly associated with cigarette smoking. It commonly arises centrally, causes bulky hilar and mediastinal disease, and frequently produces superior vena cava syndrome.

Pulmonary squamous cell carcinoma.description: A non-small-cell lung carcinoma associated with smoking that often arises in central bronchi. It can form an endobronchial obstructing mass and invade mediastinal structures, including the superior vena cava.

BCL11B-related severe combined immunodef.description: A genetic disorder caused by pathogenic BCL11B variants, characterized by impaired thymic T-cell development, severe T-cell lymphopenia or SCID, craniofacial dysmorphism, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, skin findings, and occasionally congenital anomalies.

FOXN1 deficiency (nude severe combined i.description: FOXN1 deficiency is an autosomal-recessive thymic epithelial-cell disorder causing profound T-cell immunodeficiency, absent or severely reduced TRECs, and ectodermal abnormalities involving hair, skin, and nails.

PAX1 deficiency (otofaciocervical syndro.normalized_text: PAX1 deficiency (otofaciocervical syndrome type 2 with severe T-cell immunodeficiency)
PAX1 deficiency (otofaciocervical syndro.description: Biallelic PAX1 deficiency can cause a syndromic form of severe T-cell immunodeficiency due to abnormal thymic development, often accompanied by craniofacial, skeletal, and other congenital developmental abnormalities.

22q11.2 deletion syndrome with severe th.normalized_text: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome with severe thymic hypoplasia or athymia
22q11.2 deletion syndrome with severe th.description: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome can cause variable T-cell lymphopenia from thymic hypoplasia; rare patients have congenital athymia and a SCID-like phenotype. Congenital heart defects, craniofacial differences, and neurologic abnormalities may coexist.

Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic RAG1/R.normalized_text: Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic RAG1/RAG2 or related SCID genes
Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic RAG1/R.description: Omenn syndrome is a form of leaky severe combined immunodeficiency in which impaired lymphocyte development is accompanied by inflammatory erythroderma, activated oligoclonal T cells, lymphadenopathy, and susceptibility to severe infection.

Primary colorectal extramedullary plasma.description: A rare localized plasma-cell neoplasm arising outside the bone marrow, which can involve the rectum or colon. The endoscopic lesions and biopsy appearance of dense plasma-cell infiltration support this diagnosis; normal serum protein studies and bone marrow findings support a primary extramedullary lesion rather than multiple myeloma.

Colonic plasmacytosis.description: A benign or reactive disorder characterized by prominent plasma-cell infiltration of colonic or rectal mucosa, potentially causing erythema, nodularity, mucus production, and defecatory urgency. Demonstration of polyclonal plasma cells would favor this over plasmacytoma.

Colorectal mucosa-associated lymphoid ti.normalized_text: Colorectal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation
Colorectal mucosa-associated lymphoid ti.description: An indolent extranodal B-cell lymphoma that may involve the colon or rectum and can show extensive plasmacytic differentiation. It may produce mucosal nodules or masses and can mimic a plasma-cell neoplasm on limited biopsy.

Ulcerative proctitis or ulcerative colit.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum. Plasma cells may be prominent in the lamina propria, particularly in chronic disease, and rectal involvement can cause tenesmus and mucus.

Intestinal tuberculosis involving the co.normalized_text: Intestinal tuberculosis involving the colon or rectum
Intestinal tuberculosis involving the co.description: Gastrointestinal infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can cause ulceration, strictures, nodules, and inflammatory bowel symptoms. Prior pulmonary tuberculosis increases clinical consideration, although the pathology shown would more typically demonstrate granulomatous inflammation rather than a predominantly plasma-cell infiltrate.

Acute pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial branches by thrombus, usually embolized from a deep venous thrombosis. The chest CT image shows intraluminal filling defects in bilateral pulmonary arterial branches consistent with pulmonary emboli.

Acute extensive left iliofemoral deep ve.normalized_text: Acute extensive left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
Acute extensive left iliofemoral deep ve.description: Acute thrombosis involving the deep veins of the left lower extremity and pelvic/iliac venous system. The pelvic CT image is consistent with thrombosis of the left iliac venous region, and the clinical presentation strongly supports extensive proximal DVT.

May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein co.normalized_text: May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein compression syndrome) with acute thrombosis
May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein co.description: An anatomic venous outflow disorder in which the left common iliac vein is compressed by the overlying right common iliac artery and adjacent spine, predisposing young women to left-sided iliofemoral DVT. The pelvic imaging and extensive left-sided proximal thrombosis are compatible with this condition.

Phlegmasia alba dolens due to extensive.normalized_text: Phlegmasia alba dolens due to extensive proximal DVT
Phlegmasia alba dolens due to extensive.description: A severe form of extensive iliofemoral deep venous thrombosis causing marked limb edema and pain from major venous outflow obstruction. It may progress to phlegmasia cerulea dolens if cyanosis and threatened limb perfusion develop.

X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by defective NADPH oxidase in phagocytes, resulting in impaired oxidative burst and susceptibility to recurrent severe bacterial and fungal infections. The absent/markedly reduced rhodamine oxidation response on flow cytometry and sequencing image are highly supportive.

Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatou.description: CGD can also result from autosomal recessive defects in NADPH oxidase components such as NCF1, NCF2, NCF4, or CYBA. It produces defective neutrophil oxidative burst and recurrent serious pulmonary and systemic infections.

Myeloperoxidase deficiency.description: A neutrophil enzyme deficiency that can cause abnormal oxidation-dependent fluorescence testing and, rarely, increased susceptibility to Candida infection. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic or have mild infections.

Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome).description: A primary immunodeficiency, often due to STAT3-pathway abnormalities, characterized by recurrent bacterial pneumonias, skin infections, markedly elevated IgE, eczema, and characteristic skeletal or dental findings.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A primary adenocarcinoma arising from the intrahepatic bile ducts. It commonly produces a desmoplastic gland-forming tumor on pathology and can present as multifocal liver masses with elevated CA 19-9.

Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcin.normalized_text: Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to the liver
Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcin.description: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is an aggressive gland-forming malignancy that frequently elevates CA 19-9 and metastasizes to the liver. It may cause epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma inv.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma involving the liver
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma inv.description: Colorectal adenocarcinoma commonly spreads hematogenously to the liver and can show gland-forming malignant cells on histology. A family history of early colon cancer raises concern for a hereditary colorectal cancer predisposition.

Parotid gland leiomyoma (vascular leiomy.description: A rare benign smooth-muscle tumor arising in or adjacent to the parotid gland, often from vascular smooth muscle. Histology typically shows bland spindle cells arranged in interlacing fascicles or whorls, with smooth-muscle-marker positivity and no malignant cytologic features.

Schwannoma of the intraparotid facial ne.normalized_text: Schwannoma of the intraparotid facial nerve or adjacent peripheral nerve
Schwannoma of the intraparotid facial ne.description: A benign nerve-sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells. It may present as a slow-growing parotid-region mass, usually with preserved facial nerve function, and histology can show spindle cells in fascicular arrangements.

Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.description: The most common benign salivary-gland tumor, generally presenting as a slow-growing, well-circumscribed and mobile parotid mass. It contains epithelial and myoepithelial elements in a variable stromal background.

Myoepithelioma of the parotid gland.description: A benign salivary-gland neoplasm composed predominantly of myoepithelial cells, which can have spindle-cell morphology and may resemble mesenchymal tumors on routine microscopy.

Low-grade fibromatosis or other benign f.normalized_text: Low-grade fibromatosis or other benign fibroblastic spindle-cell tumor
Low-grade fibromatosis or other benign f.description: Benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumors may form infiltrative or circumscribed spindle-cell masses in the head and neck. They can show fascicular spindle-cell proliferation but usually lack the vascular smooth-muscle differentiation of angioleiomyoma.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (Sanfilip.description: A lysosomal storage disorder causing progressive accumulation of heparan sulfate, with early developmental delay followed by severe neurodegeneration; somatic features may be milder than in other mucopolysaccharidoses. Brain MRI can show delayed or abnormal white-matter maturation, cerebral atrophy, and ventricular enlargement.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: An X-linked lysosomal disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, producing dermatan- and heparan-sulfate accumulation. It causes coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, developmental delay, and progressive neurologic decline; neuroimaging may demonstrate white-matter lesions and ventriculomegaly.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syn.normalized_text: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome / severe MPS I)
Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syn.description: A lysosomal storage disorder due to alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency. The severe form causes progressive developmental delay, coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, skeletal disease, and progressive neurologic involvement. MRI can show white-matter signal abnormalities, enlarged perivascular spaces, atrophy, and hydrocephalus or ventriculomegaly.

GM1 gangliosidosis type II (late-infanti.normalized_text: GM1 gangliosidosis type II (late-infantile GM1 gangliosidosis)
GM1 gangliosidosis type II (late-infanti.description: A neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disease caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency. The late-infantile form often begins between 1 and 3 years with developmental regression, progressive cognitive decline, dystonia, spasticity, hearing impairment, and coarse facial features. MRI may show delayed myelination, diffuse white-matter signal change, and cerebral atrophy.

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency. It produces intellectual disability, speech delay, hearing loss, coarse facies, skeletal abnormalities, immune dysfunction, and progressive motor impairment; MRI may show white-matter abnormalities and cerebral or cerebellar atrophy.

diagnoses.name: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis
diagnoses.icd11_title: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx[Bilateral]

Bilateral vocal fold paralysis.description: Immobility of both vocal folds, usually in a paramedian position, causing a markedly narrowed glottic airway. In neonates it can be congenital or associated with neurologic injury, hypoxic-ischemic injury, or birth trauma. The endoscopic images are compatible with a narrow glottic opening and impaired vocal-fold abduction.

Congenital bilateral vocal cord paralysi.description: A neonatal form of bilateral vocal-fold immobility present from birth or becoming apparent shortly after extubation. It commonly presents with stridor, respiratory distress, and difficulty weaning from ventilatory support; some cases are idiopathic and others are neurologic.

Posterior glottic stenosis or cricoaryte.normalized_text: Posterior glottic stenosis or cricoarytenoid fixation after intubation
Posterior glottic stenosis or cricoaryte.description: Scarring, inflammation, or fixation involving the posterior glottis and cricoarytenoid joints can prevent vocal-fold abduction and mimic bilateral vocal-fold paralysis. It may occur after traumatic or prolonged endotracheal intubation.

Laryngomalacia.description: A common congenital dynamic supraglottic airway disorder caused by collapse of immature supraglottic structures during inspiration. It usually causes inspiratory stridor that is worse with feeding, crying, or supine positioning.

Left piriform sinus fistula (third or fo.normalized_text: Left piriform sinus fistula (third or fourth branchial pouch anomaly) with recurrent cervical abscess
Left piriform sinus fistula (third or fo.description: A congenital epithelial tract arising from the piriform sinus, most often on the left, can permit pharyngeal bacteria to enter the neck or thyroid region and cause recurrent deep neck infections/abscesses. The CT appearance of a tract or air-containing inflammatory focus near the left hypopharynx supports this diagnosis.

Infected second branchial cleft cyst.description: A branchial cleft cyst is a congenital lateral neck cyst that may become infected, producing a tender neck mass, fever, and abscess formation. Second branchial cleft anomalies are the most common type and usually occur in the upper lateral neck.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis with thyro.normalized_text: Acute suppurative thyroiditis with thyroid abscess
Acute suppurative thyroiditis with thyro.description: Acute bacterial infection of the thyroid gland is uncommon but can cause fever, painful anterior neck swelling, and abscess formation. In young patients with recurrent left-sided disease, it may be secondary to an underlying piriform sinus fistula.

Drug-induced urticarial vasculitis (norm.description: A small-vessel immune-mediated skin vasculitis presenting with urticarial-appearing lesions that are painful or burning, persist for at least 24 hours, and may leave bruising or hyperpigmentation. It may be triggered by medications or supplements and can cause systemic symptoms.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: A medication-associated hypersensitivity reaction characterized by fever, urticarial or morbilliform rash, joint pain, muscle aches, and sometimes angioedema. Unlike true serum sickness, complement levels are often normal and major organ involvement is uncommon.

Acute drug-induced urticaria with angioe.description: An acute mast-cell-mediated eruption of transient itchy wheals, often caused by drugs, foods, infections, or supplements, with possible swelling of deeper tissues such as the hands, feet, lips, or eyelids.

Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.description: A systemic form of urticarial vasculitis associated with low complement levels and potentially with joint, eye, lung, kidney, or gastrointestinal involvement.

Adult-onset Still disease.description: A systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by high spiking fever, arthritis or arthralgia, myalgia, elevated inflammatory markers, and a transient salmon-colored rash.

Rapunzel syndrome (gastric trichobezoar.normalized_text: Rapunzel syndrome (gastric trichobezoar with intestinal extension)
Rapunzel syndrome (gastric trichobezoar.description: A large mass of swallowed hair (trichobezoar) fills the stomach and extends beyond the pylorus into the small intestine. The endoscopic and CT images show a large hair-containing gastric mass with a long tail, characteristic of Rapunzel syndrome.

Gastric trichobezoar.description: A trichobezoar is a compact intragastric accumulation of swallowed hair. It can cause gastric irritation, partial outlet obstruction, malnutrition, anemia, and vomiting; in this case the images indicate an exceptionally large trichobezoar.

Small-bowel obstruction due to bezoar ex.normalized_text: Small-bowel obstruction due to bezoar extension
Small-bowel obstruction due to bezoar ex.description: The intestinal tail of a gastric trichobezoar can mechanically obstruct the duodenum or small bowel, producing intermittent crampy pain, vomiting, constipation, dehydration, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Gastric outlet obstruction secondary to.normalized_text: Gastric outlet obstruction secondary to a large gastric bezoar
Gastric outlet obstruction secondary to.description: A large intragastric bezoar can obstruct gastric emptying at the pylorus, causing upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, poor oral intake, dehydration, and nutritional deficiencies.

Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with intestinal ileal tuberculosis and perforation
Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.description: Systemic infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing granulomatous disease in multiple organs. Ileal tuberculosis can produce ulceration, transmural inflammation, perforation, and fatal peritonitis; pulmonary and renal nodules may represent disseminated involvement.

Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria.normalized_text: Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, especially Mycobacterium avium complex
Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria.description: A systemic infection caused by environmental mycobacteria, often occurring in immunocompromised individuals. It may involve lungs, gastrointestinal tract, bone, kidney, and other organs, with abundant acid-fast bacilli in tissue.

Intestinal tuberculosis causing tubercul.description: Localized or disseminated tuberculosis involving the ileum, where it causes ulcerative granulomatous inflammation. Deep ulceration can penetrate the bowel wall and result in perforation, diffuse peritonitis, and sepsis.

Crohn disease with ileal ulceration and.normalized_text: Crohn disease with ileal ulceration and perforation
Crohn disease with ileal ulceration and.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that commonly affects the terminal ileum and may cause transmural inflammation, deep ulcers, strictures, fistulas, and rarely free bowel perforation. Granulomas can be present but are noncaseating and acid-fast organisms are not expected.

Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (refl.normalized_text: Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (reflex syncope with sinus pause)
Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (refl.description: A neurally mediated reflex causing increased vagal tone, producing hypotension, bradycardia or transient sinus arrest, and presyncopal symptoms. It is often triggered by pain, nausea, vomiting, emotional stress, dehydration, or medical procedures.

Acute coronary syndrome.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by reduced coronary blood flow, ranging from unstable angina to myocardial infarction. It commonly causes central chest discomfort with autonomic symptoms.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation of the myocardium and/or pericardium, often following a viral illness. It can cause chest pain, ECG repolarization changes, arrhythmias, and occasionally hemodynamic instability.

Gastroenteritis with dehydration trigger.normalized_text: Gastroenteritis with dehydration triggering a vasovagal episode
Gastroenteritis with dehydration trigger.description: An acute gastrointestinal infection can cause nausea, vomiting, reduced oral intake, and volume depletion. These factors can precipitate hypotension and reflex syncope in susceptible individuals.

Panic attack or hyperventilation syndrom.description: An acute anxiety-related episode may produce chest discomfort, dyspnea, sweating, dizziness, nausea, and paresthesias, particularly in the hands. Hyperventilation can amplify tingling and presyncope.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum (Hamman sy.description: Free air in the mediastinum occurring without trauma or an invasive procedure, often from alveolar rupture with air tracking along bronchovascular sheaths (the Macklin effect). The CT image shows mediastinal air adjacent to the trachea, and the clinical precordial crepitus with cervical subcutaneous emphysema is highly characteristic.

Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndro.normalized_text: Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome or other esophageal rupture)
Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndro.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus causing leakage of air and/or gastrointestinal contents into the mediastinum. It can produce pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema but usually follows forceful vomiting, instrumentation, or severe retching and may rapidly cause mediastinitis.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse, often presenting in young adults with sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. A pneumothorax can occasionally coexist with pneumomediastinum, but the provided radiograph does not show a pleural line or lung collapse.

Erythema migrans (early localized Lyme d.description: The characteristic expanding annular skin lesion of Lyme borreliosis, caused by Borrelia infection transmitted by Ixodes ticks. Serology can be negative early in infection and erythema migrans is primarily a clinical diagnosis.

Tinea corporis (ringworm).description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection that commonly causes an itchy, enlarging ring-shaped rash with a more active red edge and central clearing.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory skin eruption producing slowly enlarging annular red plaques, often on the trunk or proximal limbs; lesions may be mildly itchy and can persist for weeks to months.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis that forms annular plaques, usually from grouped papules, most often on hands, feet, elbows, or other extremities.

Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) w.normalized_text: Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) with transient coronary artery spasm
Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) w.description: Episodic myocardial ischemia caused by transient vasoconstriction of an epicardial coronary artery, often occurring at rest in the early morning. Smoking and alcohol can precipitate coronary spasm. Angiographic narrowing that resolves and intravascular imaging without major fixed plaque support this diagnosis.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction d.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction due to coronary vasospasm (vasospasm-related MINOCA)
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction d.description: A myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) can result from prolonged coronary vasospasm, causing transient ischemia and troponin release without a persistent occlusive atherosclerotic lesion.

Acute coronary syndrome from atheroscler.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome from atherosclerotic coronary artery disease
Acute coronary syndrome from atheroscler.description: Acute coronary syndrome occurs when coronary atherosclerotic plaque rupture, erosion, or thrombosis causes reduced coronary blood flow and myocardial ischemia or infarction.

Type 2 myocardial infarction or demand-r.normalized_text: Type 2 myocardial infarction or demand-related myocardial injury associated with anemia
Type 2 myocardial infarction or demand-r.description: Reduced oxygen delivery from significant anemia can contribute to myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch, producing ischemic chest discomfort and mild troponin elevation, particularly when another trigger such as tachycardia or coronary spasm is present.

Split-hand/foot malformation (ectrodacty.description: A congenital limb malformation characterized by absence or underdevelopment of central fingers and toes, producing a split-hand/split-foot appearance; it can occur with congenital absence of multiple teeth (oligodontia).

Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefti.normalized_text: Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting syndrome (EEC syndrome, TP63-related disorder)
Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefti.description: A TP63-related developmental disorder commonly causing split-hand/split-foot malformation, abnormalities of teeth and enamel, and variable ectodermal or cleft lip/palate findings. Expression is highly variable.

Acetazolamide embryopathy (teratogenic f.normalized_text: Acetazolamide embryopathy (teratogenic fetal exposure to acetazolamide)
Acetazolamide embryopathy (teratogenic f.description: A pattern of congenital abnormalities potentially associated with prenatal acetazolamide exposure. Reported concerns include fetal growth restriction and limb or craniofacial developmental abnormalities, although causality in individual cases can be difficult to establish.

TP63-related acro-dermato-ungual-lacrima.description: A TP63-related ectodermal dysplasia syndrome that may include ectrodactyly or syndactyly, hypodontia/oligodontia, enamel defects, nail abnormalities, skin findings and lacrimal-duct abnormalities; clefting is usually absent.

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.description: An intermittent cardiac arrhythmia characterized by chaotic atrial electrical activity and irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm that spontaneously terminates within 7 days, often causing episodic palpitations and breathlessness.

Alcohol-triggered atrial fibrillation (h.description: A form of atrial arrhythmia, commonly atrial fibrillation, precipitated by recent alcohol consumption, sometimes occurring even without chronic heavy alcohol use or structural heart disease.

Frequent premature atrial contractions w.normalized_text: Frequent premature atrial contractions with atrial tachyarrhythmia
Frequent premature atrial contractions w.description: Premature atrial contractions are early beats originating in the atria. A high burden of atrial ectopy, including couplets and short runs, can cause palpitations and may trigger atrial fibrillation or other supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.

Primary colorectal diffuse large B-cell.normalized_text: Primary colorectal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary colorectal diffuse large B-cell.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that can infiltrate the colon diffusely and cause ulceration, inflammatory-appearing mucosa, abdominal symptoms, and weight loss. The dense atypical lymphoid infiltrate and immunohistochemical staining in the images support a lymphoproliferative process.

Colorectal T-cell lymphoma / intestinal.normalized_text: Colorectal T-cell lymphoma / intestinal T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder
Colorectal T-cell lymphoma / intestinal.description: A lymphoid neoplasm involving the gastrointestinal tract that may present with chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and multifocal mucosal ulcers. Histology may show prominent atypical lymphocytic infiltration of the colonic mucosa.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous colonic mucosal inflammation, edema, loss of vascular pattern, granularity, friability, and superficial ulceration; it usually begins in the rectum and may involve the entire colon.

Crohn colitis.description: A form of Crohn disease limited predominantly to the colon, characterized by patchy inflammation, aphthous or irregular ulcers, weight loss, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. It can mimic infection or lymphoma endoscopically.

Cytomegalovirus colitis.description: An opportunistic viral colitis that can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and large irregular colonic ulcers, especially in immunocompromised patients or those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Diagnosis requires characteristic viral inclusions or positive CMV testing in biopsy tissue.

Left spontaneous hydropneumothorax.description: Presence of both air and fluid in the left pleural space, causing partial collapse of the left lung. The radiographs show a large left-sided horizontal air-fluid level and a visible pleural line with compressed lung.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with pl.normalized_text: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with pleural effusion
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with pl.description: A spontaneous leak of air into the pleural space, often from rupture of a subpleural bleb, accompanied by pleural fluid. In this case, the air-fluid level indicates a pneumothorax with associated effusion.

Spontaneous hemopneumothorax.description: A pneumothorax associated with blood in the pleural cavity, producing an air-fluid level and potentially causing acute respiratory compromise. It may occur from bleeding associated with rupture of pleural adhesions or a bleb.

Pyopneumothorax (empyema with bronchople.description: Air and infected fluid within the pleural space, usually resulting from pneumonia, empyema, or a bronchopleural fistula. It can produce a pleural air-fluid level and reduced breath sounds.

diagnoses.name: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
diagnoses.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver

Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.description: A localized monoclonal plasma-cell tumor occurring outside the bone marrow. Primary hepatic involvement is very rare. The liver lesion and plasma-cell-rich histology with plasma-cell immunophenotype support this diagnosis, while normal marrow, serum/urine immunoelectrophoresis, calcium, and skeletal survey support a solitary extramedullary process rather than systemic myeloma.

Multiple myeloma with hepatic plasmacyto.description: A systemic malignant plasma-cell disorder that may rarely involve the liver as a focal plasmacytoma or diffuse infiltration. It usually has bone marrow involvement, monoclonal protein production, lytic bone lesions, anemia, renal impairment, or hypercalcemia.

Primary hepatic lymphoma.description: A rare lymphoma predominantly involving the liver, usually presenting as a solitary or multiple hepatic mass. Imaging can overlap with other liver tumors, but histology generally shows atypical lymphoid cells rather than a monomorphic plasma-cell neoplasm.

Chlamydial cervicitis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis that may cause inflammation of the cervix and abnormal vaginal discharge; many cases are asymptomatic.

Gonococcal cervicitis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae that can cause cervicitis, mucopurulent vaginal discharge, pelvic discomfort, or urinary symptoms.

Trichomoniasis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, commonly producing vaginal discharge, irritation, odor, and sometimes painful urination or intercourse.

Bacterial vaginosis.description: An imbalance of normal vaginal bacteria that often causes thin vaginal discharge and a fishy odor; it is associated with sexual activity but is not necessarily a sexually transmitted infection.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis.description: A yeast infection, usually caused by Candida species, that commonly causes thick vaginal discharge with vulvar itching, redness, and irritation.

Vanishing lung syndrome (giant bullous e.description: A severe form of bullous emphysema in which giant air-filled bullae, usually upper-lobe predominant, occupy a large portion of a hemithorax and compress residual functioning lung. It is strongly associated with cigarette smoking and cannabis use.

Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.normalized_text: Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with bullous emphysema
Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.description: COPD/emphysema is chronic irreversible airflow obstruction caused most commonly by smoking. Destruction of alveolar walls may form bullae, including very large bullae in advanced disease.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.normalized_text: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to rupture of an emphysematous bulla
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.description: A spontaneous pneumothorax can occur when a subpleural bleb or emphysematous bulla ruptures, allowing air into the pleural space. It commonly presents with sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness and is more likely in smokers with emphysema.

Cannabis-associated bullous lung disease.description: Heavy cannabis inhalation has been associated with early-onset paraseptal emphysema, apical blebs, giant bullae, and spontaneous pneumothorax, especially when combined with tobacco smoking.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with an extremely high proliferation rate. It commonly produces bulky abdominal/retroperitoneal disease, marrow involvement, spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome, and a 'starry-sky' histologic pattern; the image findings are consistent with a high-grade CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults and may present with constitutional symptoms, abdominal masses, marrow involvement, elevated LDH, and tumor lysis syndrome. It is generally composed of larger atypical B cells rather than the classic uniform medium-sized cells of Burkitt lymphoma.

Plasma cell myeloma (multiple myeloma).description: A clonal plasma-cell malignancy that commonly causes anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and elevated serum protein due to monoclonal immunoglobulin production. It can cause bone lesions and marrow failure but does not usually produce a high-grade abdominal lymphoma mass or profound spontaneous tumor lysis.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoblast.description: A rapidly proliferative precursor lymphoid neoplasm that can cause cytopenias, high LDH, tumor lysis syndrome, organ infiltration, and occasionally bulky nodal or abdominal disease. It is distinguished from Burkitt lymphoma by precursor-cell morphology and immunophenotypic markers such as TdT.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.normalized_text: Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneous PAN) with mononeuritis multiplex
Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized arteries confined predominantly to the skin, sometimes with peripheral nerve involvement. The image shows livedoid/purpuric lesions, and the biopsy is compatible with necrotizing vasculitis of a muscular vessel.

Systemic polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that can cause skin purpura or livedo reticularis and mononeuritis multiplex, often with renal, gastrointestinal, muscular, or constitutional involvement.

ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy (f.normalized_text: ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy (for example microscopic polyangiitis)
ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy (f.description: Small-vessel systemic vasculitis may produce palpable purpura and painful asymmetric peripheral neuropathy or mononeuritis multiplex; it commonly affects the kidneys and/or lungs.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis that can cause lower-extremity purpura, peripheral neuropathy, arthralgia, renal disease, and systemic symptoms, often associated with hepatitis C or autoimmune disease.

Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.normalized_text: Classical homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency
Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of sulfur amino-acid metabolism causing markedly elevated homocysteine. It commonly produces a marfanoid skeletal phenotype, ectopia lentis/high myopia, osteoporosis, scoliosis, chest-wall deformity, and thromboembolic risk.

Homocystinuria due to a remethylation de.normalized_text: Homocystinuria due to a remethylation defect (for example, MTHFR deficiency or cobalamin-processing disorder)
Homocystinuria due to a remethylation de.description: A group of inherited disorders that impair conversion of homocysteine to methionine, producing severe hyperhomocysteinemia with normal or low methionine. Neurologic, psychiatric, hematologic, and vascular manifestations are common, although presentations vary.

Marfan syndrome.description: An autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder, usually caused by FBN1 variants, characterized by skeletal overgrowth, pectus deformity, scoliosis, ectopia lentis, myopia, and aortic-root disease.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome.description: A heritable connective-tissue disorder involving TGF-beta signaling, characterized by arterial aneurysm/tortuosity risk, pectus deformity, scoliosis, craniofacial abnormalities, and sometimes myopia.

Pontine hemorrhage due to a brainstem ca.normalized_text: Pontine hemorrhage due to a brainstem cavernous malformation (cavernoma)
Pontine hemorrhage due to a brainstem ca.description: A cavernous malformation is a cluster of fragile, low-flow blood vessels that can bleed repeatedly. In the pons, even a small hemorrhage can cause prominent long-tract, cerebellar, sensory, and ocular symptoms. The CT images show a focal hyperdense pontine lesion consistent with acute hemorrhage, with associated ventricular enlargement; MRI supports a focal brainstem hemorrhagic lesion.

Primary hypertensive pontine intracerebr.description: A pontine hemorrhage is bleeding within the pons, commonly related to chronic hypertension and rupture of small penetrating arteries. The focal pontine hyperdensity on CT is compatible with acute blood, and ventricular dilatation may reflect obstructive hydrocephalus from posterior fossa hemorrhage.

Posterior circulation ischemic stroke fr.normalized_text: Posterior circulation ischemic stroke from vertebral artery dissection, with hemorrhagic transformation
Posterior circulation ischemic stroke fr.description: Vertebral artery dissection can occur in young adults and often presents with unilateral neck pain or headache followed by posterior-circulation ischemia involving the brainstem or cerebellum. Infarcted tissue can occasionally undergo hemorrhagic transformation, producing a focal hyperdense area on CT.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with bone ma.normalized_text: Disseminated histoplasmosis with bone marrow involvement
Disseminated histoplasmosis with bone ma.description: Systemic infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. The images are compatible with small intracellular yeast forms within macrophages in bone marrow, highlighted by fungal staining, which is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania species, acquired through sandfly exposure. Amastigotes may be seen within macrophages in bone marrow and can resemble Histoplasma on routine microscopy.

Iliopsoas or pelvic pyomyositis with sep.normalized_text: Iliopsoas or pelvic pyomyositis with sepsis
Iliopsoas or pelvic pyomyositis with sep.description: Bacterial infection of pelvic or paraspinal muscles, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, producing fever, systemic illness, abdominal or back pain, and pain radiating to the groin. The pelvic imaging suggests inflammatory change involving pelvic musculature.

Genitourinary bacterial infection with a.normalized_text: Genitourinary bacterial infection with acute prostatitis or epididymo-orchitis
Genitourinary bacterial infection with a.description: A bacterial infection of the prostate, epididymis, testis, or urinary tract can cause fever, dysuria, pelvic pain, groin pain, scrotal pain, and systemic inflammatory symptoms. Negative gonorrhea and chlamydia testing reduces the likelihood of common sexually transmitted causes but does not exclude enteric urinary pathogens.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.normalized_text: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), likely antiresorptive-associated
Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.description: Progressive jawbone necrosis with exposed nonhealing bone, commonly associated with bisphosphonates or denosumab used for skeletal metastases. It may occur without acute infection and can affect reconstructed bone.

Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.normalized_text: Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstructed mandible
Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.description: Chronic infection and inflammation of bone that can cause sequestration, bone exposure, fistula formation, and progressive osseous destruction, particularly after major mandibular surgery or reconstruction.

Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.normalized_text: Recurrent or progressive metastatic clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma involving the mandible/fibular graft
Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.description: Clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma can metastasize to bone and may produce destructive, often hypervascular osteolytic lesions. Local recurrence or metastatic involvement of the reconstructed mandibular region could cause bone destruction and mucosal breakdown.

Ischemic necrosis or failure of the fibu.normalized_text: Ischemic necrosis or failure of the fibular free-flap bone graft
Ischemic necrosis or failure of the fibu.description: Compromised perfusion, chronic vascular insufficiency, mechanical stress, or impaired healing of a vascularized osseous flap can lead to graft bone necrosis, exposure, and progressive loss of reconstructed mandibular bone.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive inflammatory myocarditis characterized histologically by multinucleated giant cells, extensive myocardial inflammation, and myocyte necrosis. It can cause fulminant heart failure, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and can mimic acute coronary syndrome. The myocardial biopsy image is highly supportive, showing inflammatory infiltrates, myocyte injury, and giant cells.

Acute lymphocytic myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the heart muscle, often viral or immune mediated, producing chest pain, heart failure, arrhythmias, and occasionally shock. Biopsy typically shows lymphocytic inflammation with myocyte necrosis; however, the presence of numerous giant cells would favor giant cell myocarditis over routine lymphocytic myocarditis.

Acute myocardial infarction with cardiog.normalized_text: Acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock
Acute myocardial infarction with cardiog.description: Acute coronary artery occlusion causes myocardial ischemia and necrosis, typically presenting with chest pressure, diaphoresis, dyspnea, ECG ischemic changes, and potentially cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema and functional mitral regurgitation. The clinical syndrome strongly resembles this condition, but biopsy evidence of inflammatory giant-cell myocarditis argues against infarction as the primary diagnosis.

Eosinophilic myocarditis.description: An inflammatory myocardial disease caused by eosinophil-rich infiltration, sometimes related to medications, hypersensitivity reactions, infections, autoimmune disease, or hypereosinophilic syndromes. It may present with chest pain, heart failure, arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock. Histology generally demonstrates prominent eosinophils rather than giant cells.

Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.normalized_text: Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long QT syndrome type 8)
Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.description: A rare autosomal-dominant calcium-channel disorder caused by pathogenic CACNA1C variants, classically including marked QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias/sudden cardiac arrest, syndactyly, characteristic facial appearance, and variable developmental or extracardiac abnormalities. The depicted heterozygous CACNA1C c.1216G>A (p.Gly406Arg) variant is the classic Timothy syndrome variant.

Atypical Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-relat.normalized_text: Atypical Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related disorder without syndactyly)
Atypical Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-relat.description: An atypical form of CACNA1C-related long QT syndrome in which severe QT prolongation and malignant ventricular arrhythmias occur with some Timothy syndrome facial features but without the classic syndactyly. This phenotype can be associated with the p.Gly406Arg CACNA1C variant depending on transcript involvement and tissue expression.

Congenital long QT syndrome due to CACNA.normalized_text: Congenital long QT syndrome due to CACNA1C (LQT8)
Congenital long QT syndrome due to CACNA.description: A congenital cardiac channelopathy caused by CACNA1C variants that prolong ventricular repolarization and predispose to torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, syncope, and sudden cardiac arrest. Timothy syndrome is the syndromic form of LQT8.

Strongyloidiasis (Strongyloides stercora.description: A soil-transmitted intestinal nematode infection acquired in tropical and subtropical regions. Chronic infection can cause intermittent diarrhea, abdominal symptoms, rash, weight loss, and prominent eosinophilia; gastrointestinal biopsies may show eosinophil-rich inflammation.

Secondary hypereosinophilic syndrome due.normalized_text: Secondary hypereosinophilic syndrome due to parasitic infection
Secondary hypereosinophilic syndrome due.description: A marked and persistent elevation in eosinophils caused by a reactive process, commonly helminth infection. Eosinophils may infiltrate the gastrointestinal tract, skin, liver, spleen, and bone marrow, producing systemic symptoms and organ dysfunction.

Eosinophilic colitis / eosinophilic gast.description: An eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorder in which eosinophils infiltrate the bowel wall and cause diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, malabsorption, protein loss, and sometimes peripheral eosinophilia. It may be primary or secondary to parasites, drugs, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Intestinal schistosomiasis.description: A trematode infection acquired through freshwater exposure in endemic regions. Intestinal disease may cause diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, eosinophilia, and hepatosplenic involvement; diagnosis is supported by ova in stool or tissue biopsy.

Ulcerative colitis flare.description: A relapse of chronic ulcerative colitis causes colonic mucosal inflammation, diarrhea, urgency, abdominal pain, and systemic effects such as fatigue and weight loss. However, pronounced eosinophilia should prompt evaluation for a superimposed parasitic or eosinophilic disorder.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (hemorrhagic.description: An aggressive diffuse astrocytic glioma that can present as a necrotic, ring-enhancing intra-axial mass with extensive vasogenic edema and intratumoral hemorrhage. The pathology images show glial-marker positivity (GFAP and Olig2), absent IDH1 staining, retained ATRX expression, p53 positivity, and elevated proliferative activity, supporting a high-grade IDH-wildtype glioma.

Epithelioid glioblastoma.description: A histologic variant of glioblastoma that often affects relatively younger patients and may present as a superficially located cerebral hemispheric mass with hemorrhage, necrosis, edema, and seizures. Molecular testing, particularly for BRAF V600E mutation, would be needed for confirmation.

Anaplastic astrocytoma / diffuse high-gr.description: A malignant infiltrating astrocytic tumor that can cause seizures and may enhance after contrast administration. Some tumors can undergo necrosis or hemorrhage, although the marked ring enhancement and central necrosis in this case favor glioblastoma over a lower-grade or grade 3 astrocytoma.

Cerebral metastasis with intratumoral he.description: Metastatic tumors can produce a sharply demarcated ring-enhancing brain lesion with marked vasogenic edema, seizures, and hemorrhage. However, the young age, absence of known systemic cancer, solitary frontal lesion, and glial-marker-positive pathology make metastasis substantially less likely than a primary glioma.

Blastomycosis with lumbar vertebral oste.description: Disseminated infection with Blastomyces species, a dimorphic fungus that can begin as pulmonary disease and spread hematogenously to bone, causing destructive vertebral osteomyelitis and paraspinal soft-tissue infection. The imaging shows destructive lumbar endplate/vertebral changes with adjacent soft-tissue abnormality, and the histology is consistent with thick-walled budding yeast.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine, typically causing an indolent destructive spondylodiscitis with paravertebral soft-tissue collections, constitutional symptoms, and possible pulmonary involvement.

Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/disciti.description: Bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral endplates, commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus or gram-negative organisms. It causes back pain and may produce epidural or paraspinal inflammatory collections.

Coccidioidomycosis with vertebral osteom.description: Disseminated infection with Coccidioides species can cause pulmonary disease followed by skeletal dissemination, including destructive vertebral osteomyelitis. Tissue usually shows characteristic spherules containing endospores rather than budding yeast.

Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy involving the lumbar spine
Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.description: Metastatic cancer can produce progressive, activity-related or nocturnal back pain, weight loss, and destructive vertebral lesions. Common primary sites in older men include prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid, and multiple myeloma-related disease.

Disseminated cryptococcosis (Cryptococcu.description: A systemic fungal infection that commonly begins in the lungs after inhalation and can disseminate to skin, lymph nodes, eyes/orbits, and the central nervous system. The pulmonary CT pattern of multiple nodules and the tissue images showing yeast-like organisms are highly compatible.

Disseminated talaromycosis (Talaromyces.description: A systemic dimorphic fungal infection that may cause fever, weight loss, diffuse pulmonary disease, lymphadenopathy, and skin or soft-tissue lesions, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Histology may show numerous small yeast-like organisms in tissue.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that can produce constitutional symptoms, diffuse pulmonary nodules, lymph-node enlargement, and dissemination to skin and soft tissue. Tissue typically shows small intracellular yeast forms in macrophages.

Disseminated nocardiosis.description: An opportunistic infection caused by Nocardia bacteria that can cause nodular or cavitary lung disease and can spread to skin, soft tissue, brain, and eyes. It may resemble fungal infection on imaging and can cause prolonged fever and weight loss.

Congenital Zika syndrome due to in utero.normalized_text: Congenital Zika syndrome due to in utero Zika virus infection
Congenital Zika syndrome due to in utero.description: A congenital viral infection caused by transplacental Zika virus transmission, associated with fetal brain injury including ventriculomegaly, cortical malformations, corpus callosum/cavum septum pellucidum abnormalities, calcifications, and sometimes microcephaly. Maternal infection is often mild and may be sexually transmitted.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: Congenital CMV is a common fetal viral infection that can cause ventriculomegaly, periventricular calcifications, cortical developmental abnormalities, growth restriction, microcephaly, hearing loss, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstru.normalized_text: Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstru.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct can cause enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles, producing severe ventriculomegaly and dangling choroid plexuses. It may be isolated, genetic, or secondary to infection or hemorrhage.

diagnoses.name: Complex hereditary spastic paraplegia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Autosomal recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia

SPG11-associated hereditary spastic para.normalized_text: SPG11-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia (Spastic paraplegia type 11, Kjellin syndrome spectrum)
SPG11-associated hereditary spastic para.description: An autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG11 mutations. It commonly produces progressive lower-limb spasticity, cognitive decline, dysphagia/dysarthria, peripheral neuropathy, and characteristic thinning of the corpus callosum with periventricular white-matter abnormalities on MRI.

SPG15-associated hereditary spastic para.normalized_text: SPG15-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia (Spastic paraplegia type 15)
SPG15-associated hereditary spastic para.description: A complicated autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by ZFYVE26 mutations. It can closely resemble SPG11, with progressive spastic paraparesis, cognitive decline, dysphagia, peripheral neuropathy, and thinning of the corpus callosum.

SPG47-associated hereditary spastic para.normalized_text: SPG47-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia (Spastic paraplegia type 47)
SPG47-associated hereditary spastic para.description: An autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by AP4B1 mutations. It is associated with spastic paraplegia, intellectual disability, speech or swallowing difficulties, and sometimes corpus callosum or white-matter abnormalities, although onset is usually earlier in childhood.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy / adrenomy.description: A peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 mutations that may cause progressive spastic paraparesis, gait impairment, bladder dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, and cerebral white-matter disease. Female carriers can develop myelopathy, but severe early cognitive disease is less typical in women.

Functional mediastinal paraganglioma (ca.description: A rare extra-adrenal neuroendocrine tumor arising from sympathetic paraganglia in the mediastinum, often near the heart or great vessels. It can secrete norepinephrine and cause catecholamine crises. The intensely avid mediastinal mass on functional imaging and the enhancing para-cardiac mass on MRI support this diagnosis.

Cardiac paraganglioma.description: A subtype of mediastinal paraganglioma located in or adjacent to the heart, commonly near the left atrium, aortic root, pulmonary artery, or coronary vessels. Functional cardiac paragangliomas can produce predominantly norepinephrine and present with episodic adrenergic symptoms.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumor of the adrenal medulla that classically causes episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, and severe hypertension. It is an important consideration in pregnancy but is less supported here because the apparent juxta-adrenal lesion was brown fat and imaging identifies a mediastinal lesion.

Pre-eclampsia with severe hypertension.description: A pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder occurring after 20 weeks of gestation, usually associated with proteinuria and/or maternal end-organ dysfunction. It is a critical alternative diagnosis for third-trimester severe hypertension but does not explain marked catecholamine excess or the mediastinal functional mass.

Nocardia brain abscess (cerebral nocardi.normalized_text: Nocardia brain abscess (cerebral nocardiosis, possibly Nocardia farcinica)
Nocardia brain abscess (cerebral nocardi.description: An opportunistic bacterial infection caused by Nocardia species, often occurring in patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity. It can produce a multiloculated, ring-enhancing cerebral abscess with surrounding edema, hemorrhage, and neutrophilic inflammation. The imaging and microbiology images are compatible with a brain abscess caused by branching gram-positive organisms.

Pyogenic bacterial brain abscess.description: A localized intracranial collection of pus caused by bacterial infection. MRI commonly shows a ring-enhancing lesion with central restricted diffusion, surrounding vasogenic edema, and mass effect; pathology typically demonstrates extensive neutrophilic inflammation.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis.description: Toxoplasma gondii reactivation can cause ring-enhancing brain lesions in immunocompromised patients, particularly those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Lesions may cause focal neurologic deficits, cognitive changes, seizures, and headache.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: Primary CNS lymphoma is a malignant lymphoid tumor of the brain that is more common in immunosuppressed patients. It can produce focal neurologic deficits, neurocognitive symptoms, and enhancing brain masses, although lesions are more often solidly enhancing than abscess-like.

Glioblastoma.description: Glioblastoma is an aggressive primary brain tumor that may appear as an irregular ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and extensive surrounding edema. It can cause headache, aphasia, confusion, and focal weakness.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: A severe atypical bacterial pneumonia caused by Legionella species, often acquired by inhaling aerosolized contaminated freshwater from plumbing, spas, fountains, or other water systems. Imaging may show rapidly progressive, patchy or multilobar consolidation.

Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia,.normalized_text: Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, especially pneumococcal pneumonia
Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia,.description: An acute bacterial infection of the lung parenchyma, commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, producing fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, focal bronchial breathing, and lobar or segmental consolidation.

Acute pulmonary melioidosis.description: A potentially severe pneumonia caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired from contaminated soil or surface water in endemic regions. Diabetes is a major risk factor, and disease can cause multifocal, rapidly progressive pulmonary consolidation.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It commonly produces prolonged cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, and upper-lobe infiltrates or cavitation, although lower-lobe disease can occur in some patients, including those with diabetes.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to RA.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to RAPSN deficiency
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to RA.description: An inherited postsynaptic neuromuscular-junction disorder caused by impaired clustering of acetylcholine receptors. It commonly presents at birth or in infancy with severe weakness, respiratory failure, ptosis, and fatigable bulbar weakness. Ultrastructural studies may show abnormal neuromuscular-junction architecture and simplified postsynaptic folds.

MuSK-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: A rare inherited congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in MUSK, impairing formation and maintenance of the neuromuscular junction. It can cause severe neonatal respiratory and bulbar weakness, ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, and abnormal postsynaptic junctional folds. This is distinct from autoimmune MuSK-antibody myasthenia gravis.

LRP4-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: An inherited postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome due to impaired agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling, which is necessary for acetylcholine-receptor clustering and postsynaptic-fold maturation. Severe early-onset cases can have respiratory failure, ocular and bulbar weakness, and structural abnormalities at the endplate.

Agrin-related congenital myasthenic synd.description: A congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by AGRN variants that disrupt agrin signaling at the neuromuscular junction. It produces impaired acetylcholine-receptor clustering and may lead to neonatal or childhood-onset fatigable weakness, ptosis, respiratory involvement, and abnormal endplate morphology.

DOK7 congenital myasthenic syndrome.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by defective DOK7-MuSK signaling. It often causes limb-girdle and axial weakness, respiratory compromise, scoliosis, and a decremental response on nerve stimulation; ocular symptoms are usually mild or absent compared with other congenital myasthenic syndromes.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolal gap, acute kidney injury, and calcium oxalate crystal deposition in urine.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion that produces an elevated osmolal gap followed by high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis due to formic acid accumulation, often causing neurologic and visual toxicity.

Lactic acidosis due to tissue hypoperfus.normalized_text: Lactic acidosis due to tissue hypoperfusion or sepsis
Lactic acidosis due to tissue hypoperfus.description: Accumulation of lactate from impaired oxygen delivery or severe systemic illness, producing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and compensatory hyperventilation.

Diabetic ketoacidosis.description: A diabetic metabolic emergency caused by insulin deficiency, leading to hyperglycemia, ketone production, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, dehydration, and Kussmaul respirations.

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Q.normalized_text: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain thyroiditis), likely post-viral
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Q.description: A self-limited inflammatory thyroid disorder, often following a viral upper-respiratory illness, that can cause fever, constitutional symptoms, diffuse thyroid enlargement, and inflammatory changes within the thyroid on CT.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis (infectiou.description: A rare bacterial infection of the thyroid that produces fever, neck swelling, and thyroid inflammation; CT may show thyroid enlargement, heterogeneous enhancement, edema, or an evolving abscess.

Acute coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever).normalized_text: Acute coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever) with associated inflammatory thyroiditis
Acute coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever).description: Coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection acquired in the southwestern United States. Acute illness commonly causes fever, fatigue, headache, sore throat, and respiratory symptoms; thyroid involvement is uncommon but systemic inflammation may trigger or coincide with thyroiditis.

Viral thyroiditis associated with an acu.normalized_text: Viral thyroiditis associated with an acute viral infection
Viral thyroiditis associated with an acu.description: Viruses such as enteroviruses, adenovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, Epstein-Barr virus, or other respiratory viruses can precede thyroid inflammation and cause fever, malaise, neck discomfort, and diffuse thyroid enlargement.

Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei inf.description: A rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, usually involving the small intestine and causing malabsorption. The CT appearance of mesenteric lymphadenopathy and small-bowel involvement, together with biopsy showing lamina propria packed with macrophage-like cells, is highly suggestive.

Celiac disease.description: An immune-mediated gluten-sensitive enteropathy causing chronic inflammation and malabsorption of the small intestine. It can produce diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal discomfort, and nutritional deficiency, although the illustrated biopsy and nodal findings are more supportive of Whipple disease.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possibl.normalized_text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possible acute-on-chronic intestinal ischemia
Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possibl.description: Reduced intestinal blood flow caused by atherosclerotic mesenteric arterial disease. His known coronary artery disease and dyslipidemia increase risk. It can cause postprandial abdominal symptoms, food avoidance, diarrhea, and weight loss; acute worsening can cause sudden abdominal pain.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Inflammation of the pancreas that classically causes acute epigastric or left upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with nausea and elevated pancreatic enzymes. The enzyme elevations here are only mild, and the chronic diarrhea, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and biopsy findings suggest an additional underlying intestinal disorder.

Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.normalized_text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with gonococcal septic arthritis
Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.description: Hematogenous dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae that can cause migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, or purulent septic arthritis. The recent unprotected sexual exposure and microbiologic images consistent with diplococcal bacterial growth strongly support this diagnosis.

Nongonococcal bacterial septic arthritis.description: Infection of a joint by pyogenic bacteria, commonly Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci, producing acute painful swelling, warmth, effusion, and restricted movement. Bacteremia can occasionally cause more than one involved joint.

Reactive arthritis triggered by a sexual.normalized_text: Reactive arthritis triggered by a sexually transmitted infection
