Reactive arthritis triggered by a sexual.description: A sterile inflammatory arthritis occurring after genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection, classically associated with Chlamydia trachomatis. It often affects the lower extremities asymmetrically and may be accompanied by urethritis, conjunctivitis, mucocutaneous lesions, or enthesitis.

Rheumatoid arthritis.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that usually causes symmetric small-joint synovitis, prolonged morning stiffness, and progressive joint damage if untreated.

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type

Disseminated histoplasmosis with bilater.normalized_text: Disseminated histoplasmosis with bilateral adrenal involvement
Disseminated histoplasmosis with bilater.description: Systemic infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, which can involve the reticuloendothelial system, bone marrow, liver, spleen, lungs, and adrenal glands. Imaging may show bilateral adrenal enlargement and multiple small hepatic and splenic lesions.

Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral adrenal tuberculosis
Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.description: Hematogenous Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can affect the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and adrenal glands. Bilateral adrenal enlargement may occur and can eventually lead to adrenal insufficiency.

Primary adrenal lymphoma with systemic i.normalized_text: Primary adrenal lymphoma with systemic involvement
Primary adrenal lymphoma with systemic i.description: Aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present as bilateral adrenal masses and may involve the liver, spleen, lungs, and bone marrow. It is often associated with fever, cytopenias, and markedly elevated LDH.

Disseminated visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection that infiltrates macrophage-rich organs, especially the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, producing prolonged fever, cytopenias, and elevated inflammatory markers. Adrenal involvement is uncommon but possible in disseminated disease.

Complex pulmonary arteriovenous malforma.normalized_text: Complex pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (pulmonary arteriovenous fistula) of the left lung
Complex pulmonary arteriovenous malforma.description: A congenital abnormal direct connection between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein, bypassing the normal capillary bed. The CT angiographic images show markedly enlarged, tortuous left hilar pulmonary vessels consistent with a high-flow vascular malformation.

Pulmonary artery aneurysm involving the.normalized_text: Pulmonary artery aneurysm involving the left pulmonary arterial circulation
Pulmonary artery aneurysm involving the.description: A pulmonary artery aneurysm is abnormal focal or diffuse enlargement of the pulmonary artery, sometimes associated with congenital shunts or pulmonary vascular malformations. The imaging appearance of prominent enlarged left hilar pulmonary vessels may represent aneurysmal dilatation in a high-flow lesion.

Patent ductus arteriosus with pulmonary.normalized_text: Patent ductus arteriosus with pulmonary arterial dilatation
Patent ductus arteriosus with pulmonary.description: Patent ductus arteriosus is persistence of a fetal communication between the aorta and pulmonary artery, producing a left-to-right shunt and increased pulmonary blood flow. It can cause enlarged pulmonary arteries and a thoracic continuous murmur or bruit.

IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: A fibroinflammatory manifestation of IgG4-related disease in which retroperitoneal soft tissue surrounds major vessels and/or ureters. The CT appearance is consistent with infiltrative retroperitoneal soft tissue, which can compress the inferior vena cava or iliac veins and produce severe bilateral leg edema.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Orm.description: A chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disorder producing a plaque-like retroperitoneal mass, often centered around the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels. It can obstruct venous or ureteric structures; in this case, venous compression could account for bilateral leg swelling.

Retroperitoneal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can present as infiltrative retroperitoneal soft tissue or confluent lymphadenopathy that encases vessels and causes venous obstruction. Compression of the inferior vena cava or iliac veins may result in marked bilateral lower-limb edema.

Malignant retroperitoneal or pelvic veno.normalized_text: Malignant retroperitoneal or pelvic venous obstruction
Malignant retroperitoneal or pelvic veno.description: A retroperitoneal malignancy, metastatic nodal disease, or pelvic cancer can compress the inferior vena cava or iliac veins, producing bilateral pitting edema. Such processes may also cause anemia, inflammation, and nonspecific abdominal symptoms.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or near-complete collapse of a lung, occurring without trauma or known underlying lung disease; it is most common in young men. The radiograph shows a large left pneumothorax with absent peripheral lung markings and a collapsed left lung medially.

Tension pneumothorax.description: A pneumothorax in which intrapleural pressure rises sufficiently to compress the affected lung and potentially shift mediastinal structures, impairing venous return and causing hemodynamic compromise. A very large left pneumothorax is visible on the radiograph.

Giant pulmonary bulla (bullous lung dise.description: A large air-filled space within the lung caused by destruction of alveolar tissue, which can mimic a pneumothorax on chest radiography. In this case, the visible collapsed lung edge and lack of peripheral markings favor pneumothorax rather than a bulla.

Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.normalized_text: Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic carditis causing severe mitral regurgitation
Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.description: An immune-mediated complication of prior group A streptococcal streptococcal infection. It commonly causes migratory polyarthritis and carditis, with mitral-valve inflammation leading to mitral regurgitation and acute heart failure. The echocardiographic images are consistent with significant mitral regurgitation.

Infective endocarditis with mitral-valve.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with mitral-valve regurgitation and heart failure
Infective endocarditis with mitral-valve.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, that can produce fever, a new regurgitant murmur, embolic or immune-mediated joint manifestations, and heart failure when valve destruction is severe.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman-Sacks endocarditis or lupus-associated valvular disease
Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause constitutional symptoms, inflammatory polyarthralgia or arthritis, and nonbacterial valvular lesions. Valvular involvement may cause regurgitation, although severe acute mitral regurgitation is less typical than in rheumatic carditis or infective endocarditis.

Disseminated gonococcal infection with m.normalized_text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with migratory polyarthritis
Disseminated gonococcal infection with m.description: Hematogenous spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae that may cause fever, migratory arthralgias, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and occasionally septic arthritis of a single joint. It does not usually cause valvular disease or heart failure.

Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtaf.normalized_text: Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtafacet cyst), likely at L3-L4
Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtaf.description: A fluid-filled degenerative cyst arising from a lumbar facet joint that can protrude into the spinal canal or lateral recess and compress a nerve root. The MRI appearance of a well-circumscribed posterior-lateral cystic lesion adjacent to the facet joint is most consistent with this diagnosis.

Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerative facet arthropathy with lateral recess compression
Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.description: Degenerative enlargement of facet joints, ligamentous tissues, and disc-related changes can narrow the spinal canal or lateral recess, causing compression of lumbar nerve roots. The facet-associated cyst seen on MRI may be a focal contributor to stenosis.

Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopath.description: Protrusion or extrusion of intervertebral disc material can compress a lumbar nerve root and produce sciatica. Disc degeneration is present on the images, although the focal cystic facet-adjacent lesion is more suggestive of a synovial cyst than a primary disc extrusion.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with possible cervical lymph-node metastasis
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with.description: A malignant tumor of squamous cells, commonly presenting as a persistent nonhealing, crusted or ulcerated lesion on the lip. Regional lymph-node enlargement can indicate spread.

Herpes simplex virus infection (persiste.normalized_text: Herpes simplex virus infection (persistent herpes labialis)
Herpes simplex virus infection (persiste.description: HSV-1 commonly causes recurrent painful grouped blisters and crusted erosions on or around the lips, often called cold sores. Persistent or unusually severe disease may occur with immune dysfunction.

Basal cell carcinoma of the perioral ski.normalized_text: Basal cell carcinoma of the perioral skin
Basal cell carcinoma of the perioral ski.description: Basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing skin cancer that can present as a persistent ulcerated, crusted, or bleeding lesion on sun-exposed facial skin, including the area around the lips.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.description: An inherited hamartomatous polyposis syndrome characterized by multiple gastrointestinal polyps, especially in the small bowel, which can cause bleeding, anemia, intussusception, obstruction, diarrhea, and protein loss.

Juvenile polyposis syndrome.description: A hamartomatous polyposis disorder with multiple juvenile polyps, usually involving the colon and stomach, causing rectal bleeding, chronic anemia, diarrhea, and protein-losing enteropathy.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and may cause diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, bowel narrowing, and inflammatory arthritis.

Intestinal lymphangiomatosis (primary in.description: A disorder of dilated intestinal lymphatic vessels causing protein-losing enteropathy, chronic diarrhea, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and occasionally gastrointestinal bleeding or polypoid intestinal lesions.

Common variable immunodeficiency with no.normalized_text: Common variable immunodeficiency with nodular lymphoid hyperplasia
Common variable immunodeficiency with no.description: An immune-deficiency disorder that can produce chronic infectious or inflammatory diarrhea, malabsorption, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the intestine, anemia, and low serum protein levels.

Dupuytren disease (Dupuytren contracture.description: A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia causing nodules and cord formation, progressively pulling the fingers into flexion. It commonly affects the ring and little fingers in older men and may be familial.

Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosyn.description: Inflammation and thickening around the flexor tendon pulley, usually at the metacarpophalangeal joint, causing painful clicking, catching, or locking during finger movement.

Camptodactyly.description: A congenital or developmental condition characterized by a flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal joint, most often affecting the little finger.

Flexor tendon contracture or adhesions a.normalized_text: Flexor tendon contracture or adhesions after hand trauma
Flexor tendon contracture or adhesions a.description: Scarring or shortening of flexor tendons and surrounding tissues can limit finger extension after laceration, fracture, surgery, or prolonged immobilization.

Syphilitic lymphadenitis (secondary syph.normalized_text: Syphilitic lymphadenitis (secondary syphilis with inguinal lymph-node involvement)
Syphilitic lymphadenitis (secondary syph.description: Lymph-node inflammation caused by Treponema pallidum, often occurring in secondary syphilis. It can produce prominent regional or generalized lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, follicular hyperplasia, plasmacytosis, and detectable spirochetes on immunostaining.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV).description: An invasive sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3. It may cause painful inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy, systemic symptoms, and inflammatory lymph-node disease, especially in men with HIV.

HIV-associated lymphoma (such as diffuse.normalized_text: HIV-associated lymphoma (such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
HIV-associated lymphoma (such as diffuse.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurs at increased frequency in people with HIV and may present with enlarging lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, and extranodal disease. Inguinal nodes can be involved, although isolated regional painful adenopathy is less specific.

Mycobacterial lymphadenitis, including r.normalized_text: Mycobacterial lymphadenitis, including recurrent Mycobacterium avium complex infection
Mycobacterial lymphadenitis, including r.description: Mycobacterial infection can cause lymph-node enlargement, fever, night sweats, and constitutional symptoms in immunocompromised patients. Disseminated MAC is most common with advanced HIV immunosuppression, while localized mycobacterial lymphadenitis may occur at higher CD4 counts.

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

Solitary eosinophilic granuloma of the r.normalized_text: Solitary eosinophilic granuloma of the rib (osseous Langerhans cell histiocytosis)
Solitary eosinophilic granuloma of the r.description: A localized form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis causing a destructive lytic bone lesion, commonly involving flat bones such as ribs. It can produce adjacent soft-tissue inflammation, pleural reaction, and chest pain. The imaging appearance of a focal rib lesion with adjacent pleural abnormality and the histology showing inflammatory/Langerhans-type cells support this diagnosis.

Ewing sarcoma of the rib / Askin tumor.normalized_text: Ewing sarcoma of the rib / Askin tumor
Ewing sarcoma of the rib / Askin tumor.description: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant small round cell tumor that can arise from a rib and extend into adjacent soft tissue or pleura. It may cause a chest-wall mass, pleural effusion, chest pain, and respiratory symptoms in adolescents.

Rib osteomyelitis with pleuritis or empy.normalized_text: Rib osteomyelitis with pleuritis or empyema
Rib osteomyelitis with pleuritis or empy.description: Infection of a rib can cause focal bony destruction, chest-wall pain, adjacent pleural inflammation, pleural effusion, and reduced expansion of the affected hemithorax. Infection can occasionally be indolent and present without marked systemic symptoms.

Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the rib wit.normalized_text: Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the rib with a chest-wall cold abscess
Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the rib wit.description: Tuberculosis can rarely involve a rib, producing chronic localized pain, lytic rib destruction, chest-wall soft-tissue inflammation or abscess, and pleural disease. Constitutional symptoms may be absent, particularly in localized disease.

Pathologic rib fracture or stress injury.normalized_text: Pathologic rib fracture or stress injury with reactive pleural effusion
Pathologic rib fracture or stress injury.description: A rib stress injury or pathologic fracture can cause focal chest-wall pain after strenuous physical activity and may be associated with pleural irritation, small effusion, or reduced expansion. A destructive-appearing rib lesion, however, would raise concern for an underlying bone disorder rather than an uncomplicated athletic injury.

Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lym.normalized_text: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lym.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma arising predominantly in the spleen. It can present as a solitary splenic mass with constitutional B symptoms and may occur without peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Primary splenic angiosarcoma.description: A rare, highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor of the spleen that may form a splenic mass and cause systemic symptoms, anemia, coagulopathy, and splenomegaly.

Primary splenic Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A rare lymphoma confined mainly to the spleen at presentation. It may cause B symptoms, splenomegaly, anemia, and a focal splenic lesion, sometimes without palpable lymph nodes.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic parasitic infection caused by Leishmania species, classically producing prolonged fever, weight loss, splenomegaly, anemia, hyperferritinemia, and macrophages containing intracellular organisms in tissue aspirates.

Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) w.normalized_text: Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) with cardiac involvement
Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) w.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, resulting in globotriaosylceramide accumulation in the kidneys, heart, nervous system, skin, and eyes. Cardiac involvement commonly produces concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, and myocardial fibrosis.

Hypertensive heart disease with concentr.normalized_text: Hypertensive heart disease with concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertensive heart disease with concentr.description: Long-standing systemic hypertension can cause concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, reduced ventricular compliance, diastolic dysfunction, left-atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, and myocardial oxygen-demand ischemia with mild troponin elevation.

Cardiac amyloidosis.description: An infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular amyloid protein deposition. It can produce increased ventricular wall thickness, restrictive physiology, atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, proteinuria, renal dysfunction, and elevated cardiac biomarkers.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disease characterized by otherwise unexplained left-ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetric but sometimes concentric, with diastolic dysfunction, myocardial ischemia, atrial enlargement, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias.

Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.normalized_text: Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left middle cerebral artery territory infarction)
Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.description: An acute interruption of arterial cerebral blood flow causing focal brain infarction. The diffusion-weighted MRI shows a focal area of restricted diffusion in the left cerebral hemisphere, consistent with an acute ischemic infarct, likely in a left middle cerebral artery cortical territory.

Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke due t.normalized_text: Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke due to left middle cerebral artery branch occlusion
Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke due t.description: A subtype of neonatal stroke caused by thrombotic or embolic occlusion of a cerebral artery around the time of birth. Vascular imaging may show reduced visualization or narrowing of a left middle cerebral artery branch, while MRI demonstrates acute infarction.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) wi.description: Brain injury from impaired oxygen delivery and/or blood flow around birth. It commonly causes neonatal seizures, but classic HIE usually produces diffuse or bilateral brain injury rather than a sharply focal unilateral arterial-territory lesion.

Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage.description: Bleeding into the brain parenchyma, ventricles, or subarachnoid space can provoke seizures in newborns. However, the described MRI diffusion abnormality and apparent vascular-territory distribution are more suggestive of ischemic infarction than hemorrhage.

Takayasu arteritis with severe aortic re.normalized_text: Takayasu arteritis with severe aortic regurgitation and heart failure
Takayasu arteritis with severe aortic re.description: A chronic large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, typically in young women. Imaging is consistent with diffuse aortic wall disease and branch-vessel stenoses; aortic-root involvement can cause severe aortic regurgitation and acute decompensated heart failure.

Severe chronic aortic regurgitation caus.normalized_text: Severe chronic aortic regurgitation causing acute decompensated heart failure
Severe chronic aortic regurgitation caus.description: Aortic valve incompetence causes diastolic blood flow from the aorta back into the left ventricle. Severe regurgitation produces a murmur, wide pulsatile circulation, pulmonary congestion, dyspnea, and eventual heart failure. In this case, the likely cause is inflammatory aortic-root disease from Takayasu arteritis.

Infective endocarditis involving the aor.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis involving the aortic valve
Infective endocarditis involving the aor.description: Infective endocarditis is microbial infection of the endocardial surface, often involving a cardiac valve. Aortic-valve infection can cause new severe aortic regurgitation, heart failure, systemic inflammation, and embolic or musculoskeletal pain. It is an important alternative because of the murmur, inflammatory markers, and recent dental procedure.

Aortitis due to another inflammatory vas.normalized_text: Aortitis due to another inflammatory vasculitis, such as Behcet disease or isolated idiopathic aortitis
Aortitis due to another inflammatory vas.description: Inflammatory aortitis can thicken the aortic wall, cause aneurysmal or stenotic changes, involve major branches, and produce aortic-valve regurgitation. Behcet disease and isolated idiopathic aortitis can occasionally mimic Takayasu arteritis, although the demographic and vascular pattern favor Takayasu disease.

Giant cell arteritis with aortitis.description: Giant cell arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that can involve the thoracic aorta and cause aortic regurgitation or aortic aneurysmal disease. It can produce elevated inflammatory markers and constitutional illness, but it overwhelmingly affects adults older than 50 years.

Torsion and infarction of an accessory s.normalized_text: Torsion and infarction of an accessory spleen (torsed splenunculus)
Torsion and infarction of an accessory s.description: An accessory spleen can remain after traumatic splenectomy and may rarely twist on its vascular pedicle, causing venous congestion, infarction, local inflammation, and acute abdominal pain. The CT appearances of an inflamed mesenteric mass with a twisted vascular pedicle are highly suggestive.

Infarction of accessory splenic tissue w.normalized_text: Infarction of accessory splenic tissue without torsion
Infarction of accessory splenic tissue w.description: Accessory splenic tissue may become infarcted because of compromised arterial or venous supply. It produces localized abdominal pain and inflammatory-marker elevation, with CT potentially showing poorly enhancing or inflamed ectopic splenic tissue.

Mesenteric panniculitis (sclerosing mese.description: Mesenteric panniculitis is inflammatory change within mesenteric fat that can cause abdominal pain, nausea, low-grade fever, and raised inflammatory markers. CT typically demonstrates mesenteric fat stranding, soft-tissue nodules, and inflammatory change around mesenteric vessels.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas commonly causes severe epigastric pain with nausea and elevated pancreatic enzymes; CT may show peripancreatic inflammatory change in established disease.

Hematometrocolpos due to imperforate hym.description: Obstruction of menstrual outflow by an imperforate hymen causes accumulation of blood in the vagina and often uterus (hematocolpos/hematometra). Ultrasound may show a large midline pelvic cystic structure containing homogeneous low-level internal echoes consistent with retained blood.

Obstructed hemivagina with hematometroco.normalized_text: Obstructed hemivagina with hematometrocolpos (OHVIRA syndrome or other Müllerian outflow obstruction)
Obstructed hemivagina with hematometroco.description: A congenital Müllerian anomaly, such as an obstructed hemivagina, can lead to retained menstrual blood in one side of the vagina and uterus. It may present after menarche with cyclic or recurrent pelvic pain and a complex fluid-filled pelvic mass on ultrasound.

Ovarian endometrioma.description: An endometrioma is an ovarian cyst containing old blood from endometriosis. On ultrasound it commonly has homogeneous low-level 'ground-glass' internal echoes, although it is uncommon at 12 years of age.

Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion associated with an ovarian cyst
Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.description: Ovarian torsion is twisting of the ovary and its vascular pedicle, often around a cyst or enlarged ovary. It causes acute pelvic pain and requires urgent evaluation; ultrasound may show an enlarged cystic ovarian mass, though Doppler findings are needed for assessment.

Acute appendicitis.description: Acute appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix and is a common cause of acute abdominal pain in children. Pain often begins centrally and localizes to the right lower quadrant, although pelvic appendicitis can produce hypogastric pain.

Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.description: A contiguous gene-deletion syndrome caused by deletion of 11p11.2, commonly involving EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It is characterized by multiple osteochondromas/exostoses, parietal foramina or other skull ossification defects, developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, growth retardation, and distinctive craniofacial features.

Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, usually caused by pathogenic variants in EXT1 or EXT2, producing multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near the metaphyses of long bones during childhood.

Langer-Giedion syndrome (trichorhinophal.description: A contiguous gene-deletion disorder involving 8q23-q24, typically including EXT1 and TRPS1. It causes multiple exostoses, short stature, characteristic facial features, sparse hair, and variable developmental delay.

Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei infestation).description: A contagious infestation by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. The biopsy image directly shows a mite within the stratum corneum, supporting this diagnosis.

Crusted scabies (Norwegian scabies).description: A severe, highly contagious form of scabies occurring most often in patients with impaired immune function or reduced ability to scratch. It may cause extensive crusted, hyperkeratotic, erosive, or ulcerated lesions and can be minimally pruritic.

Secondary bacterial infection of scabeti.normalized_text: Secondary bacterial infection of scabetic lesions (impetiginized scabies/ecthyma)
Secondary bacterial infection of scabeti.description: Scabies lesions can become secondarily infected with bacteria, particularly Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. In a patient with severe neutropenia, superficial lesions may progress to erosions, ulcers, and crusting.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (comp.normalized_text: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy)
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (comp.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by platelet-rich microthrombi in renal vessels and glomeruli, causing thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, severe acute kidney injury, hypertension, and active urinary sediment. The biopsy image is compatible with glomerular thrombotic microangiopathy.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A severe ADAMTS13-deficiency-associated thrombotic microangiopathy causing marked thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, fever, and variable renal and neurologic involvement. Renal biopsy may show thrombotic microangiopathy.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomerular capillaries, producing endothelial damage, thrombotic microangiopathy, hematuria, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

Primary myeloid sarcoma of the extrahepa.normalized_text: Primary myeloid sarcoma of the extrahepatic bile duct (isolated granulocytic sarcoma)
Primary myeloid sarcoma of the extrahepa.description: A localized extramedullary tumor composed of immature myeloid cells. It can occur without detectable bone marrow leukemia and may infiltrate the bile duct, producing obstructive jaundice. The histology and leukocyte-marker positivity with absence of T-cell, B-cell, NK-cell, and precursor lymphoid markers support this diagnosis.

Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.normalized_text: Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the bile duct
Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: An uncommon lymphoma arising in or infiltrating the biliary tract that can mimic cholangiocarcinoma and cause obstructive jaundice. Lymphomas are generally CD45-positive, but the reported negative lymphoid immunophenotype makes a conventional B-cell or T-cell lymphoma less likely.

Cholangiocarcinoma (hilar or extrahepati.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bile ducts that commonly presents with painless obstructive jaundice and intrahepatic biliary dilatation. However, the pathology in this case favors a hematologic tumor rather than an epithelial carcinoma.
